title: Large connectivity expansion of Ising Spin Glasses on random graphs
summary: We compute a high-connectivity analytical expansion for Ising spin glasses on sparse random graphs. We expand the cavity equations around the fully-connected mean-field limit, focusing on the critical behavior of the system: our approach allows us to compute the de Almeida-Thouless line of mean-field finitely-connected systems in the temperature $T$--magnetic field $H$ plane, by means of closed analytical equations. The exact cavity solution of such systems can only be obtained by solving numerically iterative equations, so our approach brings a notable computational advantage. On the theoretical side, we are able to identify three sources of corrections to the fully-connected mean-field solution: i) the non-Gaussianity of the cavity fields, ii) the statistical correlation between the cavity fields and their fluctuations, and iii) the corrections to the cavity filter functions. These corrections are treated using two different expansions: a non-uniform expansion, where we expand all three contributions around the mean-field solution, and a uniform expansion, where we only expand the statistics but leave the cavity filters untouched. The former allows for a direct comparison with the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model but fails at low temperatures, as a consequence of the de Almeida-Thouless line diverging in the zero-temperature limit. On the other hand, the uniform expansion describes with good accuracy the critical behavior of the system. We also extend these results to the $T = 0$ limit.

AI.tldr: The authors derive a closed-form high-connectivity analytical expansion of the cavity equations for Ising spin glasses on sparse random graphs, enabling computation of the de Almeida-Thouless (AT) line in the (T,H) plane without iterative numerics, and identify three sources of corrections to the fully-connected mean-field solution.
AI.motivation: The exact cavity solution for Ising spin glasses on sparse random graphs requires numerically solving iterative equations, which is computationally costly. The authors aim for an analytical expansion around the fully-connected mean-field limit to gain computational advantage and theoretical insight into the critical behavior, particularly the AT line.
AI.method: Expand the cavity equations around the fully-connected mean-field limit at high connectivity. Three correction sources are treated: (i) non-Gaussianity of cavity fields, (ii) statistical correlation between cavity fields and their fluctuations, and (iii) corrections to cavity filter functions. Two expansions are used: a non-uniform expansion (all three contributions expanded around mean field) and a uniform expansion (only statistics expanded, cavity filters left untouched). Results are also extended to T=0.
AI.result: The approach yields closed analytical equations for the AT line of mean-field finitely-connected systems. The non-uniform expansion permits direct comparison with the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model but fails at low temperatures because the AT line diverges in the zero-temperature limit. The uniform expansion describes the critical behavior with good accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A high-connectivity analytical expansion provides a computationally efficient alternative to iterative cavity numerics and, via the uniform expansion, accurately captures the critical behavior of finitely-connected Ising spin glasses down to T=0.

title: Spectral theory of large data with power-law latent features
summary: Power-law eigenvalue spectra of covariance matrices estimated from data appear in diverse domains ranging from neural populations to proteins. We introduce a generative latent feature model for such data, optionally corrupted by measurement noise, and develop its spectral theory. We derive closed leading-order self-consistent equations for the Stieltjes transform of the covariance matrix from which the bulk eigenvalue density is obtained and provide a variational principle for the self-consistent equations. We also compute the positions and fluctuations of isolated top eigenvalues. The theory is validated in known algebraic limits and tested against simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a generative latent feature model for data whose sample covariance matrices exhibit power-law eigenvalue spectra and develops a spectral theory for it, deriving self-consistent equations for the Stieltjes transform (yielding the bulk eigenvalue density), a variational principle, and the positions/fluctuations of isolated top eigenvalues, validated against known limits and simulations.
AI.motivation: Power-law eigenvalue spectra of covariance matrices estimated from data arise across diverse domains (e.g., neural populations to proteins), yet a principled generative model with accompanying spectral theory for such data—especially under measurement noise—is lacking.
AI.method: Proposes a generative latent feature model for data with power-law covariance spectra, optionally corrupted by measurement noise. Develops spectral theory via closed leading-order self-consistent equations for the Stieltjes transform of the covariance matrix, providing the bulk eigenvalue density and a variational principle for the self-consistent equations; also computes positions and fluctuations of isolated top eigenvalues.
AI.result: Closed leading-order self-consistent equations for the Stieltjes transform yield the bulk eigenvalue density; the self-consistent equations admit a variational characterization; positions and fluctuations of isolated top eigenvalues are obtained. The theory reproduces known algebraic limits and agrees with simulations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed latent feature model and its spectral theory provide a tractable, validated framework for describing power-law covariance spectra, including measurement noise and outlier eigenvalue behavior.

title: Tunable periodic cascade of delocalization transitions in non-Hermitian IAAF model
summary: Cascade of delocalization transitions provides a route to multi-step control of delocalization, yet achieving a programmable periodic cascade remains a challenge. Here, we demonstrate a tunable periodic cascade of delocalization transitions in a non-Hermitian interpolating Aubry-André-Fibonacci (IAAF) model by introducing an imaginary phase shift into the quasiperiodic potential. Such a periodic cascade of delocalization transitions arises from the competition between kinetic-energy-facilitated delocalization and gain-loss-regulated localization. In numerical static localization characterizations, successive regular stripe patterns for localized and extended states emerge in phase diagrams. We also derive an analytical expression for the cascade period and find that it relies solely on the imaginary phase shift. This provides a direct way of continuously tuning the cascade period via a single control parameter. Complementary static and dynamical diagnostics consistently confirm this periodic cascade of delocalization transitions in the non-Hermitian IAAF system. Our findings identify a novel class of delocalization transitions with tunable cascading periods, opening a route toward experimentally programmable control of delocalization.

AI.tldr: A non-Hermitian interpolating Aubry-André-Fibonacci model with an imaginary phase shift hosts a tunable periodic cascade of delocalization transitions, whose period depends only on the imaginary phase shift, enabling single-parameter control of delocalization.
AI.motivation: Cascades of delocalization transitions enable multi-step control of delocalization, but a programmable periodic cascade has not been achieved. The authors aim to realize and tune such a cascade.
AI.method: Introduce an imaginary phase shift into the quasiperiodic potential of a non-Hermitian interpolating Aubry-André-Fibonacci (IAAF) model. Static diagnostics (phase diagrams of localized vs. extended states) and dynamical diagnostics are combined, plus an analytical derivation of the cascade period.
AI.result: Successive regular stripe patterns of localized and extended states appear in the phase diagram; the cascade originates from competition between kinetic-energy-facilitated delocalization and gain-loss-regulated localization. The derived analytical cascade period depends solely on the imaginary phase shift, allowing continuous tuning with a single control parameter. Static and dynamical diagnostics agree.
AI.conclusion: A novel class of delocalization transitions with tunable cascading periods is identified, offering a route to experimentally programmable control of delocalization.

title: Microscopic Mechanism and Control of Reentrant Localization
summary: Increasing quasiperiodic modulation can restore extended states after localization, raising the question of how the same modulation drives both localization and recovery. We identify a microscopic mechanism in quasiperiodic dimer chains by resolving scattering between Fourier channels. Specifically, scattering into neighboring channels and back shifts the spectral edge relative to a localization boundary determined by a neutral auxiliary resonance. Their successive crossings drive the same spectral packet with fixed integrated-density-of-states (IDS) labels into localization and back into an extended regime. This recovery persists across finite parameter ranges in both gap-opening families, including relative-phase detuning. Furthermore, an exact sublattice mapping enables compensated control of the recovery window and predicts recovery thresholds for individual IDS labels.

AI.tldr: The paper explains how the same quasiperiodic modulation both localizes and delocalizes states in dimer chains via a channel-scattering mechanism, and uses an exact sublattice mapping to control and predict the recovery window.
AI.motivation: Increasing quasiperiodic modulation can restore extended states after localization, raising the puzzle of how a single modulation drives both localization and recovery. The authors seek a microscopic mechanism underlying this dual behavior.
AI.method: They resolve scattering between Fourier channels in quasiperiodic dimer chains. The mechanism involves scattering into neighboring channels and back, which shifts the spectral edge relative to a localization boundary set by a neutral auxiliary resonance. An exact sublattice mapping is constructed for analysis.
AI.result: Successive crossings of the shifted spectral edge with the localization boundary drive the same spectral packet (with fixed IDS labels) into localization and back into an extended regime. Recovery persists across finite parameter ranges in both gap-opening families, including relative-phase detuning. The sublattice mapping enables compensated control of the recovery window and predicts recovery thresholds for individual IDS labels.
AI.conclusion: The dual localization-recovery behavior is explained by channel-scattering-induced spectral-edge shifts relative to a fixed localization boundary; an exact sublattice mapping provides controllable and predictive description of the recovery, including per-IDS thresholds.

title: Defining 2-group symmetries on lattices and extracting their anomalies
summary: Ordinary $0$-form symmetries $G$ can mix with $1$-form symmetries $Π_2$ to form a $2$-group $\mathcal{G}$. We give a concrete lattice definition for a class of finite $2$-group symmetries in terms of local relations among symmetry operators. These relations identify the Postnikov class $[ρ]\in H^3(BG,Π_2)$ that characterizes the mixing. We develop a method to extract anomalies of these symmetries in one spatial dimension by restricting symmetry operations to an interval and comparing their composition near its endpoints. We also construct explicit qubit symmetry actions in $d=1,2,3$ spatial dimensions for a $2$-group with $G=Π_2=\mathbb{Z}_2$. These actions share the same nontrivial Postnikov class but include both anomaly-free and anomalous realizations. Their cohomological anomalies are classified by $H^{d+2}(B\mathcal G,U(1))$, which is $\mathbb{Z}_2$ for $d=1,2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ for $d=3$, and our constructions realize every class in these dimensions. Our results connect higher-group symmetry and its anomalies to concrete lattice operations, providing a microscopic framework for studying anomalous symmetries.

AI.tldr: This paper gives a concrete lattice formulation of finite 2-group symmetries (a 0-form group G mixed with a 1-form symmetry Π₂ via a Postnikov class) using local relations among symmetry operators, develops a method to extract their anomalies in d=1 by interval restriction and endpoint comparison, and constructs explicit qubit realizations for G=Π₂=ℤ₂ in d=1,2,3 that realize every cohomological anomaly class in H^{d+2}(B𝒢,U(1)).
AI.motivation: Higher-group symmetries and their 't Hooft anomalies are usually described abstractly via Postnikov classes and cohomology, but lack a concrete microscopic (lattice) definition. The authors aim to connect the abstract higher-group anomaly framework to explicit lattice symmetry operators and operations, enabling microscopic study of anomalous symmetries.
AI.method: They define a class of finite 2-group symmetries on the lattice through local relations among symmetry operators, which explicitly identify the Postnikov class [ρ]∈H³(BG,Π₂) encoding the mixing. To extract anomalies in one spatial dimension, they restrict symmetry operations to an interval and compare their composition near the two endpoints. They also construct explicit qubit symmetry actions in d=1,2,3 for G=Π₂=ℤ₂ sharing the same nontrivial Postnikov class, and classify their cohomological anomalies via H^{d+2}(B𝒢,U(1)).
AI.result: The lattice relations correctly encode the Postnikov class, and the interval-composition method extracts anomalies in d=1. The cohomological anomalies are classified by H^{d+2}(B𝒢,U(1)), which is ℤ₂ for d=1,2 and ℤ₂×ℤ₂ for d=3. For G=Π₂=ℤ₂ with the same nontrivial Postnikov class, the constructions yield both anomaly-free and anomalous realizations, and realize every anomaly class in these dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Higher-group symmetries and their anomalies can be concretely realized through lattice operations, providing a microscopic framework for studying anomalous symmetries and connecting abstract higher-group symmetry to explicit qubit constructions.

title: Dynamical mean-field theory for associative memory with block-correlated patterns
summary: In associative memories storing correlated patterns, retrieval of individual memories can compete with symmetric mixed states. A dynamical description is needed to determine how the initial state selects between these outcomes. We extend the generating-functional dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for independent patterns to independent blocks of correlated binary patterns of fixed finite size. The resulting effective single-neuron process has a self-consistent cross-talk noise covariance and self-feedback coefficients that depend on the block-covariance eigenvalues. For hierarchically correlated patterns with nonmonotonic transfer, increasing the loading can permit retrieval from an imperfect initial state before further loading prevents it. DMFT reproduces the retrieval trajectories and basin geometry found in direct simulations. Near the lower boundary of this re-entrant region, direct networks reveal stationary saddles separating coexisting mixed and target-retrieval states. Parameter sensitivities of DMFT trajectories predict nearby shifts of this boundary. At the tested upper boundary, retrieval remains accessible from initial states with larger target overlap, indicating a change in basin access. Under fixed-point convergence assumptions, the theory recovers the equations of generalized self-consistent signal-to-noise analysis.

AI.tldr: Extends generating-functional DMFT from independent patterns to finite-size blocks of correlated binary patterns, yielding a self-consistent single-neuron process whose noise covariance and feedback depend on block-covariance eigenvalues; the theory captures retrieval dynamics, re-entrant retrieval, and basin geometry, and reduces to generalized self-consistent signal-to-noise analysis at fixed points.
AI.motivation: In associative memories storing correlated patterns, retrieval of individual memories competes with symmetric mixed states, so a dynamical description is needed to determine how the initial state selects between these outcomes.
AI.method: Extend generating-functional dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for independent patterns to independent blocks of correlated binary patterns of fixed finite size. The effective single-neuron process acquires self-consistent cross-talk noise covariance and self-feedback coefficients depending on the block-covariance eigenvalues; fixed-point convergence recovers generalized self-consistent signal-to-noise analysis.
AI.result: For hierarchically correlated patterns with nonmonotonic transfer, increasing loading permits retrieval from an imperfect initial state before further loading prevents it (re-entrant region). DMFT reproduces direct-simulation retrieval trajectories and basin geometry. Near the lower boundary, direct networks show stationary saddles separating coexisting mixed and target-retrieval states; parameter sensitivities of DMFT trajectories predict shifts of this boundary. At the upper boundary, retrieval remains accessible from initial states with larger target overlap, indicating a change in basin access.
AI.conclusion: DMFT for block-correlated patterns quantitatively describes retrieval dynamics and basin structure in correlated associative memories, predicts re-entrant retrieval and boundary shifts, and is consistent with generalized self-consistent signal-to-noise analysis at fixed points.

title: Fundamental limits on photonic state preparation from phase-space majorization
summary: Preparing complex quantum states of light for quantum information processing tasks often proceeds by converting from simpler states via experimentally accessible operations. We provide fundamental bounds on such probabilistic conversions, both exact and approximate. To do so, we establish a theory of weak, fully relative majorization that compares the disorder of phase-space functions. Our framework is versatile and can be tailored to different systems and sets of allowed operations. Focusing on Wigner functions in multimode photonic systems, we establish rigorous no-go results and tradeoff relations for exact and approximate conversions involving squeezed states, cat states, Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill states, and Fock states. In doing so, we derive novel bounds and recover known tight ones. Our results demonstrate that phase-space disorder imposes strong limitations on photonic state preparation.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a theory of weak, fully relative majorization for comparing phase-space disorder, yielding fundamental bounds on probabilistic (exact and approximate) conversions of photonic quantum states.
AI.motivation: Preparing complex quantum states of light typically relies on converting simpler states via experimentally accessible operations. Understanding the fundamental limitations on such probabilistic conversions is essential, yet general bounds—especially for approximate conversions—were lacking.
AI.method: The authors establish a theory of weak, fully relative majorization that compares the disorder of phase-space functions. The framework is versatile and adaptable to different systems and allowed operation sets; they apply it to Wigner functions in multimode photonic systems.
AI.result: They derive rigorous no-go results and tradeoff relations for exact and approximate conversions involving squeezed states, cat states, Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill states, and Fock states, obtaining novel bounds while recovering known tight bounds.
AI.conclusion: Phase-space disorder imposes strong fundamental limitations on photonic state preparation, and relative majorization of phase-space functions provides a powerful, general tool for bounding probabilistic state conversions.

title: Structural signatures of primary and secondary relaxation during physical aging of a metallic glass
summary: Physical aging drives glasses toward equilibrium and changes their thermodynamic and mechanical properties, but the accompanying microscopic structural evolution remains poorly understood. Here, using our recently developed low-background setup combining fast scanning calorimetry with \emph{in-situ} X-ray total scattering, we investigate microscopic structural changes during physical aging in Pd$_{42.5}$Cu$_{30}$Ni$_{7.5}$P$_{20}$ metallic glass. The measurements span an unprecedented six orders of magnitude in time and a temperature range extending from above the glass transition temperature to more than 150\,K below it. We observe dominant structural changes near the first and second peaks of the structure factor. Near and above the glass transition temperature, changes in the first sharp diffraction peak closely follow enthalpy relaxation and are associated predominantly with increasing degrees of medium-range ordering. At lower temperatures, the enthalpy evolution can no longer be described by this contribution alone, revealing an additional, faster relaxation process that correlates with changes near the second diffraction peak and thus short-range structural rearrangements, including increased Pd--Pd correlations. These results establish a direct connection between thermodynamic relaxation and structural evolution, providing strong evidence that primary and secondary aging processes are associated with distinct structural length scales.

AI.tldr: Physical aging in a Pd-Cu-Ni-P metallic glass was tracked over six orders of time and >150 K below Tg using fast scanning calorimetry combined with in-situ X-ray total scattering, linking enthalpy relaxation to distinct structural length scales.
AI.motivation: Physical aging drives glasses toward equilibrium and alters thermodynamic and mechanical properties, yet the microscopic structural evolution accompanying it is poorly understood. Existing work lacks a direct, time- and temperature-resolved connection between thermodynamic relaxation and structural change.
AI.method: A low-background setup combining fast scanning calorimetry with in-situ X-ray total scattering was used to monitor structural changes during aging in Pd42.5Cu30Ni7.5P20 metallic glass. Measurements spanned six orders of magnitude in time and temperatures from above Tg to >150 K below Tg, with changes tracked at the first sharp diffraction peak and second structure factor peak alongside enthalpy relaxation.
AI.result: Dominant structural changes occur near the first and second structure-factor peaks. Near and above Tg, first-peak changes closely track enthalpy relaxation and mainly reflect increasing medium-range order. At lower temperatures, enthalpy evolution cannot be explained by this contribution alone; an additional faster process correlates with second-peak changes, indicating short-range rearrangements and increased Pd-Pd correlations.
AI.conclusion: Thermodynamic relaxation is directly linked to structural evolution, providing strong evidence that primary and secondary aging processes in metallic glasses are associated with distinct structural length scales: medium-range ordering and short-range rearrangements, respectively.

title: Magic in Grover's Algorithm and the Role of Oracle Synthesis
summary: Grover's algorithm is a textbook example of quantum advantage, providing a quadratic query speedup over classical methods for unstructured search. In this Letter, we characterize the non-stabilizerness, or magic, developed throughout Grover's protocol, quantifying quantum complexity with respect to the efficiently simulable stabilizer states. First, we compute the compilation-independent magic at the end of each Grover iteration, deriving an analytic prediction for the stabilizer Rényi entropy and proving that it remains intensive as the system size grows. We then investigate the magic overhead due to decomposing the circuit into elementary gates. When the solution to the search problem is known, we show that an efficient decomposition exists that keeps magic bounded despite using an extensive number of Toffoli gates. In contrast, agnostic implementations are expected to generate volume-law non-stabilizerness, as we confirm for the 3-SAT problem, which rules out efficient simulation by stabilizer-based methods in practically relevant cases. Our findings clarify the growth of magic in Grover's algorithm and the role of solution-awareness in its circuit compilation.

AI.tldr: This Letter quantifies the non-stabilizerness ("magic") generated throughout Grover's algorithm, showing it stays intensive across iterations yet can become volume-law depending on how the circuit is compiled.
AI.motivation: Grover's algorithm exemplifies quantum advantage, but its quantum complexity relative to efficiently simulable stabilizer states (its magic/non-stabilizerness) was not characterized, nor was the impact of circuit decomposition into elementary gates on that magic.
AI.method: The authors compute the compilation-independent magic at the end of each Grover iteration, deriving an analytic prediction for the stabilizer Rényi entropy. They then analyze the magic overhead from decomposing the circuit into elementary gates, contrasting solution-aware versus agnostic decompositions, with 3-SAT as a testbed for the agnostic case.
AI.result: The stabilizer Rényi entropy at the end of each Grover iteration is derived analytically and proven to remain intensive as system size grows. A solution-aware efficient decomposition keeps magic bounded despite using an extensive number of Toffoli gates, whereas agnostic implementations (confirmed for 3-SAT) generate volume-law non-stabilizerness.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify how magic grows in Grover's algorithm and highlight the role of solution-awareness in circuit compilation; volume-law magic in agnostic cases rules out efficient stabilizer-based simulation in practically relevant settings.

title: Entanglement measures and LOCC conversion criteria from Schur-Weyl duality
summary: The characterization of possible transformations between quantum states and the quantification of entanglement are central for understanding quantum resources. Explicit results are, however, scarce since they require complicated optimizations over transformation protocols or state decompositions. We introduce a method to optimize functions of the entanglement spectrum of bipartite states over mixed-state decompositions with arbitrary accuracy. Our results are based on a convergent semidefinite programming hierarchy of optimizations over entanglement spectra using a natural polynomial basis and Schur-Weyl duality. Our approach can also be used to determine non-polynomial measures, such as the entanglement of formation, and to characterize the dimensionality of entanglement. Moreover, extracting the decomposition allows us to formulate criteria to determine state transformations under local operations and classical communication (LOCC). In particular, we provide a hierarchy of certificates of LOCC non-convertibility from pure to mixed states in any dimension and a heuristic approach for LOCC convertibility.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a convergent semidefinite programming (SDP) hierarchy to optimize functions of the entanglement spectrum of bipartite states over mixed-state decompositions, enabling computation of entanglement measures and LOCC conversion criteria.
AI.motivation: Characterizing transformations between quantum states and quantifying entanglement are central to understanding quantum resources, but explicit results are scarce because they require complicated optimizations over transformation protocols or state decompositions. The authors seek a tractable, provably convergent method to handle these optimizations.
AI.method: The authors build a convergent SDP hierarchy for optimizing functions of the entanglement spectrum over mixed-state decompositions to arbitrary accuracy. The hierarchy uses a natural polynomial basis together with Schur-Weyl duality to reduce the optimization to a tractable semidefinite program.
AI.result: The framework optimizes entanglement-spectrum functions with arbitrary accuracy and can also determine non-polynomial measures such as the entanglement of formation and characterize the dimensionality of entanglement. Extracting the optimal decomposition yields criteria for state transformations under LOCC, including a hierarchy of certificates of LOCC non-convertibility from pure to mixed states in any dimension, plus a heuristic approach for LOCC convertibility.
AI.conclusion: A single convergent SDP-based hierarchy over entanglement spectra provides a unified, accurate tool for quantifying entanglement, computing non-polynomial measures, and certifying or heuristically testing LOCC convertibility between pure and mixed bipartite states in arbitrary dimensions.

title: Topological Quantum Error-Correcting Thresholds of a Symmetry-Enriched Toric Code
summary: We study the error thresholds of a new topological quantum error-correcting code under the independent bit-flip and phase-flip noisy channel. By mapping to classical spin-glass models, we find that if Pauli X and Z errors are equally probable, the threshold of vertex syndromes is improved by 30% compared to that of the toric code, while the threshold of plaquette syndromes is lowered. Both thresholds increase when the Z component is less likely than the X component, reaching 0.5 if the Z component is absent. An analytical proof justifies this special case of perfect correctability, and a disordered version of Peierls's argument establishes a lower bound for the vertex-syndrome threshold.

AI.tldr: The authors analyze error thresholds of a new topological quantum code under independent bit-flip and phase-flip noise, mapping the problem to classical spin-glass models. The vertex-syndrome threshold improves by 30% over the toric code when X and Z errors are equiprobable, and both thresholds rise when Z errors are less likely, reaching 0.5 in the absence of Z errors.
AI.motivation: Understanding how a new topological quantum error-correcting code performs under realistic independent bit-flip and phase-flip noise is essential for benchmarking it against the well-known toric code, particularly in terms of syndrome-specific error thresholds.
AI.method: The error thresholds are studied by mapping the code's decoding problem onto classical spin-glass models, enabling threshold evaluation via statistical-mechanics techniques. An analytical proof establishes perfect correctability in the limiting case, and a disordered version of Peierls's argument is used to derive a rigorous lower bound on the vertex-syndrome threshold.
AI.result: For equally probable Pauli X and Z errors, the vertex-syndrome threshold exceeds the toric code by 30%, while the plaquette-syndrome threshold is lower. When Z errors are less likely than X errors, both thresholds increase, reaching 0.5 when the Z component is absent. An analytical proof justifies this perfect-correctability case, and the disordered Peierls argument yields a lower bound for the vertex-syndrome threshold.
AI.conclusion: The new code offers an improved vertex-syndrome threshold relative to the toric code under symmetric depolarizing-like noise, with a trade-off of a reduced plaquette-syndrome threshold, and exhibits perfect correctability in the limit of purely bit-flip noise, supported by analytical and rigorous lower-bound arguments.

title: Lower Bound for Region of Non-Distillable Magic States
summary: Magic states are a leading proposal for realizing fault-tolerant and universal quantum computation. At the present moment, much of the theory of magic states is not understood. Even simple questions such as what single qubit states have magic remain open. In Campbell and Browne's seminal paper on bound magic states, they prove the existence of states outside of the stabilizer octahedron which cannot be used to achieve universal computation. In this paper we expand upon their proof and determine a lower-bound on this region.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits Campbell and Browne's proof on bound magic states, expands the argument, and derives a lower bound on the region of states lying outside the stabilizer octahedron yet still non-universal (bound magic).
AI.motivation: Magic states underpin fault-tolerant universal quantum computation, yet their theory is poorly understood; even classifying which single-qubit states possess magic is open. Campbell and Browne showed states outside the stabilizer octahedron can still fail to enable universality, but this bound-magic region was not quantitatively characterized.
AI.method: The authors expand upon Campbell and Browne's original proof for the existence of bound magic states outside the stabilizer octahedron and use this extended argument to establish a quantitative lower bound on the bound-magic region.
AI.result: A lower bound is determined on the region of single-qubit states that lie outside the stabilizer octahedron but cannot achieve universal computation.
AI.conclusion: The work sharpens understanding of the geometry of magic states by quantifying a subset of non-universal states beyond the stabilizer octahedron, contributing to the broader open problem of classifying magic in single-qubit states.

title: Stellar Representation of Gottesman Kitaev Preskill States on the Double Discrete Cylinder
summary: Covariant integral quantization is developed on the double discrete cylinder phase space, with the torus as configuration space, and yields the Wigner distribution and the stellar representation. This phase space is particularly well suited to translationally invariant states, such as the Gottesman Kitaev Preskill (GKP) states. These states are central to fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures, yet their quantum resources are still under investigation. The stellar representations of ideal GKP logical states, which behave as phase eigenstates of the double discrete cylinder, have no zeros on this phase space, whereas those of their superpositions have infinitely many. The vacuum, although Gaussian, has zeros on this phase space, and the zeros of finitely squeezed GKP states move with the widths of the peaks and of the envelope, and reach this phase space for fine-tuned widths. These features echo the role of the vacuum as the resource that makes GKP-based architectures hard to simulate.

AI.tldr: Covariant integral quantization on the double discrete cylinder phase space (with the torus as configuration space) yields a Wigner distribution and stellar representation, used to analyze zeros of GKP states and the vacuum.
AI.motivation: GKP states are central to fault-tolerant quantum computing, but their quantum resources remain under investigation; a phase-space framework suited to translationally invariant states is needed to characterize them.
AI.method: Develop covariant integral quantization on the double discrete cylinder phase space, deriving the Wigner distribution and stellar (zero) representation, then apply it to ideal and finitely squeezed GKP logical states, their superpositions, and the vacuum.
AI.result: Ideal GKP logical states, behaving as phase eigenstates of the double discrete cylinder, have no zeros on this phase space, while their superpositions have infinitely many zeros; the vacuum, although Gaussian, exhibits zeros, and the zeros of finitely squeezed GKP states shift with peak and envelope widths, reaching the phase space for fine-tuned widths.
AI.conclusion: The zero structure of the stellar representation distinguishes GKP states and superpositions, and the vacuum's zeros reflect its role as the resource making GKP-based architectures hard to simulate classically.

title: Shor's algorithm compiled on cat qubits: 22 593 qubits for RSA-2048 in 3.14 days
summary:
We present an end-to-end resource estimation of Shor's algorithm on superconducting cat qubits, from its mathematical description to the allocation and scheduling of physical qubits on a chip layout. We review modern versions of Shor's algorithm for RSA, ECDLP and FFDLP, and make their logical circuits and trade-offs explicit. We compile the dominant subroutines down to physical-qubit operations on two architectures: one based on repetition cat codes and one on LDPC cat codes. We design a parity-Cnot gate for cat qubits, extend a multi-target Cnot gate to the LDPC-cat architecture, and adapt an active injection procedure to cat qubits. Building on these primitives, we adapt to cat qubits the adder from Gidney's 2025 resource estimate for factoring RSA-2048. We combine our adder compilation and a coarser estimate for the phaseup with the factory designs and lookup compilation from the FeMoco resource estimation of Kroell et al. Together, these lead to chip layouts and schedules for factoring RSA-2048.
  Assuming a 1$μ$s error-correction cycle time, a 10$μ$s reaction time, circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability $p_Z = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ and no bit-flips, factoring RSA-2048, the configuration we compile in full, requires about 23 000 cat qubits and 3.14 days. Reusing the compiled operations, solving ECDLP on secp256k1 requires at most 30 000 cat qubits and 1 hour, and FFDLP-512, which we propose as an intermediate benchmark, about 6 700 cat qubits and 21 minutes. Trading space for time, RSA-2048 runs in 1.25 hours on about 611 000 cat qubits. The no-bit-flip requirement (a bit-flip time of about 100 years) can be relaxed to a bit-flip time of about one hour by adding a concatenation layer with a distance-3 bit-flip code, in which case RSA-2048 needs about 45 000 cat qubits.

AI.tldr: End-to-end resource estimation of Shor's algorithm (RSA, ECDLP, FFDLP) on superconducting cat qubits yields chip layouts and schedules: factoring RSA-2048 needs ~23,000 cat qubits and 3.14 days under stated noise assumptions.
AI.motivation: Provide a full-stack, mathematically grounded resource estimate for Shor's algorithm on cat qubits, bridging logical circuits to physical-qubit allocation and scheduling on realistic chip layouts, and covering multiple cryptographic problems rather than RSA alone.
AI.method: Review modern Shor variants for RSA, ECDLP, FFDLP and make their logical circuits and trade-offs explicit; compile dominant subroutines to physical-qubit operations on two cat-qubit architectures (repetition codes and LDPC codes). Introduce a parity-Cnot gate for cat qubits, extend a multi-target Cnot gate to the LDPC-cat architecture, and adapt an active injection procedure. Adapt Gidney's 2025 RSA-2048 adder to cat qubits, and combine this with a coarser phaseup estimate plus factory designs and lookup compilation from Kroell et al.'s FeMoco estimation to produce chip layouts and schedules.
AI.result: Assuming 1 μs error-correction cycle, 10 μs reaction time, circuit-level phase-flip noise p_Z = 5×10⁻⁴ and no bit-flips: RSA-2048 requires ~23,000 cat qubits and 3.14 days; ECDLP on secp256k1 requires ≤30,000 cat qubits and 1 hour; FFDLP-512 (proposed intermediate benchmark) ~6,700 cat qubits and 21 minutes. Space-time trade-off: RSA-2048 in 1.25 hours on ~611,000 cat qubits. Relaxing the no-bit-flip requirement to a ~1-hour bit-flip time via a concatenated distance-3 bit-flip layer yields RSA-2048 in ~45,000 cat qubits.
AI.conclusion: Cat-qubit architectures enable competitive, layout-aware resource estimates for Shor's algorithm across RSA, ECDLP, and FFDLP, with favorable space-time trade-offs; a modest concatenation layer relaxes the stringent bit-flip requirement at moderate qubit overhead. FFDLP-512 is offered as a practical intermediate benchmark.

title: Ground-state energy estimation compiled on cat qubits: 7 164 qubits for FeMoco-54 in 23.5 hours
summary: We provide a detailed resource estimate of the state-of-the-art sum-of-squares block encoding algorithm for electronic structure Hamiltonians of Low et al. on superconducting cat qubits. To achieve this, we present compilations with closed-form costs of the dominant subroutines such as skew-tree Qrom, a Swap network and a Phaseup for both a repetition-cat and an LDPC-cat architecture. Our compilation represents algorithmic qubits in the $X$ basis, taking advantage of the asymmetric cost of $X$ and $Z$ access that the concatenation of cat qubits with phase-flip classical code brings. Additionally, we provide a protocol for $\vert i \rangle$-state distillation and a two-level Toffoli-like $\vert \text{C}_X\text{C}_X X \rangle$ magic state distillation protocol, including three factory layouts. To minimize the cost of Clifford corrections induced by magic state injections we tailor injection gadgets to each subroutine. Combining our compilation work with the adder compilation from the companion work Pappalardo et al., we provide global layouts for the block encoding in both architectures which we use to obtain resource estimates for ground-state energy estimation for the benchmarks of FeMoco-54 and FeMoco-76. Assuming a cycle time of 1$μ$s, a reaction time of 10$\mathrmμ$s, a phase estimation precision of 1 mHa and circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability $p_Z = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ with negligible bit-flip error, FeMoco-54 requires fewer than $7\,500$ cat qubits with an expected runtime of under one day for a single phase estimation run using an LDPC-cat architecture. Relaxing the bit-flip requirement to $p_X = 10^{-11}$ with an additional layer of elevator codes raises this to an estimated $13\,000$ cat qubits.

AI.tldr: A detailed resource estimate of Low et al.'s sum-of-squares block encoding for electronic-structure Hamiltonians on superconducting cat qubits, with closed-form compilations for skew-tree QROM, Swap networks and Phaseup in repetition-cat and LDPC-cat architectures, yielding FeMoco-54 ground-state energy estimation in under 7,500 cat qubits and under one day.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art Sum-of-Squares (SoS) block encoding algorithms for electronic-structure Hamiltonians need realistic, architecture-aware resource estimates on a fault-tolerant hardware platform. Cat qubits offer asymmetric X/Z error costs when concatenated with a phase-flip classical code, a property not exploited by generic compilations, so tailored compilation and magic-state protocols are needed to assess feasibility for chemistry benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors build closed-form cost compilations of the dominant subroutines—skew-tree QROM, Swap network, and Phaseup—for both a repetition-cat and an LDPC-cat architecture, representing algorithmic qubits in the X basis to exploit the asymmetric X/Z access cost of cat qubits concatenated with a phase-flip code. They design an |i⟩-state distillation protocol and a two-level Toffoli-like |C_X C_X X⟩ magic-state distillation protocol with three factory layouts, and tailor injection gadgets to each subroutine to minimize Clifford-correction cost. Combined with the adder compilation from Pappalardo et al., they construct global block-encoding layouts and derive end-to-end estimates for FeMoco-54 and FeMoco-76.
AI.result: For FeMoco-54, under a 1 μs cycle time, 10 μs reaction time, 1 mHa phase-estimation precision, and circuit-level phase-flip noise p_Z = 5×10⁻⁴ with negligible bit-flip error, fewer than 7,500 cat qubits are required with an expected single-run runtime under one day using the LDPC-cat architecture. Relaxing the bit-flip requirement to p_X = 10⁻¹¹ with an additional layer of elevator codes raises the estimate to about 13,000 cat qubits.
AI.conclusion: Tailored, X-basis, cat-qubit-aware compilation of SoS block encoding makes ground-state energy estimation for FeMoco-54 feasible within under 7,500 cat qubits and under one day per phase-estimation run, with robustness to stricter bit-flip noise (p_X = 10⁻¹¹) achievable at roughly 13,000 cat qubits via elevator codes. The results quantify the resource impact of architecture choice, magic-state distillation, and Clifford-correction overhead.

title: Exact verification of Givens rotation circuits for efficient quantum phase estimation of iron-sulfur clusters
summary: Givens rotations with angles stored in quantum registers account for much of the cost of published quantum phase estimation algorithms based on double-factorized tensor hypercontraction and spectral amplification. These rotations create superpositions and cannot be verified directly by the basis-state evaluators used to optimize classical reversible circuits. We give an exact verification method that separates out a fixed Clifford change of basis and tracks basis states and phases in the remaining circuit. Integer conditions establish correctness of the full coherent action, including measurement-based uncomputation and restoration of the phase-gradient resource state. Under our interpretation of Low et al.'s angle grid and rotation convention, simplifying the adders lowers the rotation cost relative to the published accounting; fusing the two additions into one masked addition gives an additional saving. We verify both implementations exhaustively at every precision used in the published walks and prove the fused circuit correct for all widths. For benchmarks including FeMoco and other iron-sulfur clusters, replacing only the rotation term lowers total phase-estimation Toffoli counts by 9.5-14.3% under the published error budget, with the walk operator unchanged.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an exact verification method for Givens rotation circuits that use register-stored angles. By separating a fixed Clifford basis change and tracking basis states plus phases, the authors verify coherent actions (including measurement-based uncomputation). Their reformulated adders lower rotation cost versus published accounting, and fusing two additions into one masked addition yields further savings; for FeMoco and other iron-sulfur clusters, replacing only the rotation term cuts total phase-estimation Toffoli counts by 9.5–14.3%.
AI.motivation: Givens rotations with angles stored in quantum registers dominate the cost of published quantum phase estimation based on double-factorized tensor hypercontraction and spectral amplification. These rotations create superpositions and cannot be directly verified by the basis-state evaluators used to optimize classical reversible circuits, creating a verification gap.
AI.method: An exact verification method that isolates a fixed Clifford change of basis and tracks basis states and phases in the remaining circuit. Integer conditions are used to establish correctness of the full coherent action, including measurement-based uncomputation and restoration of the phase-gradient resource state. Within the authors' interpretation of Low et al.'s angle grid and rotation convention, adders are simplified (reducing rotation cost) and two additions are fused into a single masked addition.
AI.result: Both implementations are verified exhaustively at every precision used in the published walks, and the fused circuit is proved correct for all widths. For benchmarks including FeMoco and other iron-sulfur clusters, replacing only the rotation term lowers total phase-estimation Toffoli counts by 9.5–14.3% under the published error budget, with the walk operator unchanged.
AI.conclusion: A practical exact verification framework enables cost reductions in register-angle Givens rotation circuits without altering the walk operator. Simplifying and fusing adders yields measurable Toffoli savings on realistic chemistry benchmarks.

title: Quantum Foundations Beyond Bell's Theorem: A Topical Review
summary: We review a series of recent no-go theorems that extend the methodological and conceptual framework introduced by Bell's theorem to more sophisticated operational scenarios involving independent sources, quantum networks, joint measurements, and multiple observers. Many of these results were originally developed within quantum information science and are scattered across the literature, where their technical and application-driven success has partly obscured their broader foundational significance. We organize them around a common Bell-inspired methodology that extends beyond quantum nonlocality, and emphasize how increasingly rich operational structures change which physical assumptions can be tested.

AI.tldr: A review organizing recent no-go theorems that generalize Bell's methodology to independent sources, quantum networks, joint measurements, and multiple observers, highlighting their shared foundational significance.
AI.motivation: No-go results developed in quantum information science are scattered across the literature, and their technical/application-driven success has obscured their broader foundational importance. The paper aims to consolidate them and show that they share a common Bell-inspired methodology extending beyond quantum nonlocality.
AI.method: A conceptual and methodological review: the authors collect and organize recent no-go theorems around a common Bell-style framework, generalizing the Bell scenario to richer operational structures (independent sources, quantum networks, joint measurements, multiple observers), and analyze how these structures determine which physical assumptions can be tested.
AI.result: The review identifies a unified Bell-inspired methodology spanning diverse no-go theorems and clarifies how increasingly rich operational scenarios alter the set of assumptions that become experimentally testable.
AI.conclusion: Recent no-go theorems from quantum information science carry substantial foundational significance; viewing them through a generalized Bell framework clarifies the relationship between operational structure and testable physical assumptions.

title: The Geometry of Quantum Teleportation in Phase Space
summary: We formulate the standard quantum teleportation protocol within the framework of deformation quantization, employing the Stratonovich--Weyl (SW) correspondence and the associated star product on the coadjoint orbits of $SU(2)$. Each qubit is represented by a spherical phase space $S^2$ endowed with the Kirillov--Kostant--Souriau (KKS) symplectic structure. Within this setting, we explicitly construct the phase space representations of the entangled Bell resource, the controlled-NOT and Hadamard operators, the projective measurements, and the conditional Pauli corrections. We demonstrate how the quantum information initially encoded in the Wigner function for the input qubit is redistributed through bipartite and tripartite phase space correlations. Upon consideration of a conditional unitary transformation, the measurement outcome produces a Wigner function on the receiver's coadjoint orbit that is related to the input by an outcome-dependent rotation, which can subsequently be inverted through the implementation of an appropriate Pauli correction. The covariance of the SW correspondence provides a geometric interpretation of this process, in which quantum information is redistributed and reconstructed without transferring the underlying symplectic geometry. Our formulation can also be extended to study quantum teleportation in more general phase space geometries equipped with suitable star products.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates standard qubit quantum teleportation in deformation quantization using the Stratonovich–Weyl correspondence and star products on SU(2) coadjoint orbits, showing information redistribution via Wigner-function correlations and its restoration by outcome-dependent Pauli corrections.
AI.motivation: Standard teleportation is usually described algebraically in Hilbert space; the authors seek a geometric, phase-space formulation that clarifies how quantum information (non the underlying geometry) is transferred, using the KKS symplectic structure of qubit phase spaces.
AI.method: Each qubit is mapped to a spherical phase space S^2 with KKS symplectic form; the SW correspondence and star product are used to construct phase-space representations of the Bell resource, CNOT and Hadamard gates, projective measurements, and conditional Pauli corrections. Wigner-function redistribution is tracked through bipartite and tripartite correlations.
AI.result: After measurement and conditional unitary transformation, the receiver's Wigner function relates to the input by an outcome-dependent rotation on the coadjoint orbit, which Pauli corrections invert; covariance of the SW correspondence gives a geometric account in which information is redistributed and reconstructed without transferring symplectic geometry.
AI.conclusion: Teleportation admits a consistent deformation-quantization description, and the framework can be extended to more general phase-space geometries equipped with suitable star products.

title: Are quantum measurements universal?
summary: With D. Aerts, we showed in 2014, within the extended Bloch representation of quantum mechanics, that the Born rule can be understood as resulting from a universal average over all the possible ways in which the measurement-interactions can be selected. The cellular construction used there was since questioned, in the context of Bertrand's paradox, by N. Shackel, who observed that the result depends on the discretization adopted, that the sequence of averages is constant, and that the sense in which the average is taken over "all" densities remains unclear. Taking these criticisms as a stimulus, we re-examine the notion. The key is to recognize that a universal measurement is a random way of selecting a measurement which does not privilege any portion of the structure describing the available interactions, a property we call indifference. We prove that every indifferent universal measurement, however constructed, produces exactly the Born probabilities: the universal average is unique, and the cellular construction of 2014 is one among infinitely many ways of obtaining it, exact at every finite resolution. Non-trivial indifferent universal measurements exist, but must involve deterministic measurements: Dirichlet processes are indifferent universal measurements reaching every way of selecting an interaction, whereas an indifferent universal measurement free of deterministic components necessarily selects the uniform density, so that the Born rule holds not only on average but with certainty. Deviations from the quantum statistics in sequences of measurements are governed by a single parameter, in principle accessible to experiment. The only geometric inputs are the Euclidean length of the membrane and the orthogonal landing of the point-particle on it; the latter is where the content of Gleason's theorem lies. Generalizations to N outcomes and to Bertrand's paradox are discussed.

AI.tldr: Re-examines the 2014 derivation of the Born rule from a "universal average" over measurement-interactions in the extended Bloch representation, reframing it via an "indifference" principle to answer Bertrand-paradox criticisms and proving the Born probabilities are the unique universal average.
AI.motivation: The 2014 cellular construction of the Born rule was criticized by N. Shackel in the context of Bertrand's paradox: results depend on discretization, the sequence of averages is constant, and the sense of averaging over "all" densities is unclear. The paper treats these criticisms as a stimulus to re-examine and rigorize the notion of universal measurement.
AI.method: Introduces an "indifference" principle: a universal measurement is a random selection of a measurement that privileges no portion of the structure describing available interactions. Proves that every indifferent universal measurement yields exactly the Born probabilities, making the universal average unique (with the 2014 cellular construction as one of infinitely many instances, exact at every finite resolution). Uses Dirichlet processes as indifferent universal measurements, and analyzes deterministic components and a single deviation parameter.
AI.result: The universal average is unique and equals the Born probabilities. Non-trivial indifferent universal measurements exist but must involve deterministic measurements; Dirichlet processes reach every interaction selection, while an indifferent universal measurement free of deterministic components necessarily selects the uniform density, so the Born rule holds with certainty, not merely on average. Deviations in measurement sequences are governed by one experimentally accessible parameter. The only geometric inputs are the Euclidean membrane length and orthogonal landing of the point-particle, the latter carrying the content of Gleason's theorem.
AI.conclusion: The Born rule is robustly derivable as a unique universal average under the indifference principle, resolving the Bertrand-paradox objections. The framework extends to N outcomes and to Bertrand's paradox, and predicts a single-parameter family of deviations from quantum statistics testable in experiment.

title: Twisted Fourier Analysis of Quantum Weight Enumerators
summary: A unified Fourier framework for quantum weight enumerators of prime-power-dimensional qudits is developed in this paper. We introduce the notions of Weyl power spectrum and Weyl-conjugation autocorrelation for the Weyl-operator quantities nderlying the Shor--Laflamme weight enumerators. Representing these quantities as formal vectors, we show that they form a symplectic Fourier transform pair, from which the quantum MacWilliams identity follows by applying the Hamming-weight functional. This framework extends to a family of twisted Fourier transforms, including the Rains shadow transform. We show that identical-copy Bell sampling corresponds to a twisted autocorrelation related to the shadow enumerator through Weyl translation and Hamming projection. We further prove that all twisted Fourier transforms are Weyl translations of either the ordinary MacWilliams transform or the Rains shadow transform. This two-class reduction implies that the twists yield no additional independent coefficientwise positivity constraints under compatible projections. Nevertheless, the framework leads to refined MacWilliams and shadow identities that retain more Fourier information than ordinary Hamming weight enumerators. We employ these refined identities in linear programming, together with simplex mapping and shadow-coset counting, to exclude surviving candidate weight distributions. These techniques yield tighter bounds for binary and qutrit quantum codes, including nonexistence results for specific code parameters.

AI.tldr: A unified symplectic Fourier framework for quantum weight enumerators of prime-power qudits is developed, showing that Weyl power spectra and autocorrelations form Fourier pairs, that all twisted transforms reduce to two classes (ordinary MacWilliams or Rains shadow), and that refined identities yield improved linear-programming bounds and nonexistence results for binary and qutrit codes.
AI.motivation: Quantum weight enumerators (Shor–Laflamme) and their MacWilliams-type identities are the main analytic tool for bounding quantum codes, but the underlying Weyl-operator quantities, the various twisted/shadow transforms, and their relation to sampling protocols lack a single unifying algebraic framework. The authors aim to explain these transforms uniformly and to extract stronger constraints than ordinary Hamming-weight enumerators provide.
AI.method: The paper defines Weyl power spectrum and Weyl-conjugation autocorrelation for the Weyl-operator quantities underlying Shor–Laflamme enumerators, representing them as formal vectors. It proves they form a symplectic Fourier transform pair, derives the quantum MacWilliams identity via a Hamming-weight functional, and extends to twisted Fourier transforms including the Rains shadow transform. A connection is drawn between identical-copy Bell sampling and a twisted autocorrelation (shadow enumerator) via Weyl translation and Hamming projection. Refined MacWilliams and shadow identities are then used in linear programming with simplex mapping and shadow-coset counting to rule out candidate weight distributions.
AI.result: All twisted Fourier transforms are proven to be Weyl translations of either the ordinary MacWilliams transform or the Rains shadow transform (a two-class reduction), implying no additional independent coefficientwise positivity constraints under compatible projections. The refined identities nonetheless retain more Fourier information and, in linear programming, exclude surviving candidate weight distributions, giving tighter bounds for binary and qutrit quantum codes and nonexistence results for specific parameters.
AI.conclusion: The symplectic Fourier viewpoint unifies quantum weight enumerators and their twisted variants, revealing a two-class structure of transforms while still providing strictly stronger constraints than ordinary Hamming-weight enumerators; combined with LP, simplex mapping, and shadow-coset counting it tightens code bounds and establishes new nonexistence results.

title: Ontology without states: PBR as an argument for dynamics-first realism
summary: The Pusey--Barrett--Rudolph (PBR) theorem is commonly taken to establish that a pure quantum state represents a physical property of the system to which it is assigned, rather than merely encoding knowledge. In this work, I distinguish between state-first and dynamics-first physical theories, and argue that this reading presupposes the former. These two types of theories support different approaches to causal explanation, and one of PBR's stated assumptions depends on the state-first approach. Using a recent interpretation of quantum theory as a concrete example, I show how a dynamics-first theory can explain the PBR correlations while maintaining a broadly epistemic reading of quantum states. I conclude that the PBR theorem supports a dilemma: either the quantum state is part of reality, or reality is not fundamentally built out of states.

AI.tldr: The PBR theorem's anti-epistemic conclusion depends on a "state-first" framing; a "dynamics-first" theory can reproduce PBR correlations while treating quantum states as broadly epistemic, so PBR yields a dilemma rather than a refutation of epistemic readings.
AI.motivation: The standard reading of the PBR theorem as proving that pure quantum states are ontic (physical properties) rather than epistemic (states of knowledge) is widely accepted; the paper challenges this reading by exposing a hidden framing assumption and showing that the theorem's force is more limited than usually claimed.
AI.method: Conceptual/philosophical analysis. The author distinguishes state-first theories (fundamental ontology given by states, with dynamics defined on them) from dynamics-first theories (fundamental ontology given by dynamical laws/processes, with states as derived or effective descriptions), and argues these support different models of causal explanation. The paper identifies which of PBR's stated assumptions presupposes the state-first approach, then uses a recent dynamics-first interpretation of quantum theory as a worked example to show the PBR correlations can be explained while retaining a broadly epistemic reading of states.
AI.result: One of PBR's stated assumptions is shown to be a state-first presupposition rather than a neutral premise. A concrete dynamics-first interpretation reproduces the PBR correlations without assigning ontic status to the quantum state, undermining the claim that PBR alone establishes ontic states.
AI.conclusion: PBR should be read as supporting a dilemma: either the quantum state is part of reality, or reality is not fundamentally built out of states. Consequently, the theorem does not by itself refute epistemic readings of the quantum state; escaping the ontic conclusion requires abandoning state-first ontology rather than abandoning epistemicism.

title: Reducing the cost of ancilla purification for Majorana quantum computation
summary: Braiding Majorana zero modes does not by itself provide a universal set of quantum gates. Additional operations can be supplied through ancillary states, whose preparation need not have the same protection as braiding. Here, we consider purification of the non-Gaussian ancilla used for an entangling gate in Bravyi's scheme. We keep his elementary braid-and-fusion comparison and change how its outputs are combined. An additional layer compares the product of the three stabilizer signs. The first accepted errors giving an incorrect output then require three faulty input blocks rather than two. As a result, the preparation error decreases cubically instead of quadratically, and the asymptotic raw-copy overhead is reduced. We also construct a preliminary sequence in which a processed block is paired with a fresh copy from the same noisy source. For independent inputs supported in the even-parity sector and ideal purification operations, this sequence establishes a sufficient distillability fidelity of 59.95 percent after free Gaussian twirling. At a common source fidelity, it reduces the expected cost of preparing an input for the recurrence by more than seven orders of magnitude relative to the balanced construction studied here. Finally, we examine imperfect purification operations in an effective syndrome-noise model. The additional layer leaves the leading operation-error coefficient unchanged, although a nonzero error floor remains.

AI.tldr: Bravyi's ancilla-purification scheme for an entangling gate is modified so that errors are accepted only when three (rather than two) faulty input blocks conspire, reducing the preparation error from quadratic to cubic and lowering raw-copy overhead, with a preliminary mixed fresh/processed-block sequence achieving 59.95% distillability fidelity and >7 orders of magnitude cost reduction at a common source fidelity.
AI.motivation: Braiding Majorana zero modes alone is non-universal; ancilla states enable entangling gates but their preparation lacks braiding-level protection, so the ancilla purification (distillation) procedure must be made more error-tolerant to reduce reliance on high-fidelity source states.
AI.method: Retains Bravyi's elementary braid-and-fusion comparison but changes output combination: an additional layer compares the product of the three stabilizer signs, so accepted incorrect outputs require three faulty input blocks. Also constructs a preliminary sequence pairing a processed block with a fresh copy from the same noisy source, analyzed for independent even-parity-sector inputs under ideal purification and free Gaussian twirling, plus a study of imperfect purification in an effective syndrome-noise model.
AI.result: Preparation error scales cubically rather than quadratically, reducing asymptotic raw-copy overhead. The fresh-copy sequence yields a sufficient distillability fidelity of 59.95% after free Gaussian twirling and, at a common source fidelity, cuts expected input-preparation cost by more than seven orders of magnitude versus the balanced construction. In the syndrome-noise model, the extra layer leaves the leading operation-error coefficient unchanged while a nonzero error floor persists.
AI.conclusion: Modifying the output-combination rule of Bravyi's purification improves error scaling and resource overhead, and a mixed processed/fresh-block recurrence offers dramatic cost savings under ideal operations; however, imperfect purification introduces an error floor, so operation-level noise must be addressed for practical benefit.

title: Sample Complexity for Generative Learning of Quantum Measurement Data
summary: Generative learning of a quantum measurement distribution from finite data requires choosing a model capacity that balances representation accuracy against estimation cost. We develop a bias-variance framework that decomposes the expected population Kullback-Leibler error at model capacity $s$ and sample size $N$ as $\mathcal E(s,N)=B(s)+V(s,N)$, with representation bias $B$ and a variance term $V$ capturing the mean estimation error. In the well-sampled regime, $V(s,N)\simeq[NC(s)]^{-1}$, and exponential or algebraic laws for $B$ and $C$ yield four scaling templates for the optimal error, from inverse powers of $N$ to inverse powers of $\ln N$. For local autoregressive models, the context radius sets the model capacity, and $B$ is the summed conditional mutual information lost by truncating the context. For a smoothed histogram learner, we derive an exact finite-sample estimation cost that accounts for rarely observed contexts and recovers the parameter-count law in the well-sampled regime. For transverse-field Ising Born distributions, the independently evaluated bias and estimation cost predict both the optimal context radius and the optimal error. In the well-sampled regime, the estimation cost grows exponentially with context radius. Its competition with approximately exponential bias decay in the gapped regimes predicts power-law error decay in $N$, while algebraic bias decay at criticality predicts asymptotic inverse-power decay in $\ln N$. Bulk-site results are consistent with the corresponding finite-sample predictions. These results connect the structure of quantum measurement distributions to the model capacity justified by finite data.

AI.tldr: A bias-variance framework decomposes the population KL error of generative learning of quantum measurement distributions into bias B(s) and variance V(s,N), yielding four scaling templates for optimal error; when applied to local autoregressive models and smoothed histogram learners on transverse-field Ising Born distributions, it predicts the optimal context radius and optimal error.
AI.motivation: Learning quantum measurement distributions generatively from finite data requires choosing a model capacity that balances representation accuracy against estimation cost, but a principled account linking the structure of the distribution to the justified capacity was missing.
AI.method: Expected population KL error is decomposed as E(s,N)=B(s)+V(s,N), with V≈[NC(s)]^{-1} in the well-sampled regime; exponential or algebraic laws for B and C give four scaling templates. For local autoregressive models, capacity is set by context radius and B equals the summed conditional mutual information lost to context truncation; for a smoothed histogram learner an exact finite-sample estimation cost is derived. Both are evaluated on transverse-field Ising Born distributions.
AI.result: For TFIM Born distributions the independently evaluated bias and estimation cost predict both the optimal context radius and optimal error. Estimation cost grows exponentially with context radius; competing with approximately exponential bias decay in gapped regimes gives power-law error decay in N, while algebraic bias decay at criticality gives inverse-power decay in ln N. Bulk-site results agree with finite-sample predictions.
AI.conclusion: The bias-variance decomposition connects the structure of quantum measurement distributions to the model capacity justified by finite data, providing scaling laws for optimal error and optimal capacity that match numerical results for TFIM Born distributions.

title: Continuous variable quantum key distribution through a fading channel with minimal information leakage
summary: Continuous variable quantum key distribution enables two parties to extract provably secure keys for cryptography by exploiting aspects of quantum mechanics. A central challenge in achieving QKD over long distances is overcoming optical loss, which limits the secret key rates and achievable transmission distances. Recent work has illustrated how to perform continuous variable quantum key distribution while eliminating information leakage to an eavesdropper in a pure-loss channel and minimizing information leakage in a noisy channel. In this work, we analyse this protocol under conditions where the quantum channel linking the sender and receiver is a fading channel, which can be used to model free-space links. We find that the protocol maintains strong performance over fading channels and outperforms comparable protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes a continuous-variable QKD protocol that suppresses eavesdropper information leakage over fading (free-space-like) channels, showing it retains strong performance and beats comparable protocols.
AI.motivation: Long-distance CV-QKD is limited by optical loss, which caps secret key rates and reach. Recent protocols eliminate leakage in pure-loss channels and minimize it in noisy channels, but their behavior over fading channels—relevant for free-space links—was unexamined.
AI.method: The authors analytically/statistically evaluate the recently proposed low-leakage CV-QKD protocol under fading-channel conditions, which model free-space links, and benchmark it against comparable CV-QKD protocols.
AI.result: The protocol maintains strong performance over fading channels and outperforms comparable protocols.
AI.conclusion: The leakage-minimizing CV-QKD protocol is a robust candidate for free-space/ fading-channel deployment, retaining advantages over standard schemes.

title: Perspective on AI and quantum open-source software
summary: Quantum open-source software provides essential infrastructure for quantum science, and artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping its capabilities and transforming its development. However, verifying quantum software at scale remains difficult, and AI-generated contributions can increase the workload of maintainers. In this Perspective, we examine verification as a central requirement for reliable AI-assisted quantum software development and research. We analyze public repositories, records covering 110 repositories from five annual quantum open-source hackathons that we organize, and responses from more than 1600 participants in a community survey. Our analysis connects limitations in automated verification with the review burden on quantum software maintainers. We propose verification practices and contribution standards that require contributors to support their changes with reproducible evidence for maintainer review. We also examine how quantum open-source software can provide infrastructure for AI-driven research whose results the community can independently verify and build upon. We maintain an open-source companion repository to support reproducibility and help projects adopt and refine these proposals. Together, these contributions help the quantum open-source software community translate advances in AI into reliable quantum research through reproducible verification.

AI.tldr: This Perspective argues that verification is the central requirement for reliable AI-assisted quantum open-source software development, analyzing repositories, hackathon records, and survey data to link weak automated verification with maintainer review burden and proposing evidence-based contribution standards.
AI.motivation: Quantum open-source software is critical infrastructure for quantum science, and AI is rapidly reshaping its capabilities and development. However, verifying quantum software at scale remains difficult, and AI-generated contributions can overload maintainers. The paper therefore frames verification as the cornerstone for trustworthy AI-assisted quantum software development and research.
AI.method: The authors combine multiple empirical sources: analysis of public repositories, records from 110 repositories across five annual quantum open-source hackathons they organize, and responses from more than 1,600 community survey participants. They relate limitations in automated verification to the review burden on maintainers, and propose verification practices and contribution standards requiring contributors to back changes with reproducible evidence for maintainer review. An open-source companion repository supports reproducibility and adoption of these proposals.
AI.result: The analysis connects shortcomings in automated verification to increased review burden on quantum software maintainers, and shows how reproducible, evidence-supported contributions can reduce that load. The proposals also position quantum open-source software as infrastructure for AI-driven research whose results the community can independently verify and build upon.
AI.conclusion: Verification should be treated as a central requirement for AI-assisted quantum software. By adopting reproducible-evidence contribution standards and shared verification infrastructure, the quantum open-source community can translate advances in AI into reliable, independently verifiable quantum research.

title: Exact Positive-P Simulation of Open Quantum Spin Systems with Generalized Density Matrix Formalism
summary: The positive-P representation for bosons allows scalable exact simulations of many-body open quantum systems, provided dissipation is strong enough to stabilise stochastic trajectories. Designing analogous methods for spin systems, relevant to quantum technologies, remains challenging, as previous spin positive-P formulations can exhibit systematic errors even when simulations are numerically stable. Here, we develop a phase-space representation that maps spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ degrees of freedom onto parameters of a local generalized density matrix (GDM), rather than SU(2) coherent states. In all stable regimes, we observe no deviations from exact solutions, restoring the positive-P property: stable solutions are exact up to stochastic sampling noise. The GDM representation combines seamlessly with bosonic positive-P, enabling highly scalable treatment of coupled spin-boson systems. We map simulation stability versus spin and boson dissipation in the Jaynes-Cummings model and apply the method to a Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard quasi-Lieb lattice, showing how spin dissipation and driving can destroy or restore excitation incompressibility.

AI.tldr: A generalized density-matrix (GDM) phase-space representation for spin-1/2 systems restores the exactness property of positive-P: stable stochastic trajectories reproduce exact many-body dynamics, and it composes with bosonic positive-P for scalable spin-boson simulations.
AI.motivation: Bosonic positive-P enables scalable exact open-quantum-simulation but requires strong dissipation to keep trajectories stable. Spin analogues are needed for quantum technologies, yet earlier spin positive-P formulations based on SU(2) coherent states can yield systematic errors even when numerically stable.
AI.method: Map each spin-1/2 degree of freedom onto parameters of a local generalized density matrix (GDM) instead of SU(2) coherent states, constructing a phase-space representation. Combine it with bosonic positive-P for coupled spin-boson models. Map simulation stability against spin and boson dissipation in the Jaynes-Cummings model, then apply the method to a Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard quasi-Lieb lattice.
AI.result: In all stable regimes, no deviations from exact solutions are observed: stable solutions are exact up to stochastic sampling noise, restoring the positive-P property. Stability maps versus spin and boson dissipation are produced for Jaynes-Cummings, and lattice simulations show spin dissipation and driving can destroy or restore excitation incompressibility.
AI.conclusion: The GDM representation gives an exact-when-stable phase-space method for spins and integrates seamlessly with bosonic positive-P, providing a scalable framework for coupled spin-boson open quantum systems and lattice-level physics of spin dissipation and driving.
