title: A Coherent Neutron-Nucleus Hybrid System Mediated by the Strong Interaction
summary: A coherent ensemble of polarized helium-3 nuclei and free neutrons are coupled, forming a neutron-nucleus hybrid system. The nuclei are prepared in a spin superposition, while a magnetic field induces Zeeman splitting. The resulting nuclear energy phase is coherently transferred to the neutron, producing an intensity beat at the nuclear Zeeman frequency. Finally, the incident neutron is prepared in a spin-energy superposition state. The nuclear and neutron phases then heterodyne coherently, producing a signal at the sum or difference frequency depending on their relative helicity.

AI.tldr: A polarized helium-3 nucleus ensemble is coherently coupled to free neutrons to form a neutron-nucleus hybrid system; nuclear Zeeman phase is transferred to neutrons, generating intensity beats and heterodyne signals at sum/difference frequencies.
AI.motivation: The abstract implies a need to coherently link nuclear spin phases with neutron spin-energy superposition states, enabling frequency-mixing interference signals that could extend precision metrology or spin-based sensing using hybrid neutron-nuclear systems.
AI.method: Prepare polarized helium-3 nuclei in a spin superposition; apply a magnetic field to induce Zeeman splitting; coherently transfer the nuclear energy phase to free neutrons via coupling, producing an intensity beat at the nuclear Zeeman frequency; prepare incident neutrons in a spin-energy superposition so nuclear and neutron phases heterodyne coherently.
AI.result: An intensity beat appears at the nuclear Zeeman frequency; the coherent heterodyning of nuclear and neutron phases yields a signal at the sum or difference frequency, selected by the relative helicity of the two phases.
AI.conclusion: Coherent neutron-nucleus hybrid coupling enables phase transfer and heterodyne frequency mixing, with the output frequency set by relative helicity; this provides a basis for spin-phase interferometry in polarized neutron-helium systems.

title: Experimental Observation of Error-Resilience Phase Transition on Superconducting Quantum Processor
summary: Random unitaries scramble quantum information into highly nonlocal degrees of freedom, thereby providing protection from local noise. However, as demonstrated by Turkeshi and Sierant (Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 140401, 2024 and arXiv:2603.00235), this protection may fail once local noise grows sufficiently strong. These works describe a phase transition in a noisy random encoding-decoding circuit model between an error-protecting phase, in which encoded information is recoverable, and an error-vulnerable phase, in which encoded information is lost, with the transition occurring at a critical coherent noise angle $α_c \approx 1.14$. Here, we present the first experimental observation of this transition, conducted on IBM's ibm_pittsburgh Heron r3 device for system sizes of up to $N = 26$ qubits. We detect this transition via three order parameters: fidelity, Rényi-2 entanglement entropy, and stabilizer Rényi-2 entropy. For the latter two, we employ randomized measurement protocols to construct estimators, and for all three, we rely on zero-noise extrapolation and M3 SPAM error mitigation. We then jointly model the finite-size scaling collapse across all three order parameters with a Gaussian process regression, yielding a critical angle $α_c \approx 1.01$, well below the theoretical value. Inputting noiseless simulated data into the same model yields $α_c \approx 1.05$, implying that the discrepancy between experiment and theory is due to our encoding circuits, which are not deep enough to be truly Haar-random. Finally, we observe that the same model cannot adequately identify critical behavior in unmitigated, raw experimental data. This indicates that error mitigation techniques are crucial for detecting the transition on hardware.

AI.tldr: First experimental observation of a noise-induced phase transition in random encoding-decoding circuits on IBM hardware (up to 26 qubits), identifying a critical coherent noise angle α_c ≈ 1.01 via three order parameters.
AI.motivation: Random unitaries provide protection from local noise by scrambling information, but prior theory (Turkeshi & Sierant) predicts this protection fails at strong enough local noise, with a recoverable-to-vulnerable transition at critical angle α_c ≈ 1.14. This transition had not been experimentally observed.
AI.method: Implemented the noisy random encoding-decoding circuit on IBM's ibm_pittsburgh Heron r3 device up to N=26 qubits. Detected the transition with three order parameters: fidelity, Rényi-2 entanglement entropy, and stabilizer Rényi-2 entropy (the latter two estimated via randomized measurement protocols). Applied zero-noise extrapolation and M3 SPAM error mitigation. Jointly modeled finite-size scaling collapse across all order parameters using Gaussian process regression.
AI.result: Measured critical angle α_c ≈ 1.01, below the theoretical 1.14. Noiseless simulated data fed through the same model gives α_c ≈ 1.05, indicating the gap arises from encoding circuits not being deep enough to be truly Haar-random. The same model fails to identify critical behavior in unmitigated raw data.
AI.conclusion: The phase transition is experimentally confirmed, but error mitigation is essential to detect it on hardware, and finite-depth (non-Haar) encoding circuits shift the observed critical angle below theory.

title: Quantum advantage by designing beneficial dissipation from lossless dynamics
summary: Passive loss removes probability from a system and therefore seems unable to improve an unconditional target. This intuition is exact for classical population dynamics under sink-only removal: passive killing obeys a finite-strength monotonicity principle even after optimization over the remaining controls. Here we show that coherent quantum dynamics can violate this classical monotonicity because coherent contributions to the final target can interfere destructively. We derive a trajectory-level criterion that determines when such a detrimental contribution is physically accessible to passive loss and accumulates into a net unconditional benefit. The criterion is encoded in a response operator constructed entirely from the lossless dynamics: its spectrum determines whether weak passive loss can help, while its principal eigenvector identifies the optimal environmental mode. Applying this criterion to vibronically assisted transfer, we identify a beneficial mode formed by coherently combining two individually detrimental local loss directions. The predicted mode remains near-optimal at finite loss, producing an \(8.73\%\) enhancement over the independently optimized lossless benchmark, compared with \(9.52\%\) under full finite-loss optimization. Our results establish how coherent quantum dynamics can evade classical passive-loss monotonicity and provide a general task-dependent principle for designing beneficial passive environments from lossless dynamics.

AI.tldr: Passive (sink-only) loss seems unable to improve an unconditional target, but coherent quantum dynamics can violate the classical monotonicity via destructive interference of detrimental coherent contributions. A response operator built from the lossless dynamics determines when weak loss helps (its spectrum) and which environmental mode is optimal (its principal eigenvector).
AI.motivation: Classical population dynamics under sink-only removal obey a finite-strength monotonicity principle: passive loss removes probability and thus cannot improve an unconditional target, even after optimizing remaining controls. The paper asks whether coherent quantum dynamics break this intuition and, if so, how to predict and design beneficial passive loss.
AI.method: Trajectory-level analysis yielding a criterion for when a detrimental coherent contribution is physically accessible to passive loss and accumulates into a net unconditional benefit. The criterion is encoded in a response operator constructed entirely from the lossless dynamics: its spectrum decides whether weak passive loss can help, and its principal eigenvector identifies the optimal environmental mode. Applied to vibronically assisted transfer.
AI.result: In vibronically assisted transfer, the optimal beneficial mode is formed by coherently combining two individually detrimental local loss directions. The predicted mode stays near-optimal at finite loss, giving an 8.73% enhancement over the independently optimized lossless benchmark, versus 9.52% under full finite-loss optimization.
AI.conclusion: Coherent quantum dynamics can evade classical passive-loss monotonicity through destructive interference. The response-operator framework provides a general, task-dependent principle for designing beneficial passive environments from lossless dynamics alone.

title: Ancilla-free randomized Toffoli gates and the T-count of Boolean oracles
summary: In fault-tolerant Clifford+T circuits, a Boolean oracle costs T gates and extra qubits, and on four or more qubits every exact Toffoli gate needs an extra qubit. Gosset, Kothari and Zhang showed that sampling a fresh random circuit for each call makes the T-count of the Toffoli gate independent of its size, but a direct implementation of their sampler uses about one extra qubit per bit of precision. We show that computing the sampled parities in place, on the gate's own controls, removes every extra qubit once the gate is large enough: each random circuit then uses about 8 T gates per bit of precision and borrows only the gate's own idle inputs. This is one T gate more per circuit than the best measurement-free variant that keeps one clean ancilla. The same holds for exclusive-ors of indicators of affine subspaces, such as equality tests and checks of linear equations. For randomized circuits that do not measure, this is within a factor of eight of optimal up to an additive constant, even with extra qubits, and when each random circuit computes a Boolean function exactly, closing the factor asymptotically is equivalent to determining the leading constant in the T-count of exact multi-controlled Toffoli gates. Finally, the oracle of the indicator of a random set of fixed density needs exponentially many T gates at constant error, while that of an affine subspace of the same density needs a constant number, and extra qubits reduce the exponential cost only quadratically.

AI.tldr: In-place computation of sampled parities on a gate's own controls eliminates all extra qubits for large Toffoli/affine-subspace indicators, giving ~8 T gates per bit of precision—within a factor of eight of optimal for measurement-free randomized circuits.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant Clifford+T implementations of Boolean oracles need T gates and extra qubits, and every exact Toffoli gate on four or more qubits requires an extra qubit. Gosset, Kothari and Zhang showed sampling a fresh random circuit makes T-count independent of gate size, but their direct sampler uses roughly one extra qubit per bit of precision. The work aims to remove these extra qubits.
AI.method: Compute the sampled parities in place, on the gate's own controls, rather than using a separate ancilla register. This lets each random circuit borrow only the gate's own idle inputs. The approach is extended to exclusive-ors of indicators of affine subspaces (equality tests, linear-equation checks).
AI.result: Once the gate is large enough, all extra qubits are removed: each random circuit uses ~8 T gates per bit of precision and borrows only the gate's own idle inputs—just one T gate more per circuit than the best measurement-free variant keeping one clean ancilla. For non-measuring randomized circuits this is within a factor of eight of optimal up to an additive constant, even with extra qubits. Closing the factor asymptotically is equivalent to determining the leading constant in the T-count of exact multi-controlled Toffoli gates. Additionally, the indicator of a random set of fixed density needs exponentially many T gates at constant error, while an affine subspace of the same density needs a constant number; extra qubits reduce the exponential cost only quadratically.
AI.conclusion: In-place parity computation removes ancilla overhead for large Toffoli and affine-subspace oracles, achieving near-optimal (~factor-eight) T-count for measurement-free randomized circuits. A sharp separation is shown between random-set and affine-subspace indicators, and the remaining asymptotic gap ties to the leading constant of exact multi-controlled Toffoli T-counts.

title: Barren Plateaus in Quantum Linear Combinations: Interference and Lie-Algebraic Control
summary: A coherent sum of quantum circuits introduces interference that can alter the training signal. We distinguish a single linear combination of unitaries (LCU) from a circuit that repeatedly alternates branch operations and ancilla mixing. For a single-pass LCU, independent branches with zero matrix means cannot erase the differentiated branch's gradient variance: the total variance is at least the branch variance times the fourth power of its coefficient magnitude. This bound holds at any gate position and does not require the circuit unitaries to be Haar-random. Beyond this lower bound, we derive exact loss and gradient formulas that quantify the additional contributions from interference between branches. One of these terms depends on relative coefficient phases and vanishes when the branch ensemble is invariant under multiplication by $i \mathbb{I}$; a four-qubit matchgate example shows that it can be nonzero. For repeated interleaving with full special-unitary ancilla control, we determine the generated Lie algebra from the associative algebra of the branches, including the available central phase directions. This control result predicts concentration only with additional assumptions on circuit sampling. Matchgate examples exhibit polynomial single-pass LCU variances and exponential concentration under joint Haar-random sampling. We also derive coefficient-selection rules and bounds for postselection, measurement error, and approximate moments.

AI.tldr: A coherent sum of quantum circuits creates interference that reshapes the training signal. The paper bounds gradient variance for single-pass linear combinations of unitaries (LCU): the total variance cannot drop below the differentiated branch's variance times the fourth power of its coefficient magnitude. It further derives exact loss/gradient interference terms, characterizes the Lie algebra generated by repeated branch-mixing, and shows matchgate examples with polynomial single-pass variance but exponential concentration under joint Haar sampling.
AI.motivation: Coherent (interferometric) sums of quantum circuits—LCUs and repeatedly interleaved branch/ancilla-mixing architectures—are increasingly used, but how interference affects trainability (gradient variance, barren plateaus, loss landscape) is poorly understood. The work aims to give rigorous, architecture-aware guarantees rather than generic concentration claims.
AI.method: Establishes a variance lower bound for single-pass LCU with zero-mean branches, requiring no Haar-randomness. Derives exact loss and gradient formulas isolating interference contributions, including a phase-dependent term vanishing under $i\mathbb{I}$-invariance of the branch ensemble, illustrated by a four-qubit matchgate example. For repeated interleaving with full special-unitary ancilla control, computes the generated Lie algebra from the associative algebra of branches, including central phase directions. Provides coefficient-selection rules and bounds for postselection, measurement error, and approximate moments.
AI.result: Single-pass LCU variance is at least the branch variance times $|c|^4$, valid at any gate position and without Haar assumptions. Exact interference terms are quantified, with one depending on relative coefficient phases and nonvanishing in a matchgate example. Repeated interleaving yields a Lie algebra determined by the branch associative algebra, predicting concentration only under additional sampling assumptions. Matchgate instances show polynomial single-pass variances yet exponential concentration under joint Haar-random sampling.
AI.conclusion: Interference in coherent circuit sums need not destroy the training signal in single-pass LCU settings, but repeated interleaving and joint-random sampling can induce barren plateaus. The results give architecture-specific, assumption-explicit criteria linking LCU structure, phase symmetries, and generated algebras to gradient behavior.

title: Noise Propagation and Effective Channels in Encrypted Quantum Cloning
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures; supplemental material included as an ancillary file
summary: We investigate noise propagation in encrypted quantum cloning by formulating the protocol in terms of effective recovery channels. For local single-qubit completely positive trace-preserving noise, a Pauli-basis expansion of the Kraus operators reveals a strong dependence on the location of the physical channel. Noise on an auxiliary signal qubit leaves the reduced recovered state unchanged, whereas noise on an auxiliary key qubit induces a Pauli-diagonal effective channel on the recovered qubit. For the core qubits, the error propagation additionally depends on the parity of the number of entangled pairs. In particular, for noise on the core key qubit with odd parity, distinct physical Pauli sectors merge into the same effective sector, converting isotropic depolarizing noise into an anisotropic recovery channel. We also relate Werner-type resource imperfections to local depolarizing noise and distinguish distributed product depolarization from genuine global depolarization. The results demonstrate that the effective recovery noise is governed not only by noise strength, but also by its physical location and by the structure of the encryption-decryption protocol.

AI.tldr: Noise propagation in encrypted quantum cloning is analyzed via effective recovery channels; error behavior depends strongly on the noise's physical location and on parity of entangled pairs, with odd-parity core-key noise merging Pauli sectors and converting isotropic depolarization into anisotropic recovery.
AI.motivation: Understand how local noise propagates through the encryption-decryption protocol of encrypted quantum cloning, and characterize the resulting effective recovery noise beyond a simple dependence on noise strength.
AI.method: Formulate the protocol in terms of effective recovery channels. For local single-qubit CPTP noise, perform a Pauli-basis expansion of the Kraus operators and analyze how noise at each qubit location (auxiliary signal, auxiliary key, core signal, core key) maps to the recovered qubit. Also relate Werner-type resource imperfections to local depolarizing noise and distinguish distributed product depolarization from genuine global depolarization.
AI.result: Noise on the auxiliary signal qubit leaves the reduced recovered state unchanged; noise on the auxiliary key qubit induces a Pauli-diagonal effective channel. For core qubits, error propagation depends additionally on the parity of the number of entangled pairs; for odd-parity noise on the core key qubit, distinct physical Pauli sectors merge into the same effective sector, turning isotropic depolarizing noise into an anisotropic recovery channel. Werner-type imperfections map to local depolarizing noise, and distributed product depolarization is distinguished from genuine global depolarization.
AI.conclusion: Effective recovery noise is governed not only by noise strength but also by its physical location and by the structure of the encryption-decryption protocol.

title: Active Approach to Fast Quantum State Preparation and Reset in Atomic Arrays
summary: Rapid preparation of a target quantum state and reset to the many-body ground state are essential for quantum information processing. Here, we investigate both processes in a waveguide-coupled emitter array in the low-excitation regime. By decomposing the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian into biorthogonal eigenmodes, we show that relaxation depends on the initial overlap with the more subradiant modes, providing a modal explanation of the Mpemba effect. Guided by this insight, we design a reset protocol in which a finite-duration local drive activelysuppresses the relatively slow-decaying components. For the parameters studied, this reduces the time to reach a fixed residual-excitation threshold by up to approximately 25% compared with free decay. To prepare a target Dicke state, we introduce a two-step protocol that initially leaves one emitter undriven before restoring the full drive that stabilizes the target. This local control redistributes spectral weight into the more subradiant modes, driving them closer to their target amplitudes, which reduces the preparation time by up to approximately 45% while consuming less driving energy than continuous driving. Finally, we show how directional waveguide coupling shifts collective modes toward a preferred boundary through the non-Hermitian skin effect, providing guidance for selecting the preferred site for local operations. We term this fundamental dependence of the relaxation dynamics on the system's chirality the ``non-Hermitian Skin-Mpemba effect.'' These results demonstrate how selective local control can accelerate state preparation and reset in open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: In a waveguide-coupled emitter array, decomposing the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian into biorthogonal eigenmodes explains relaxation via overlap with subradiant modes (a modal Mpemba effect). Exploiting this, local drives accelerate ground-state reset by ~25% and, via a two-step protocol, Dicke-state preparation by ~45% with lower energy cost; directional coupling further shifts modes via the non-Hermitian skin effect.
AI.motivation: Fast preparation of target quantum states and reset to the many-body ground state are critical for quantum information processing, yet the dynamics governing relaxation and preparation in open, waveguide-coupled emitter arrays are not fully understood, limiting the design of efficient control protocols.
AI.method: Decompose the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian of a low-excitation waveguide-coupled emitter array into biorthogonal eigenmodes; relate relaxation to initial overlap with subradiant modes; design a finite-duration local drive that suppresses slow-decaying components; introduce a two-step Dicke-state preparation protocol that leaves one emitter undriven then restores full drive; analyze directional waveguide coupling through the non-Hermitian skin effect.
AI.result: The reset protocol reduces time to reach a fixed residual-excitation threshold by up to ~25% versus free decay. The two-step Dicke-state protocol reduces preparation time by up to ~45% while consuming less driving energy than continuous driving. Directional coupling shifts collective modes toward a preferred boundary, guiding local-operation site selection.
AI.conclusion: Relaxation dynamics in open quantum systems are fundamentally governed by modal overlap and chirality, which the authors term the "non-Hermitian Skin-Mpemba effect." Selective local control leveraging this dependence accelerates state preparation and reset, offering a practical route to optimized control in waveguide-QED platforms.

title: Maximally-Matched Mixture Decoding for Correlated Atom Loss in Quantum LDPC Codes
summary: Heralded atom loss is a dominant noise channel in neutral atom quantum computing platforms, and losses at a two-qubit gate are strongly correlated: when one atom is lost, its gate partner is often lost too. This work shows how to exploit this correlation to construct a better decoder, focusing on [[144,12,12]] Gross code syndrome extraction circuits. Given a loss readout, the possible pairings of the lost qubits according to shared gates form a graph whose maximum matchings carry almost all of the conditional probability mass. Our maximal-matching-mixture (MMM) decoder builds a per-readout decoding hypergraph as a weighted mixture over exactly these loss scenarios. This decoding hypergraph can be used by an ordinary belief-propagation decoder. On the [[144,12,12]] Gross code, MMM lowers the logical error rate by as much as ~25x relative to a loss-unaware decoder and ~2x relative to a loss-aware uniform-mixture baseline from Baranes et al. (2026).

AI.tldr: Heralded atom loss is the dominant noise channel in neutral-atom quantum computing, and two-qubit-gate losses are strongly correlated. The paper exploits this correlation to build a maximal-matching-mixture (MMM) decoder for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code, reducing logical error rates by up to ~25x versus a loss-unaware decoder and ~2x versus a uniform-mixture loss-aware baseline.
AI.motivation: Atom loss is a dominant noise source in neutral-atom quantum platforms. Losses at two-qubit gates are strongly correlated: when one atom is lost, its gate partner is often lost too. Standard loss-unaware decoders ignore this structure, and even loss-aware uniform-mixture baselines do not exploit the correlation fully, leaving logical error suppression on the table.
AI.method: Given a loss readout, the possible pairings of lost qubits according to shared gates form a graph whose maximum matchings carry almost all of the conditional probability mass. The MMM decoder constructs a per-readout decoding hypergraph as a weighted mixture over exactly these maximum-matching loss scenarios. The resulting hypergraph is then passed to an ordinary belief-propagation decoder. Evaluation focuses on syndrome-extraction circuits for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code.
AI.result: On the [[144,12,12]] Gross code, MMM lowers the logical error rate by as much as ~25x relative to a loss-unaware decoder and ~2x relative to the loss-aware uniform-mixture baseline of Baranes et al. (2026).
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the strong correlation of two-qubit-gate atom losses—via a maximum-matching-weighted mixture of loss scenarios—yields a substantially better decoder for neutral-atom quantum error correction, and the approach is compatible with standard belief-propagation decoding.

title: Schur$\unicode{x2013}$Weyl Reduction of Finite-Copy Precision Bounds for Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
summary: In multiparameter quantum estimation, incompatible measurements can impose trade-offs among estimation errors. Understanding the precision attainable with a finite number of jointly measured copies is therefore important, but direct optimization becomes costly as the tensor product space grows exponentially. For independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) copies, the quantum statistical model is invariant under permutations of the copies. We exploit this symmetry through Schur--Weyl duality to remove permutation multiplicity spaces while using their dimensions as weights. This gives a reduced statistical model equivalent to the original under arbitrary collective measurements. On this reduced model, we derive an exact conic formulation of the tight Cramér--Rao bound and a semidefinite program for its Nagaoka--Hayashi (NH) relaxation. For fixed single-copy dimension, the reduced operator representation grows polynomially rather than exponentially with the number of copies. To approximate the tight bound, we use an exact quadratic identity to correct finite-ray dual solutions and obtain rigorous upper and lower bounds. For fixed copy number and parameter dimension, sufficiently fine meshes admit feasible primal points, and dual solutions with bounded objective gaps have uniformly bounded compact-search radii. These results yield quadratic convergence in the projective covering radius. Numerical examples illustrate the quadratic scaling of the mesh correction term and the computational reach of the reduced NH formulation.

AI.tldr: Exploiting Schur–Weyl symmetry reduces the i.i.d. multiparameter quantum estimation model polynomially in copy number, enabling exact conic and SDP formulations of the tight CRB and NH relaxation, with mesh-based certified bounds converging quadratically.
AI.motivation: Incompatible measurements in multiparameter quantum estimation impose trade-offs among estimation errors, so characterizing precision with a finite number of jointly measured copies matters. However, directly optimizing over collective measurements on the exponentially growing tensor-product space is computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: Uses permutation symmetry of i.i.d. copies via Schur–Weyl duality to eliminate multiplicity spaces, keeping their dimensions as weights, yielding a reduced statistical model equivalent to the original under arbitrary collective measurements. On this model, derives an exact conic formulation of the tight Cramér–Rao bound and a semidefinite program for its Nagaoka–Hayashi relaxation. Approximates the tight bound via an exact quadratic identity correcting finite-ray dual solutions to obtain rigorous upper and lower bounds.
AI.result: For fixed single-copy dimension, the reduced operator representation scales polynomially (not exponentially) in copy number. For fixed copy number and parameter dimension, sufficiently fine meshes admit feasible primal points, and dual solutions with bounded objective gaps have uniformly bounded compact-search radii, giving quadratic convergence in the projective covering radius. Numerical examples confirm quadratic scaling of the mesh correction term and the computational reach of the reduced NH formulation.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry reduction via Schur–Weyl duality makes finite-copy multiparameter quantum metrology computationally tractable, and mesh-based corrections to dual solutions yield certified, quadratically convergent approximations to the tight quantum Cramér–Rao bound.

title: Strict Frequency Bandwidths from Causal Light Cones Enable Scalable Exact Gradient Evaluation in Quantum Optimization
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables, including Appendices A-F
summary: Dynamical locality is often regarded as a limitation of shallow quantum circuits, yet we show that it can reduce the number of circuit settings required for exact evaluation of gradients with respect to shared parameters. For layered ansatze generated by commuting local terms, strict Heisenberg light cones confine energy slices obtained by varying one shared layer parameter to finite Fourier bandwidths dictated by local causal geometry. This bandlimit recasts exact gradient evaluation as a local signal recovery problem and, when the relevant frequencies lie on a known frequency lattice, yields an exact multipoint parameter-shift rule based on the discrete sine transform. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) provides a canonical realization in which this mechanism is governed by the local structure of the graph. Specifically, when a cost angle is varied, the relevant geometry is encoded by the contact region in the interaction line graph. At fixed circuit depth on graphs of bounded degree, the number of distinct circuit settings required for the corresponding derivative collapses from $O(m)$ to $O(1)$. This shows that dynamical locality is not merely a constraint on correlation propagation, but also a computational resource that enables exact gradient evaluation with fewer circuit settings in quantum optimization.

AI.tldr: Dynamical locality, usually seen as a limitation of shallow circuits, is shown to reduce the number of distinct circuit settings needed for exact gradients w.r.t. shared parameters by exploiting finite Fourier bandwidths of energy slices.
AI.motivation: Gradient evaluation via parameter-shift rules typically requires many distinct circuit settings, scaling as O(m) in the number of terms. The authors argue dynamical locality (strict Heisenberg light cones) can be reframed from a constraint into a computational resource to cut this cost.
AI.method: For layered ansätze built from commuting local terms, varying one shared layer parameter confines the resulting energy slice to a finite Fourier bandwidth set by local causal geometry. This bandlimit turns exact gradient evaluation into a local signal-recovery problem; when frequencies lie on a known lattice, an exact multipoint parameter-shift rule based on the discrete sine transform is derived. QAOA is used as the canonical instance, where the relevant geometry is encoded by the contact region in the interaction line graph.
AI.result: For QAOA at fixed depth on bounded-degree graphs, the number of distinct circuit settings required for the derivative of a cost angle collapses from O(m) to O(1), governed by the local contact-region structure of the interaction line graph.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical locality is not only a restriction on correlation propagation but also a computational resource enabling exact gradient evaluation with fewer circuit settings in quantum optimization.

title: Einstein Metrics and Quantum Control on Symmetric Tensor Product Quotients
summary: Let $M_n=(\mathrm{PU}(2)^n\rtimes S_n)\backslash\mathrm{PU}(2^n)$ be the space of projective $n$-qubit unitaries modulo local unitaries and permutations of the qubits. We prove that for all sufficiently large $n$ the manifold $M_n$ carries exactly two $\mathrm{PU}(2^n)$-invariant Einstein metrics up to scaling. Both Einstein metrics have uniformly bounded diameter after normalizing two-qubit costs, although approximating a Haar-random unitary requires exponentially many two-qubit gates. In contrast, we construct non-Einstein metrics with nonnegative Ricci curvature and exponentially growing typical control distances, and determine the sharp curvature threshold for this family.

AI.tldr: For large n, the quotient space M_n of n-qubit projective unitaries modulo local unitaries and qubit permutations carries exactly two invariant Einstein metrics up to scaling; both have uniformly bounded normalized diameter despite Haar-random unitaries needing exponentially many two-qubit gates, and non-Einstein nonnegative-Ricci metrics with exponentially growing control distances exist, with a sharp curvature threshold.
AI.motivation: The paper studies the geometry of the space of n-qubit unitaries modulo local operations and qubit permutations, connecting invariant Einstein metrics to quantum gate complexity (control distances) and to how curvature constrains the typical cost of implementing random unitaries.
AI.method: Riemannian/ homogeneous-space analysis of M_n = (PU(2)^n ⋊ S_n)\PU(2^n): classify PU(2^n)-invariant Einstein metrics via the quotient geometry, analyze normalized two-qubit costs and typical control distances under these metrics, and construct a family of non-Einstein metrics with nonnegative Ricci curvature, computing the sharp curvature threshold for this family.
AI.result: Exactly two invariant Einstein metrics exist on M_n for all sufficiently large n (up to scaling). Both have uniformly bounded diameter after normalizing two-qubit costs, even though a Haar-random unitary requires exponentially many two-qubit gates. Non-Einstein metrics with nonnegative Ricci curvature and exponentially growing typical control distances are constructed, and the sharp curvature threshold for this family is determined.
AI.conclusion: Einstein geometry of the unitary quotient does not reflect gate complexity: bounded normalized diameter coexists with exponential circuit cost, while relaxing the Einstein condition (keeping nonnegative Ricci curvature) yields exponential typical control distances up to a sharp curvature bound.

title: Symmetry-Preserving Hierarchical Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm with Subproblems Beyond the Qubit Limit
summary: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a paradigmatic variational quantum algorithm for combinatorial optimization problems, yet on current quantum devices the available qubit count and achievable circuit depth remain the main bottlenecks to its practical application. Divide-and-merge reduces the number of variables encoded in a single quantum circuit, while contraction based on coarse graining extends the effective range of shallow circuits, but existing work has not addressed both challenges simultaneously. We propose symmetry-preserving hierarchical QAOA (SP-HQAOA), in which parity sector contraction preserves the zero-field Ising structure of the effective objective at every contraction step, thereby addressing both within a single algorithm. We further prove that this reduction is the unique one with this property. Successive contractions further decouple the maximum leaf block size $B$ from the qubit limit $Q$ per quantum call, so every quantum circuit uses at most $Q$ qubits even when $B>Q$. We also establish a deterministic repair-risk bound on the possible loss in optimal value caused by each sector restriction, and the resulting bounds can be summed across contraction steps and levels of the recursive hierarchy. With depth $p=1$, SP-HQAOA attains $99.4\%$ to $99.7\%$ of the exact optimum on $N=40$ random regular MaxCut leaf blocks and, with at most $10$ qubits per circuit, $96\%$ of the classical reference for $N=500$. SP-HQAOA demonstrates the capacity to use shallow quantum circuits to address combinatorial optimization problems whose variable count far exceeds the qubit limit of a single quantum call, and may enable practical quantum optimization advantages in the near term.

AI.tldr: SP-HQAOA is a symmetry-preserving hierarchical QAOA that uses parity-sector contraction to handle qubit-count and circuit-depth bottlenecks simultaneously, with provable uniqueness and repair-risk bounds.
AI.motivation: QAOA is bottlenecked by limited qubit count and achievable circuit depth on current devices. Divide-and-merge reduces variables per circuit, and coarse-graining contraction extends effective range of shallow circuits, but prior work does not address both simultaneously.
AI.method: Parity sector contraction that preserves the zero-field Ising structure of the effective objective at every contraction step; proof that this reduction is unique with this property; successive contractions decouple maximum leaf block size B from per-call qubit limit Q, so each circuit uses at most Q qubits even when B>Q; deterministic repair-risk bound on optimal-value loss from each sector restriction, summable across contraction steps and recursion levels.
AI.result: At depth p=1, SP-HQAOA reaches 99.4%–99.7% of the exact optimum on N=40 random regular MaxCut leaf blocks, and 96% of the classical reference for N=500 using at most 10 qubits per circuit.
AI.conclusion: SP-HQAOA enables shallow quantum circuits to tackle combinatorial optimization problems whose variable count far exceeds the qubit limit of a single quantum call, potentially enabling near-term practical quantum optimization advantages.

title: Quantum change point metrology
summary: We quantify the extra Bayes risk of locating a quantum change point and estimating its amplitude with one measurement. The joint and marginal optimizations use the full record and the same joint prior, with both parameters unknown. For product records on a known pure state curve, position has clipped absolute loss in resolution units, and amplitude offset has squared loss in fixed calibrated units. Ideal steps exhibit certified conflict at finite signal strength, including in phase records of sixteen qubits, and recover both informative marginal optima at strong signal. For finite offset prior width, a retained quantum boundary region serves position, and the remaining suffix serves amplitude. Physical recovery holds when strength grows more slowly than the square root of record length. Known smooth rises also admit leading recovery in the coherent experiment as strength grows and width shrinks. For the quintic profile, we establish two residual cost scaling laws. The residual cost is $Θ(s^{-2})$ as $s\to\infty$. Taking the strong signal limit at fixed $w$ yields a limiting cost of $Θ(w^3)$ as $w\to0$. In the resolved local model, quadratic position loss admits a common optimum within the covariant class. These results link onset geometry and decision loss to Bayesian measurement compatibility in quantum change point estimation.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies the extra Bayes risk of jointly locating a quantum change point and estimating its amplitude from a single measurement, showing that joint and marginal optimizations using the same full-record prior provably conflict at finite signal strength, yet recover both informative marginal optima at strong signal, with explicit scaling laws for the residual cost.
AI.motivation: Joint estimation of a change point's position and amplitude is typically done with a single measurement, but it is unclear whether the single optimal measurement for the joint task agrees with the measurements that are individually optimal for position or amplitude. The paper aims to quantify the extra Bayes risk incurred by this trade-off and characterize when joint and marginal optimizations are compatible.
AI.method: The authors formulate a Bayesian joint estimation problem over product records on a known pure-state curve, with both position and amplitude unknown under a shared joint prior. Position is scored with clipped absolute loss in resolution units and amplitude offset with squared loss in fixed calibrated units. They compare joint versus marginal optimizations on the full record, certify conflict at finite signal strength (including 16-qubit phase records), and analyze regimes: finite offset-prior width (a retained quantum boundary region serves position, the suffix serves amplitude), strong-signal limits, smooth rising profiles, and a resolved local model with a covariant measurement class.
AI.result: Ideal steps exhibit certified conflict at finite signal strength, including in 16-qubit phase records, and recover both informative marginal optima at strong signal. For finite offset-prior width, a retained quantum boundary region serves position while the remaining suffix serves amplitude; physical recovery holds when signal strength grows more slowly than the square root of record length. Known smooth rises admit leading recovery in the coherent experiment as strength grows and width shrinks. For the quintic profile, residual cost scales as Θ(s^{-2}) as s→∞ and, taking the strong-signal limit at fixed w, as Θ(w^3) as w→0. In the resolved local model, quadratic position loss admits a common optimum within the covariant class.
AI.conclusion: Joint and marginal Bayesian optimizations for quantum change point estimation are not generally compatible: they conflict at finite signal strength but converge at strong signal. The residual cost obeys explicit scaling laws tied to onset geometry and decision loss, linking the geometry of the change onset and the choice of loss to Bayesian measurement compatibility.

title: Spectral Reduction Selects the Observable Imprint of Dirac Quantum Geometry
summary: Spectral constraints can alter the observable manifestation of quantum geometry without changing the local eigenspace. Relativistic electron vortices provide a sharp example: the spin orbit interaction redistributes spin and orbital angular momentum, yet its magnetic contribution differs between localized three-dimensional wave packets and stationary monochromatic beams. We resolve this discrepancy by showing that fixing the energy replaces ambient momentum derivatives in position-weighted current moments by shell-tangent derivatives and derive a Hermitian selection rule for first-order observables in momentum-dependent internal subspaces. Its extension-independent form applies beyond Dirac systems, including a broad class of antisymmetric first moments of scalar-charge velocity currents. For the free positive-energy Dirac doublet, the magnetic correction is an exact non-Abelian Berry-curvature contraction with a pointwise saturable quantum-metric bound. Changing the relative phase between the two $σ_z$ spinor components switches this correction from zero in a conserved transverse-helicity sector to a finite value in a radial coherent superposition. At fixed finite Lorentz factor, the radial response scales as $O(θ/γ)$, compared with $O(θ^2)$ for longitudinal polarization. Spectral reduction and internal coherence thus provide distinct controls of the observable imprint of quantum geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves an apparent discrepancy in the magnetic contribution to relativistic electron vortices stemming from the spin-orbit interaction, showing that energy constraints replace ambient momentum derivatives with shell-tangent derivatives and yielding a Hermitian selection rule for first-order observables in momentum-dependent internal subspaces.
AI.motivation: Spectral constraints can change the observable imprint of quantum geometry without altering the local eigenspace. Relativistic electron vortices exemplify this: spin-orbit interaction redistributes spin and orbital angular momentum, but its magnetic contribution differs between localized 3D wave packets and stationary monochromatic beams, motivating a principled resolution of this discrepancy.
AI.method: Fixing the energy replaces ambient momentum derivatives in position-weighted current moments with shell-tangent derivatives; the authors derive a Hermitian selection rule for first-order observables in momentum-dependent internal subspaces, formulated in an extension-independent way applicable beyond Dirac systems (including antisymmetric first moments of scalar-charge velocity currents). For the free positive-energy Dirac doublet, they characterize the magnetic correction as an exact non-Abelian Berry-curvature contraction with a pointwise saturable quantum-metric bound, and analyze phase-dependent effects.
AI.result: For the free positive-energy Dirac doublet, the magnetic correction is an exact non-Abelian Berry-curvature contraction obeying a pointwise saturable quantum-metric bound. Changing the relative phase between the two σ_z spinor components switches the correction from zero (conserved transverse-helicity sector) to finite (radial coherent superposition). At fixed finite Lorentz factor, the radial response scales as O(θ/γ) versus O(θ²) for longitudinal polarization.
AI.conclusion: Spectral reduction and internal coherence provide distinct, complementary controls over the observable imprint of quantum geometry. The energy-fixed shell-tangent framework and Hermitian selection rule are general and extend beyond Dirac systems.

title: Fermionic Unruh effect revisited: Entanglement and correlation dynamics under symmetric transformations
summary: A uniformly accelerated observer perceives the Minkowski vacuum as a thermal bath, so acceleration acts as a noise channel on correlations shared with an inertial partner. For a Dirac field in the standard treatment, the resulting map is a one-sided amplitude-damping channel, and entanglement and quantum discord survive at infinite acceleration. We introduce a symmetric Unruh-like map in which the vacuum and the one-particle state both exchange amplitude with the inaccessible Rindler region; for a Bell state it yields a bit-flip channel whose flip probability is the Fermi-Dirac occupation at the Unruh temperature. Using negativity, mutual information, and all six pairwise quantum discords, we find that the entanglement and discord between the inertial observer and the accessible mode vanish together at infinite acceleration, leaving only one bit of classical correlation. These results show that the fate of quantum correlations in noninertial frames depends on the structure of the Minkowski-Rindler map.

AI.tldr: A symmetric Unruh-like channel, unlike the standard one-sided amplitude-damping channel, causes entanglement and discord between an inertial observer and the accessible Rindler mode to vanish together at infinite acceleration, leaving only one bit of classical correlation.
AI.motivation: In the standard treatment the Minkowski-Rindler map for a Dirac field is a one-sided amplitude-damping channel, under which entanglement and discord famously survive at infinite acceleration. The authors question whether this survival is a robust physical fact or an artifact of that particular map's structure, and therefore examine how the fate of quantum correlations depends on the Minkowski-Rindler map used.
AI.method: They introduce a symmetric Unruh-like map in which both the vacuum and the one-particle state exchange amplitude with the inaccessible Rindler region. For a Bell state this yields a bit-flip channel whose flip probability equals the Fermi-Dirac occupation at the Unruh temperature. Quantum correlations are then quantified using negativity, mutual information, and all six pairwise quantum discords between the inertial observer and the accessible mode.
AI.result: Under the symmetric map, both the entanglement (negativity) and all pairwise discords between the inertial observer and the accessible mode vanish together in the infinite-acceleration limit, while one bit of classical correlation remains.
AI.conclusion: The fate of quantum correlations in noninertial frames is not universal but depends on the structure of the Minkowski-Rindler map; the survival of entanglement and discord at infinite acceleration in the standard treatment is tied to its one-sided amplitude-damping form.

title: Robustness of Magic and the Directed Geometry of State Conversion
summary: In this work, we introduce a state-space distance calibrated by stabilizer states based on the dual structure of the robustness of magic (RoM), and show that RoM is exactly represented as the distance to the free-state set. We then extend this geometry to state conversion by defining the directed conversion deficiency $C_{\mathcal F}$ as the distance between a target state and the set of states freely reachable from a given input state. The quantity $C_{\mathcal F}$ characterizes free convertibility and is related to the minimum stabilizer quasiprobability weight required to represent the conversion residual through the relation $1+2C_{\mathcal F}$. It also contains the conventional magic state resource lower bounds based on RoM and can detect stronger conversion obstructions. For single-qubit systems, we analytically construct a continuous family of mixed states with identical RoM but asymmetric convertibility.

AI.tldr: This work builds a geometry of magic (nonstabilizerness) based on the dual structure of the robustness of magic (RoM), showing RoM equals the distance to the stabilizer (free-state) set, and extends this geometry to state conversion via a directed conversion deficiency that characterizes free convertibility and yields stronger resource bounds.
AI.motivation: Magic (nonstabilizerness) is a key resource for universal quantum computation, and RoM is a standard quantifier. The authors aim to give RoM a clear geometric interpretation as a distance to the free-state set and to extend this geometry from static quantification to state conversion, addressing conversion obstructions that conventional RoM-based lower bounds may miss.
AI.method: The authors introduce a state-space distance calibrated by stabilizer states, constructed from the dual structure of the robustness of magic, and prove RoM is exactly represented as the distance to the free-state set. They extend this geometry to state conversion by defining the directed conversion deficiency C_F as the distance between a target state and the set of states freely reachable from a given input state; they relate C_F to the minimum stabilizer quasiprobability weight (via 1+2C_F) needed to represent the conversion residual, and analytically construct, for single-qubit systems, a continuous family of mixed states with identical RoM but asymmetric convertibility.
AI.result: RoM is exactly represented as a distance to the free-state set. The directed conversion deficiency C_F characterizes free convertibility, is tied to the minimum stabilizer quasiprobability weight through 1+2C_F, contains conventional RoM-based magic-state resource lower bounds, and detects stronger conversion obstructions. For single-qubit systems, a continuous family of mixed states with identical RoM but asymmetric convertibility is constructed analytically.
AI.conclusion: The dual-structure stabilizer-calibrated distance provides an exact geometric representation of RoM and, through the directed conversion deficiency, a conversion-theoretic tool that subsumes prior RoM-based bounds and reveals stronger obstructions, including asymmetric convertibility among states of equal RoM.

title: Controllability-Based Input Allocation in Quantum System
summary: Understanding how local perturbations influence global quantum dynamics is important for analyzing and designing large-scale quantum systems. Existing quantum centrality measures often rely on static correlations or entanglement and do not directly capture perturbation propagation under unitary evolution. We formulate controllability allocation scoring for quantum input-output dynamics governed by the Schrodinger equation. Using the multiobservable quantum-control Gramian, we introduce virtual local Hamiltonian perturbations along a nominal trajectory and decompose the terminal-output response into channel-wise Gramian contributions. A simplex-constrained log-determinant optimization combines these contributions to define a volumetric controllability allocation score (V-CAS), specifying an optimal allocation of virtual input intensities among local Hamiltonian perturbation directions. The score measures their cooperative dynamical influence and depends on the output and trajectory. We characterize the output Gramian's range and minimum-energy properties and derive a drift-independent sufficient condition ensuring score uniqueness for almost every terminal time at which the problem is feasible. For quantum many-body systems, we develop a matrix-product-state and time-evolving-block-decimation implementation that avoids explicitly constructing exponentially large state-transition matrices. We also derive an error bound propagating Trotter and MPS-truncation errors to the discrete output Gramian. Numerical experiments show that the score captures finite-time influence patterns distinct from those identified by static correlation- and entanglement-based measures and can inform target-independent control-channel preselection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a volumetric controllability allocation score (V-CAS) that quantifies how local Hamiltonian perturbations influence terminal outputs under unitary Schrödinger evolution, using a multiobservable quantum-control Gramian and a simplex-constrained log-determinant optimization, with an MPS/TEBD implementation and error bounds for many-body systems.
AI.motivation: Local perturbations' influence on global quantum dynamics is key for analyzing and designing large-scale quantum systems, but existing quantum centrality measures rely on static correlations or entanglement and fail to capture perturbation propagation under unitary evolution.
AI.method: Formulates controllability allocation scoring for quantum input-output dynamics from the Schrödinger equation. Uses the multiobservable quantum-control Gramian, injects virtual local Hamiltonian perturbations along a nominal trajectory, and decomposes the terminal-output response into channel-wise Gramian contributions. A simplex-constrained log-determinant optimization over these contributions defines V-CAS, an optimal allocation of virtual input intensities across local perturbation directions. Output Gramian range and minimum-energy properties are characterized, a drift-independent sufficient condition for score uniqueness is derived, and an MPS+TEBD implementation with a Trotter/MPS-truncation error bound on the discrete output Gramian is developed.
AI.result: V-CAS measures cooperative dynamical influence dependent on output and trajectory; uniqueness holds for almost every feasible terminal time under the derived condition. Numerical experiments show the score captures finite-time influence patterns distinct from static correlation- and entanglement-based measures and supports target-independent control-channel preselection.
AI.conclusion: V-CAS provides a trajectory- and output-dependent, Gramian-based allocation framework for capturing perturbation propagation in unitary quantum dynamics, scalable to many-body systems via MPS/TEBD, and useful for control-channel preselection.

title: Harnessing Non-Markovian Memory for Quantum-Battery Capacity
summary: Non-Markovianity is commonly characterized through information-theoretic signatures of memory. Here we take a thermodynamic perspective and ask whether such memory can be operationally harnessed to enhance quantum-battery capacity. Within the process-tensor framework, we compare memoryless and memory-enhanced strategies and define their performance gap as the memory-assisted capacity advantage of a multitime process. We prove that this advantage vanishes for Markovian process tensors and is bounded by a trace-distance measure of process non-Markovianity. In a complementary continuous-time setting, we show using random telegraph dephasing that memory accumulated during the evolution can enhance capacity retention relative to a matched Markovian reference under the same control class. These results identify non-Markovian memory as an operational resource for quantum-battery capacity.

AI.tldr: The paper casts non-Markovianity as an operational thermodynamic resource, showing that memory in a multitime quantum process can be harnessed to enhance quantum-battery capacity.
AI.motivation: Non-Markovianity is usually described via information-theoretic memory witnesses, but it is unclear whether such memory has operational value. The authors ask whether non-Markovian memory can be exploited to boost quantum-battery capacity.
AI.method: Using the process-tensor framework, they compare memoryless versus memory-enhanced strategies and define the memory-assisted capacity advantage of a multitime process. They prove this advantage vanishes for Markovian process tensors and is bounded by a trace-distance measure of process non-Markovianity; complementarily, they analyze a continuous-time random-telegraph dephasing model under a fixed control class.
AI.result: The memory-assisted capacity advantage is zero for Markovian process tensors and upper-bounded by a trace-distance non-Markovianity measure. In the continuous-time random-telegraph dephasing setting, memory accumulated during evolution enhances capacity retention relative to a matched Markovian reference under the same control class.
AI.conclusion: Non-Markovian memory is an operational resource for quantum-battery capacity, with its benefit quantitatively linked to a process non-Markovianity measure.

title: Coherent errors, syndrome extraction and the Robustness of Magic in stabiliser codes
summary: Coherent errors leave stabiliser-code-encoded magic states in superpositions of syndrome sectors. We ask how much magic these coherent errors add, and whether syndrome extraction depletes logical magic. Using Robustness of Magic, we show that, for a unitary error U on a correctable region which supports no stabiliser, the encoded state has the same robustness as the logical state plus one copy of the Choi state of U , in every stabiliser code encoding. Syndrome extraction removes this copy, returning the logical robustness. The removed magic is positive for every non-Clifford error: adding a non-stabiliser state to any state multiplies one plus the robustness by a (tightly- bounded) factor above one. The magic capacity of two-qubit gates Clifford-equivalent to diagonal or single-qubit gates is equal to their Choi-state robustness. We give a linear-algebraic test for when a Clifford error makes syndrome extraction measure a logical operator, and give magic lifetimes of stored single-qubit magic states under Pauli noise. Choosing the plane of the stored state extends these lifetimes about 1.5x on rotated surface codes under low code-capacity depolarising noise. We identify states and channels in odd-prime dimension for which Wigner negativity and robustness show equal lifetimes.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies how coherent errors affect the magic of encoded states and whether syndrome extraction depletes it, using Robustness of Magic (RoM). It proves the encoded magic equals the logical state's robustness plus one copy of the error's Choi-state robustness, and that syndrome extraction removes exactly this copy.
AI.motivation: Coherent (unitary) errors push stabiliser-code-encoded magic states into superpositions across syndrome sectors, raising the question of how much extra magic such errors introduce and whether syndrome extraction depletes logical magic. The authors seek a precise accounting of this magic to understand error-resilient magic-state storage and the magic cost of gates and noise.
AI.method: Using Robustness of Magic, they analyse a unitary error U acting on a correctable region supporting no stabiliser. They derive the encoded-state robustness in any stabiliser code, characterise the magic lost to syndrome extraction, bound the magic added by non-stabiliser states, compute the magic capacity of Clifford-equivalent two-qubit gates, give a linear-algebraic test for when a Clifford error causes syndrome extraction to measure a logical operator, and simulate magic lifetimes under Pauli and depolarising noise (including rotated surface codes).
AI.result: For a correctable-region unitary U with no stabiliser support, the encoded state's robustness equals the logical state's robustness plus one copy of U's Choi-state robustness, in every stabiliser encoding; syndrome extraction removes this copy and restores the logical robustness. The removed magic is positive for every non-Clifford error, with the added robustness bounded by a tight factor above one. Magic capacity of diagonal/single-qubit Clifford-equivalent two-qubit gates equals their Choi-state robustness. Choosing the stored state's plane extends magic lifetimes ~1.5x on rotated surface codes under low code-capacity depolarising noise. States/channels in odd-prime dimension are identified where Wigner negativity and robustness show equal lifetimes.
AI.conclusion: Syndrome extraction acts as a magic filter: it charges the code exactly the Choi-state magic of a coherent error, leaving the logical robustness intact. This gives a clean accounting of magic under coherent errors and gates, and provides practical recipes (e.g., plane choice) to extend stored-magic lifetimes.

title: Learning Grover mixers for constrained optimization
summary: Grover-Mixer QAOA (GM-QAOA) is a promising quantum framework for constrained combinatorial optimization. However, its practical implementation requires the efficient preparation of a uniform superposition over feasible states. In this work, we propose a two-stage variational approach. First, a parameterized quantum circuit is trained to prepare this superposition, using an entropy-based cost function that favors a uniform distribution over feasible bitstrings. The trained circuit is then embedded in GM-QAOA, where it provides both the initial state and, together with its inverse, yields the Grover mixer. The resulting method is evaluated on two representative benchmark problems: the Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) problem and the Multidimensional Knapsack Problem (MKP). While the results demonstrate consistent improvements over standard QAOA for MWIS, only marginal gains are observed for MKP, with the advantage diminishing as the problem size increases. The reduced performance on MKP reflects the growing difficulty of training the variational mixer, likely due to increasingly challenging optimization landscapes. Overall, these findings highlight both the potential of variational Grover mixers and the trade-off between their performance gains and the additional resources required for their training.

AI.tldr: A two-stage variational approach trains a parameterized circuit to prepare a uniform superposition over feasible states (entropy-based cost), then embeds it in GM-QAOA as both initial state and Grover mixer; consistent gains on MWIS but only marginal, size-shrinking gains on MKP.
AI.motivation: GM-QAOA is promising for constrained combinatorial optimization, but its practical use requires efficient preparation of a uniform superposition over feasible states—a nontrivial prerequisite.
AI.method: Stage 1: train a parameterized quantum circuit to prepare the uniform feasible-state superposition using an entropy-based cost function favoring uniform distributions over feasible bitstrings. Stage 2: embed the trained circuit in GM-QAOA, providing the initial state and, with its inverse, the Grover mixer. Evaluated on MWIS and MKP benchmarks.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over standard QAOA for MWIS; only marginal gains for MKP, with the advantage diminishing as problem size increases. Reduced MKP performance is attributed to growing difficulty of training the variational mixer, likely from harder optimization landscapes.
AI.conclusion: Variational Grover mixers show potential, but there is a trade-off between performance gains and the additional training resources required; scalability of mixer training is the key limitation.

title: Pulse-Informed Physical Placement for Parallel Two-Qubit Gates in Qubit Arrays
summary: A parallel two-qubit layer can often be realized with several nonoverlapping sets of physical couplers, but isolated calibrations do not reveal how each realization performs after optimizing its own simultaneous control pulse. We formulate physical placement and pulse synthesis as a coupled decision problem for parallel controlled-$Z$ gates in heterogeneous frequency tunable transmon arrays. The proposed processor-aware structural quantum multi-domain matrix (QMDM) links static processor, edge, incidence, and task information to a dynamic candidate response block. For each candidate placement $P$, QMDM instantiates the active Hamiltonian $H_P$; quantum optimal control (QOCT) generates a placement-specific pulse, direct coupled propagation returns the projected computational subspace overlap $F_{\rm proj}$ and computational survival; and these pulse-conditioned responses are fed back to QMDM to rank and progressively promote physical placements. This placement pulse response feedback defines pulse-informed physical placement. Here, to see the performance of the proposed method on 30 held-out synthetic $3\times3$ processors, the median final $F_{\rm proj}$ is $0.993826$ for pulse-informed placement and $0.984981$ for calibration-based placement. Also, when tested under different system conditions, the proposed pulse-informed approach uses $59.1\%$ fewer candidate QOCT optimizer iterations than the exhaustive finite-budget reference. The QMDM representation and outer search are formulated for arbitrary $L$ simultaneous two-qubit gates. Here, the present global candidate ranking validation is used for $L=2$.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates placement and pulse synthesis as a coupled decision problem for parallel controlled-Z gates in heterogeneous tunable transmon arrays, introducing a processor-aware QMDM representation with pulse-conditioned feedback to rank physical placements.
AI.motivation: A parallel two-qubit layer can be realized with several nonoverlapping coupler sets, but isolated calibrations do not reveal how each realization performs once its own simultaneous control pulse is optimized. Placement and pulse synthesis must therefore be treated jointly rather than separately.
AI.method: The authors propose a quantum multi-domain matrix (QMDM) that links static processor, edge, incidence, and task information to a dynamic candidate response block. For each candidate placement P, QMDM instantiates the active Hamiltonian H_P; quantum optimal control (QOCT) generates a placement-specific pulse; direct coupled propagation yields projected computational subspace overlap F_proj and computational survival; these pulse-conditioned responses are fed back to rank and progressively promote placements (pulse-informed physical placement).
AI.result: On 30 held-out synthetic 3x3 processors, median final F_proj is 0.993826 for pulse-informed placement versus 0.984981 for calibration-based placement. Under varied system conditions, the pulse-informed approach uses 59.1% fewer candidate QOCT optimizer iterations than the exhaustive finite-budget reference. Global candidate ranking validation is demonstrated for L=2 gates.
AI.conclusion: Pulse-informed placement outperforms calibration-based placement in fidelity and reduces optimization cost. The QMDM representation and outer search are formulated for arbitrary L simultaneous two-qubit gates, with present validation at L=2.

title: Competition and cancellation in a tilted Rice--Mele chain: exact Wannier--Stark offset and spectral readout
summary: In a tilted Rice--Mele chain, the Wannier--Stark (WS) ladder becomes staggered, \(E_n=n\Fo+(-1)^{n+1}A\). The offset \(A\) reflects the competition between the staggered onsite energy \(Δ\) and the dimerized hopping \(\dt\), and its cancellation restores spectral equidistance. We determine \(A\) through a systematic strong-field series in the WS basis and a nonperturbative two-band Floquet expression. An exact matrix element reduces the strong-field expansion to Bessel algebra; at the representative working point, truncation at seventh order locates the cancellation point with a theory-internal truncation error of \(0.010\)~Hz, against \(27.3\)~Hz at first order. The Floquet propagator gives the closed form \(A=(\Fo/π)\arcsin(-i\,\mathrm{Tr}\,U/2)\), exact within the two-band model, implying the kinematic bound \(|A|\le\Fo/2\) and identifying cancellation with maximum spectral uniformity. The same analytic structure yields a family of real zeros and complex exceptional points that set the convergence radius of the strong-field series without touching the real axis. On odd-length chains, the hidden-symmetry defect produces a pairing plateau of height \(2|A|\) that persists numerically beyond first order in the modulations, allowing the offset to be read from the static spectrum without Floquet propagation or time evolution. In the bulk, cancellation appears as the merging of two sidebands into a single line at \(\Fo\), a null measurement that requires no calibrated sideband amplitudes, although the tilt and line frequency still need calibration. These signatures provide complementary spectral tests of the staggered WS ladder and a calibration-aware route to precision force sensing.

AI.tldr: The staggered offset A of the Wannier–Stark ladder in a tilted Rice–Mele chain is determined via a strong-field Bessel series and an exact two-band Floquet formula A=(F0/π)arcsin(−i Tr U/2), yielding |A|≤F0/2, cancellation of A as maximum spectral uniformity, complex exceptional points, a pairing plateau 2|A| on odd chains, and sideband merging at F0 as spectral fingerprints.
AI.motivation: A staggered Wannier–Stark ladder with offset A (competition between staggered onsite energy Δ and dimerized hopping) breaks spectral equidistance, so accurate knowledge of A is needed both for fundamental understanding of the ladder and for calibration-aware precision force sensing.
AI.method: Strong-field perturbation series in the Wannier–Stark basis reduced via an exact matrix element to Bessel-algebra recursion; nonperturbative two-band Floquet propagator; analytic continuation to locate real zeros and complex exceptional points; numerical study of odd-length chains and bulk sideband structure.
AI.result: Seventh-order truncation locates the cancellation point with theory-internal truncation error 0.010 Hz versus 27.3 Hz at first order; the Floquet propagator gives exact closed form A=(F0/π)arcsin(−i Tr U/2) with bound |A|≤F0/2; exceptional points fix the series convergence radius off the real axis; odd chains show a 2|A| pairing plateau persisting beyond first order; cancellation appears as merger of two sidebands into one line at F0.
AI.conclusion: The staggered WS ladder admits exact and series-controlled analytic description with complementary spectral signatures (static plateau, null sideband coalescence, truncation-controlled cancellation point) enabling calibration-aware precision force sensing.

title: Quantum Gate Engineering in Superconducting NISQ Platforms: Experimental Methods and Emerging Directions
summary: This review aims to provide researchers, experimentalists, and quantum engineers with an updated and technically grounded perspective on the implementation of quantum gates in superconducting NISQ devices. The goal is to establish a comprehensive bridge between theoretical quantum circuit synthesis and its practical, experimental implementation, focusing on superconducting quantum technologies. We systematically examine the diverse landscape of superconducting qubits and processor architectures, ranging from conventional transmons to alternative and unconventional designs, evaluating their unique design trade-offs, connectivity constraints, device physics, and materials impact. Moving from theory to actual implementation, we detail how single- and two-qubit operations are synthesized via microwave-driven and flux-activated pulses. We here present our pulse engineering, wave shaping, calibration workflows, demonstrating how to bridge the gap between abstract gate models and real-world hardware limitations in the direction of a hardware-software co-design framework. To validate these operations, we choose benchmarking methodologies with the purpose to get the more efficient metric for the specific evaluation aspect, including truth tables and quantum process tomography. Therefore, we both discuss the theoretical concepts behind the gate synthesis and show experimental implementation of most fundamental gates by proposing a practical workflow.

AI.tldr: A technically grounded review bridging theoretical quantum circuit synthesis and practical implementation of quantum gates in superconducting NISQ devices, covering qubit architectures, pulse engineering, calibration, and benchmarking toward a hardware-software co-design framework.
AI.motivation: Researchers, experimentalists, and quantum engineers lack an updated, integrated perspective connecting abstract quantum gate models to real-world superconducting hardware limitations. The review aims to bridge theoretical quantum circuit synthesis and practical experimental implementation for superconducting quantum technologies.
AI.method: Systematic review of superconducting qubit landscapes (conventional transmons to alternative/unconventional designs), evaluating design trade-offs, connectivity constraints, device physics, and materials. Gate synthesis is detailed for single- and two-qubit operations via microwave-driven and flux-activated pulses, including pulse engineering, wave shaping, and calibration workflows. Validation uses benchmarking methodologies such as truth tables and quantum process tomography.
AI.result: The review presents pulse engineering, wave shaping, and calibration workflows that bridge abstract gate models and hardware limitations, and identifies benchmarking methods (including truth tables and quantum process tomography) suited to specific evaluation aspects, supported by a practical experimental workflow for fundamental gates.
AI.conclusion: An integrated, practically oriented framework connects gate synthesis theory with experimental implementation, guiding hardware-software co-design and providing a workflow for realizing and validating fundamental gates on superconducting NISQ hardware.

title: Hyperentanglement-enabled Quantum Privacy Amplification for Classical-Quantum Coexistence in Fiber Networks
summary: Integrating quantum communication into existing fiber infrastructures requires coexisting with high-power classical traffic, which generates noise in the quantum channel. Spontaneous Raman Scattering (SpRS) is the dominant noise source, generating a broadband photon background that degrades quantum states and, in Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), can entirely suppress secure key generation. In this work, we implement single-copy entanglement distillation utilizing energy-time and frequency hyperentanglement, and we exploit it to perform Quantum Privacy Amplification (QPA) directly at a physical layer. Strict frequency anti-correlations of spontaneous parametric down-conversion are used to selectively discard uncorrelated Raman photons while preserving genuine entangled pairs, suppressing accidental coincidences by a factor $1/N$, where $N$ is the number of frequency channel pairs. Using passive borosilicate-glass photonic integrated circuits and standard DWDM demultiplexers over a 20~km single-mode fiber testbed, we demonstrate a 4~dB improvement in tolerance to classical laser launch power $P_C$ when QPA is performed, extending the secure key threshold from $P_C=-13.3$ dBm to $P_C=-9.3$ dBm. The result shows that off-the-shelf telecom components can be repurposed as physical-layer quantum privacy amplifiers.

AI.tldr: Single-copy entanglement distillation with energy-time/frequency hyperentanglement realizes physical-layer quantum privacy amplification, improving classical-launch-power tolerance by 4 dB and extending the QKD secure-key threshold from −13.3 dBm to −9.3 dBm over 20 km fiber.
AI.motivation: Deploying QKD in existing fiber infrastructures means coexisting with high-power classical traffic, and spontaneous Raman scattering (SpRS) from that traffic is the dominant noise source—broadband photon background that degrades quantum states and can fully suppress secure key generation. A physical-layer means to reject this uncorrelated noise is needed.
AI.method: The authors use energy-time and frequency hyperentanglement to implement single-copy entanglement distillation, deployed as Quantum Privacy Amplification (QPA). Strict frequency anti-correlations of spontaneous parametric down-conversion let them selectively discard uncorrelated Raman photons while keeping genuine entangled pairs, suppressing accidental coincidences by 1/N (N = number of frequency channel pairs). Implementation uses passive borosilicate-glass photonic integrated circuits and standard DWDM demultiplexers on a 20 km single-mode fiber testbed.
AI.result: With QPA enabled, tolerance to classical laser launch power P_C improves by 4 dB, moving the secure-key threshold from P_C = −13.3 dBm to −9.3 dBm. Accidental coincidences are suppressed by a factor of 1/N.
AI.conclusion: Off-the-shelf telecom components (passive glass PICs, DWDM demultiplexers) can be repurposed as physical-layer quantum privacy amplifiers, enabling QKD coexistence with high-power classical channels in shared fiber.

title: Homodyne versus heterodyne detection for classifying families of optical quantum states from finite records of detection events
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Code and results: https://github.com/barkol/qmi-finite-shot
summary: Neural networks can identify an optical quantum state from an image of its phase-space function, but a real measurement gives a finite record of $N$ detection events. Heterodyne detection samples the Husimi $Q$ function directly, whereas homodyne detection gives the Wigner function only after a reconstruction from several phases.
