We ask which scheme better identifies one of seven families of states, including Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, under loss, dephasing and Gaussian noise. We simulate finite records on identical states for two sets of families, one with equal mean photon number and one built from the code of Ahmed et al. For convolutional networks, heterodyne detection outperforms homodyne detection with filtered back-projection by 14.1 percentage points at $N=100$ events and 20% dephasing in the first set (adjusted $p=0.003$ over $24$ cells across training runs), and it depends on the number of phases and on the reconstruction. At $N=10^3$ and $10^4$ no difference is significant, but the intervals are wide. At $N=100$, a homodyne network without reconstruction does not differ significantly from heterodyne detection in the first set and is nominally worse in the second. Near thermal states we show to leading order that heterodyne detection damps phase-space structure of order $n$ exponentially, whereas homodyne detection shares unit weight among $n+1$ angular components, a local result that does not explain the finite-record differences. Experimental records of a GKP state, photon-subtracted squeezed states and one mode of an Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen source are classified like simulated ones, but these low-power tests probe our counting-noise model, not the seven-class accuracy. A likelihood-ratio observer shows no such gap at $N=100$, so our evidence concerns a reconstruction-based pipeline, not homodyne detection in general.

AI.tldr: For identifying one of seven quantum-state families (including GKP states) from finite detection records under loss, dephasing and Gaussian noise, convolutional networks classify better from heterodyne records than from homodyne records processed by filtered back-projection—by 14.1 percentage points at N=100 events and 20% dephasing—whereas a likelihood-ratio observer shows no such gap.
AI.motivation: Neural networks can identify optical quantum states from phase-space images, but real measurements yield only finite records of N detection events. It is unclear which measurement scheme—heterodyne (direct Q-function sampling) or homodyne (Wigner function only after reconstruction from several phases)—better supports state identification under realistic noise and record sizes.
AI.method: Finite records are simulated on identical states for two sets of seven families (one with equal mean photon number, one built from the code of Ahmed et al.), under loss, dephasing and Gaussian noise. Convolutional networks are trained on heterodyne records versus homodyne records reconstructed by filtered back-projection; comparisons vary the number of phases and the reconstruction. A homodyne pipeline without reconstruction and a likelihood-ratio observer are tested as controls, and a leading-order analytical calculation near thermal states compares phase-space damping for the two schemes.
AI.result: At N=100 and 20% dephasing, heterodyne outperforms reconstructed homodyne by 14.1 percentage points in the first set (adjusted p=0.003 over 24 cells across training runs), and the gap depends on phase number and reconstruction. At N=10^3 and 10^4 differences are not significant but confidence intervals are wide. At N=100, unreconstructed homodyne does not differ significantly from heterodyne in the first set and is nominally worse in the second. Analytically, near thermal states heterodyne damps phase-space structure of order n exponentially, while homodyne distributes unit weight among n+1 angular components—a local result that does not explain the finite-record differences. Experimental records (a GKP state, photon-subtracted squeezed states, one mode of an EPR source) are classified like simulated ones but test only the counting-noise model. A likelihood-ratio observer shows no gap at N=100.
AI.conclusion: Heterodyne detection is preferable to reconstruction-based homodyne for convolutional-network state identification in the low-record regime, but the advantage is specific to the reconstruction pipeline, since an optimal likelihood-ratio observer shows no gap and the observed differences vanish statistically at larger N. The findings do not establish a general superiority of heterodyne over homodyne detection.

title: Goldbach Representations in Quantum Optics and Metrology
summary: We derive a relation between Goldbach representations and photon-number statistics in a quantum-optical setup. Considering an even-number Fock state injected into a stochastic beam splitter with uniformly distributed transmissivity and projections of the two output modes onto prime subspaces, we demonstrate that each successful outcome corresponds to an Goldbach representation and that the averaged detection probability is exactly proportional to the number of Goldbach representations. Then, employing the Hardy--Littlewood asymptotic formula, we demonstrate that the post-measurement state generated by a beam splitter with fixed transmissivity exhibits standard quantum limit scaling of the ultimate precision limit in terms of phase estimation, whereas an equally weighted superposition of Goldbach representations exhibits Heisenberg scaling. These results provide a quantum-optical realization of Goldbach representations and relate their statistics of with quantum metrology.

AI.tldr: A quantum-optical beam-splitter setup maps Goldbach representations of even numbers onto photon-number statistics, and the resulting post-measurement states show either standard quantum limit or Heisenberg scaling in phase estimation.
AI.motivation: Goldbach representations (ways of writing an even number as a sum of two primes) are a purely number-theoretic object whose statistics are hard to access operationally. The authors seek a physical realization of these representations and a bridge between additive number theory statistics and quantum metrology.
AI.method: An even-number Fock state is injected into a stochastic beam splitter with uniformly distributed transmissivity; the two output modes are projected onto prime subspaces. Each successful detection outcome is shown to correspond to a Goldbach representation, and the averaged detection probability is shown to be proportional to the number of representations. Using the Hardy--Littlewood asymptotic formula, the ultimate phase-estimation precision of the post-measurement states is then analyzed for (i) a fixed-transmissivity beam splitter and (ii) an equally weighted superposition of Goldbach representations.
AI.result: Successful projection events are in one-to-one correspondence with Goldbach representations, and the averaged detection probability is exactly proportional to the Goldbach representation count. Under the Hardy--Littlewood asymptotics, the fixed-transmissivity post-measurement state shows standard quantum limit scaling of the ultimate precision, whereas the equally weighted Goldbach superposition achieves Heisenberg scaling.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a quantum-optical realization of Goldbach representations and connects their statistics to quantum metrology, with the superposition structure of representations as the resource enabling Heisenberg-limited phase estimation.

title: Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization for Variable Molecular Geometries
summary: Quantum and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms have the potential to improve the accuracy and scale of quantum chemistry and impact a broad range of applications such as drug discovery and catalysis. In particular, subspace methods such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) can already tackle classically challenging systems. However, practical algorithms that go beyond the computation of electronic ground and excited states are still scarce. Here, we introduce the variable-geometry sample-based quantum diagonalization (VGSQD) algorithm, which extends SQD to variable molecular geometries by reusing quantum samples from a reference geometry at displaced ones, thus significantly reducing quantum computational cost. Using circuits of up to 124 qubits on ibm-quebec, an IBM Heron r2 quantum processor, we determine the equilibrium geometry and energy of the weakly bound, strongly correlated beryllium dimer, as well as the water molecule. Finally, we extend VGSQD to chemical reactions and compute the minimum energy path and energy barrier of a hydrogen exchange reaction. The results are comparable with state-of-the-art classical methods such as CCSD(T) and DMRG. This work broadens the scope of quantum algorithms for chemistry, from energies to geometry optimization and reaction pathways, both essential for practical applications.

AI.tldr: VGSQD extends sample-based quantum diagonalization to variable molecular geometries by reusing quantum samples from a reference geometry at displaced geometries, cutting quantum cost, and is demonstrated on up to 124 qubits for geometry optimization and reaction pathways matching CCSD(T)/DMRG.
AI.motivation: Quantum and hybrid algorithms can improve quantum chemistry accuracy and scale, and subspace methods like SQD already handle classically challenging systems, but practical algorithms beyond electronic ground/excited state energies are scarce. The authors aim to broaden quantum algorithms from energy computation to geometry optimization and reaction pathways, which are essential for drug discovery and catalysis applications.
AI.method: The variable-geometry sample-based quantum diagonalization (VGSQD) algorithm extends SQD to variable molecular geometries by reusing quantum samples obtained at a reference geometry when evaluating displaced geometries, thereby significantly reducing quantum computational cost. Experiments used circuits of up to 124 qubits on ibm-quebec (an IBM Heron r2 quantum processor).
AI.result: VGSQD determined the equilibrium geometry and energy of the weakly bound, strongly correlated beryllium dimer and of the water molecule. Extended to chemical reactions, it computed the minimum energy path and energy barrier of a hydrogen exchange reaction. Results are comparable with state-of-the-art classical methods such as CCSD(T) and DMRG.
AI.conclusion: VGSQD broadens the scope of quantum algorithms for chemistry from energies to geometry optimization and reaction pathways, both essential for practical applications, while reducing quantum computational cost through sample reuse across geometries.

title: Quenched Thermodynamics from Ancilla-Assisted Imaginary-Time Evolution
summary:
Quenched thermodynamics combines the equilibrium physics of fixed coupling configurations with a prescribed distribution of disorder. Problems related to quenched thermodynamics are generally intractable to approximate. We provide a quantum algorithm to calculate quenched disorder averages for the transverse-field Ising model, whose coupling configurations are organized into gauge classes. We show how to estimate these averages by preparing approximate Gibbs states through ancilla-assisted imaginary-time evolution. At each measurement, the ancilla record identifies the gauge class to which the energy estimate contributes.
  We validate our framework through an open $3\times3$ lattice. A one-step circuit resolves all sixteen flux classes, and a finite-shot calculation estimates the quenched energy for independently distributed bond signs. Thermodynamic integration extends the reconstruction to a quenched free-energy estimate, while comparison with exact diagonalization identifies the finite-step approximation as the dominant source of error. This use of the measurement record provides access to the thermodynamics of frustrated spin systems with a disorder distribution chosen independently of the circuit's sampling frequencies.

AI.tldr: A quantum algorithm estimates quenched disorder averages for the transverse-field Ising model by preparing approximate Gibbs states via ancilla-assisted imaginary-time evolution, using ancilla measurement records to assign each energy estimate to its gauge class.
AI.motivation: Quenched thermodynamics (equilibrium physics of fixed coupling configurations averaged over a disorder distribution) is generally intractable to approximate, motivating a quantum approach.
AI.method: Coupling configurations are organized into gauge classes. Approximate Gibbs states are prepared through ancilla-assisted imaginary-time evolution; at each measurement the ancilla record identifies the gauge class to which the energy estimate contributes. Thermodynamic integration reconstructs a quenched free-energy estimate.
AI.result: Validated on an open 3x3 lattice: a one-step circuit resolves all sixteen flux classes, and a finite-shot calculation estimates the quenched energy for independently distributed bond signs. Comparison with exact diagonalization shows the finite-step approximation is the dominant error source.
AI.conclusion: Using the measurement record gives access to the thermodynamics of frustrated spin systems with a disorder distribution chosen independently of the circuit's sampling frequencies.

title: Generalized Mean-Field Ising Model as a Benchmark Family with Exact Solutions
summary: Exactly solvable models provide opportunities to understand complex optimization problems while offering controlled benchmarks for computational methods. However, nontrivial models that combine analytical tractability with challenging optimization structure remain scarce. Here, we introduce the Generalized Mean-Field Ising (GMFI) family, a densely connected and inhomogeneous class of Ising Hamiltonians whose ground states can nevertheless be obtained exactly. This exact solution reveals a hidden low-dimensional structure and enables a complete number-theoretic classification of different system sizes and degenerate ground states. Uniquely, the GMFI family can be used to benchmark both quantum and classical optimization methods over system sizes far beyond exact diagonalization. We investigate the GMFI family using several approaches, including theoretical analysis of quantum annealing, experiments on a D-Wave quantum processor, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), imaginary-time evolution (ITE), greedy algorithm, simulated annealing, and a quantum-inspired greedy algorithm. Despite the GMFI model's exact solvability, it exhibits nontrivial algorithmic behavior: although the quantum-annealing gap is expected to decrease with increasing system size, it shows pronounced and unexpected system-size-dependent oscillatory signatures. These results establish GMFI models as a rare bridge between exact many-body theory, number theory, optimization, and quantum hardware, providing a scalable benchmark for identifying and understanding algorithmic limitations in classical and quantum computing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Generalized Mean-Field Ising (GMFI) family: densely connected, inhomogeneous Ising Hamiltonians with exactly solvable ground states, used as a scalable benchmark for classical and quantum optimizers.
AI.motivation: Exactly solvable optimization models that are both analytically tractable and structurally challenging are scarce, limiting controlled benchmarking of quantum and classical optimizers beyond exact-diagonalization scales.
AI.method: Defines the GMFI Hamiltonian class, derives its exact ground states via a hidden low-dimensional structure, and gives a number-theoretic classification of system sizes and degenerate ground states. Benchmarks it using quantum annealing theory, D-Wave hardware experiments, QAOA, imaginary-time evolution, greedy algorithms, simulated annealing, and a quantum-inspired greedy algorithm.
AI.result: The exact solution yields a complete classification of sizes and ground-state degeneracies; despite exact solvability, the quantum-annealing gap shows pronounced system-size-dependent oscillatory signatures contrary to monotonic-decrease expectations, and methods exhibit nontrivial algorithmic behavior across system sizes far beyond exact diagonalization.
AI.conclusion: GMFI models bridge exact many-body theory, number theory, optimization, and quantum hardware, providing a scalable benchmark for identifying algorithmic limitations in classical and quantum computing.

title: Generating Multipartite Entanglement via Structured-Bath Engineering
summary: We present how to dissipatively prepare genuinely multipartite-entangled steady states with mutually independent local reservoirs by harnessing an Abelian strong symmetry and temporal bath correlations. In interacting Ising chains, we demonstrate that, for a broad class of system-environment couplings, flat baths exponentially erase Ising-axis correlations. Structured baths overcome this obstruction by converting temporal bath correlations into classical spatial correlations. Strong symmetry then promotes these correlations to the quantum domain, enabling global multipartite entanglement. Within weak-coupling theory, we obtain exact steady states despite the generator's nonquadratic nature: strong symmetry reduces their construction to a classical problem for arbitrary Ising couplings. This reduction reveals an exact connection between classical distinguishability and entanglement. We then show how to engineer the bath spectrum to increase the correlation length and enable the preparation of GHZ-like states from separable initial conditions. We test the mechanism beyond the analytical regime using exact Markovian embeddings and tensor-network simulations. Our approach is particularly suited to superconducting and trapped-ion platforms, and we propose a concrete implementation for the latter using sympathetically cooled motional modes.

AI.tldr: Independent local baths plus an Abelian strong symmetry and temporal bath correlations can dissipatively stabilize genuinely multipartite-entangled steady states in interacting Ising chains, with an exact classical-to-quantum entanglement link.
AI.motivation: Dissipative state preparation typically requires correlated/engineered baths; the paper asks whether genuinely multipartite entanglement can be prepared using mutually independent local reservoirs, which usually destroy correlations.
AI.method: Weak-coupling master-equation analysis of interacting Ising chains under local baths; exploitation of an Abelian strong symmetry to reduce the exact steady-state construction (despite a nonquadratic generator) to a classical problem for arbitrary Ising couplings; engineering of bath spectra (structured vs. flat) to convert temporal bath correlations into spatial ones; validation via exact Markovian embeddings and tensor-network simulations; proposal for trapped-ion implementation with sympathetically cooled motional modes.
AI.result: Flat baths exponentially erase Ising-axis correlations, but structured baths convert temporal bath correlations into classical spatial correlations that the strong symmetry lifts into the quantum domain, yielding global multipartite entanglement. Exact steady states are obtained and reveal an exact connection between classical distinguishability and entanglement; bath-spectrum engineering increases correlation length and enables GHZ-like state preparation from separable initial conditions.
AI.conclusion: Genuinely multipartite-entangled steady states are achievable with independent local reservoirs via strong symmetry and temporal bath correlations; the mechanism is validated beyond the analytical regime and is well suited to superconducting and trapped-ion platforms.

title: Key Evaluation of a Relativistic Quantum Key Distribution Over a Turbulent Free-space Optical Channel
summary: We investigate the performance of relativistic quantum key distribution (RQKD) over turbulent free-space optical channels for both single-photon and coherent-state implementations. A theoretical model is developed to describe the effect of atmospheric turbulence on interferometric visibility and secret-key generation by incorporating turbulence-induced phase fluctuations into the key-rate analysis. Numerical simulations are performed under realistic channel conditions to evaluate the achievable communication distance and secret-key rate. The results show that atmospheric turbulence degrades the protocol performance by reducing interference visibility, with the severity of the degradation determined by the ratio between the interferometer-arm separation $r$ (or temporal separation of signal and reference states $ΔT$) and Fried's parameter. The single-photon protocol remains operational over all investigated turbulence regimes, whereas the coherent-state implementation exhibits a critical dependence on the interferometer geometry (especially on $ΔT$), leading to a threshold beyond which secure key generation is no longer possible. These findings quantify the impact of atmospheric turbulence on relativistic quantum key distribution and provide practical guidelines for the design and optimization of free-space RQKD systems.

AI.tldr: Relativistic QKD over turbulent free-space links is modeled by adding turbulence-induced phase fluctuations to the key-rate analysis; single-photon schemes stay secure across all turbulence regimes, while coherent-state schemes fail beyond a geometry-dependent threshold.
AI.motivation: Free-space RQKD must operate through atmospheric turbulence, yet the impact of turbulence on interferometric visibility and secret-key generation for relativistic protocols had not been quantified.
AI.method: A theoretical model incorporating turbulence-induced phase fluctuations into the secret-key-rate analysis, capturing visibility loss from the ratio of interferometer-arm separation r (or signal-reference temporal separation ΔT) to Fried's parameter; numerical simulations under realistic channel conditions estimate achievable distance and key rate for single-photon and coherent-state implementations.
AI.result: Turbulence degrades performance by reducing interference visibility, with severity set by r (or ΔT) relative to Fried's parameter. The single-photon protocol remains operational in all investigated turbulence regimes, whereas the coherent-state protocol depends critically on interferometer geometry (especially ΔT), exhibiting a threshold beyond which no secure key can be generated.
AI.conclusion: The work quantifies turbulence effects on RQKD and provides practical design guidelines for free-space RQKD systems, favoring single-photon implementations and careful control of interferometer geometry.

title: Memory-Induced Limits on Entanglement Distribution
summary: We investigate the operational limits of entanglement distribution through quantum channels reused without reinitialization. Building on an effective repeated-use channel description, we show that residual excitations left in the channel from previous uses act as a memory source that progressively suppresses coherent quantum transmission. To quantify this limitation, we derive an analytical lower bound on the quantum capacity and combine it with the Holevo-Werner semidefinite-programming upper bound. We also provide an analytical criterion to identify entanglement-breaking channels, with thresholds that depend jointly on chain length and reuse. For perfect-state-transfer chains, the resulting capacity window yields tighter estimates than previous bounds, with the relative improvement becoming substantially more pronounced closer to the entanglement-breaking threshold. Moreover, on the second use, our lower bound certifies a maximal relative timing-error tolerance across all chains with internal memory that lies just below 22.63% and is attained by the three-site chain. We further derive a fundamental relative timing-error threshold of 36.41%, above which we analytically guarantee zero unassisted quantum capacity for every chain with internal memory, independent of the number of uses. These results establish a clear benchmark model for repeated entanglement distribution, and identify timing precision, chain length, and memory accumulation as fundamental constraints on scalable quantum-network architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies how channel memory/residual excitations in reused spin chains degrade entanglement distribution, providing tighter quantum-capacity bounds and explicit timing-error thresholds.
AI.motivation: In scalable quantum networks, quantum channels are often reused without full reinitialization, so leftover excitations from prior uses introduce memory that may suppress coherent quantum transmission. Prior capacity estimates do not account for this reuse-induced memory, leaving the operational limits of repeated entanglement distribution unclear.
AI.method: The authors adopt an effective repeated-use channel description in which residual excitations act as a memory source. They derive an analytical lower bound on the quantum capacity and pair it with the Holevo-Werner semidefinite-programming upper bound. They also formulate an analytical entanglement-breaking criterion whose thresholds depend jointly on chain length and number of reuses, and apply the framework to perfect-state-transfer chains.
AI.result: The combined bounds yield a tighter capacity window than previous estimates, with relative improvement increasing near the entanglement-breaking threshold. On the second use, the lower bound certifies a maximal relative timing-error tolerance just below 22.63% over all chains with internal memory, attained by the three-site chain. A fundamental relative timing-error threshold of 36.41% is derived, above which unassisted quantum capacity is analytically guaranteed to be zero for every chain with internal memory, regardless of the number of uses.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a benchmark model for repeated entanglement distribution and identifies timing precision, chain length, and memory accumulation as fundamental constraints on scalable quantum-network architectures.

title: Gravitational Interactions in Nuclear Clocks
summary: Atomic clocks achieve extraordinary precision through quantum control over large ensembles of atoms, with precision increasing and atom number advancing steadily. Emerging nuclear clock technology encodes clock states in nuclear rather than electronic transitions, offering a new frontier for precision measurement. Here we study whether a large ensemble of such clock nuclei could be used to observe their mutual gravitational interaction. We investigate the gravitational redshift induced by neighboring atoms, including nuclear energy superpositions as sources of gravity, giving rise to a genuinely quantum gravitational interaction between pairs of nuclei. We find that the resulting clock frequency shift due to mutual gravity may become non-negligible for a macroscopic number of nuclei, for instance in a solid-state thorium clock, and we propose approaches to mitigate electromagnetic field effects by exploiting spatial symmetry and high-precision spectroscopy. We further discuss how energy-induced mass superpositions could be directly probed using external gravitational field sensors. By contrast, observing gravity-induced entanglement involving clocks would require substantially greater experimental advances due to decoherence from spontaneous emission. Taken together, our results suggest that nuclear clocks, either alone or in combination with complementary sensors such as optomechanical systems, may offer a future route toward probing gravity at short distances and testing gravitating quantum source masses beyond the Newtonian limit.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using large ensembles of nuclear-clock nuclei (e.g., solid-state thorium clocks) to observe mutual gravitational interaction, including gravity sourced by nuclear energy superpositions. It finds the mutual-gravity-induced clock frequency shift may become non-negligible for macroscopic nuclei numbers and discusses experimental routes.
AI.motivation: Nuclear clocks encode clock states in nuclear rather than electronic transitions, offering a new precision-measurement frontier. The authors ask whether a large ensemble of clock nuclei could be used to observe their mutual gravitational interaction, a regime largely unexplored.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of the gravitational redshift induced by neighboring atoms, treating nuclear energy superpositions as gravitational sources that yield a genuinely quantum gravitational interaction between nuclei pairs. They propose mitigating electromagnetic field effects via spatial symmetry and high-precision spectroscopy, and discuss probing energy-induced mass superpositions with external gravitational field sensors.
AI.result: The mutual-gravity-induced clock frequency shift may become non-negligible for a macroscopic number of nuclei, e.g., in a solid-state thorium clock. Observing gravity-induced entanglement involving clocks would require substantially greater experimental advances due to decoherence from spontaneous emission.
AI.conclusion: Nuclear clocks, alone or combined with complementary sensors such as optomechanical systems, may offer a future route toward probing gravity at short distances and testing gravitating quantum source masses beyond the Newtonian limit.

title: Gravitationally Mediated Entanglement in Interferometers with Repeated Splitting
summary: Proposals to probe the quantum nature of gravity through entanglement between spatially separated masses have attracted considerable interest. In such schemes, spatial superpositions are prepared through controlled splitting operations that produce several interferometric branches. Here we propose and analyse protocols involving repeated splitting stages, each of which doubles the number of occupied paths. We show that the density matrix after $n$ splitting stages is related to that of the $(n-1)$-splitting protocol through local parity dephasing. Two of the resulting sectors reproduce the preceding state, while the other two acquire additional gravitational phases. Removing the locally generated parts gives an exact lower bound on the change in negativity, expressed in terms of the preceding state's negative partial-transpose eigenspace. For two splitting stages, this leads to an explicit condition on three gravitational phases under which the additional split cannot reduce negativity. We also show that further splitting cannot shorten the lifetime of the generated entanglement. If the local internal system preserves the full branch label, the positional entanglement is retained upon recombination. We describe an implementation using a reusable two-level system and local memories, and compare it with a readout without a memory register. For the latter, we derive an exact condition for when an additional splitting stage improves the readout, based on a $2\times 2$ Schur complement. Numerical simulations show an advantage in positional negativity over the rates considered, with an improvement surviving the restricted readout at all decoherence rates considered at the final readout time.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes quantum-gravity entanglement protocols using repeated splitting stages that each double the number of occupied interferometric paths, showing the post-splitting density matrix relates to the previous one via local parity dephasing. It derives exact lower bounds on negativity change, conditions under which extra splitting cannot reduce negativity, and provides an implementation scheme with numerical evidence of advantage.
AI.motivation: Entanglement-based proposals to probe the quantum nature of gravity between spatially separated masses rely on controlled spatial-splitting operations producing multiple interferometric branches. It is unclear how adding further splitting stages affects the generated entanglement (negativity), its lifetime, and the readout, so a systematic analysis of multi-stage splitting is needed.
AI.method: Protocols with repeated splitting stages, each doubling the occupied paths, are proposed and analyzed. The n-stage density matrix is related to the (n-1)-stage state through local parity dephasing: two sectors reproduce the preceding state and two acquire additional gravitational phases. An exact lower bound on negativity change is derived from the preceding state's negative partial-transpose eigenspace. For two stages an explicit condition on three gravitational phases is obtained. Implementations using a reusable two-level system with local memories, versus a memoryless readout, are described; the memoryless case yields an exact improvement condition via a 2x2 Schur complement.
AI.result: The change in negativity from extra splitting is exactly lower-bounded in terms of the preceding state's negative partial-transpose eigenspace. For two splitting stages, an explicit condition on three gravitational phases guarantees the additional split cannot reduce negativity. Further splitting cannot shorten the entanglement lifetime; if the local internal system preserves the full branch label, positional entanglement survives recombination. For memoryless readout, an exact Schur-complement condition determines when an extra stage improves readout. Numerical simulations show a positional-negativity advantage over the considered rates, with improvement surviving the restricted readout at all considered decoherence rates at the final readout time.
AI.conclusion: Repeated splitting stages can be analyzed tractably via local parity dephasing, yielding exact bounds and conditions on negativity and entanglement lifetime. Additional splitting does not harm (and can improve) the generated positional entanglement, and memory-assisted schemes outperform memoryless readout, supporting the feasibility of multi-stage entanglement-based probes of the quantum nature of gravity.

title: Inferring the Number of Quantum State Transfers with Neural Networks
summary: Repeated-use quantum state transfer (QST) goes beyond the single-use paradigm by accounting for the memory that accumulates inside the transmission channel when it is not reset between uses. Consequently, the map governing the $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ use of the channel differs from use to use and carries a signature of each previous use. We ask whether this use number can be recovered from transmission data alone, and show that it can: a simple feed-forward neural network, given as input the Bloch vectors sent and received over a single use of an XX spin-chain channel, is able to identify the use number with an accuracy exceeding 90%. Exploiting the U(1) symmetry of the channel, we find that a reduced two-component representation of the transmitted states improves the accuracy further, to about 95%. We characterise the dependence of the classifier on the size and composition of the training data, finding that the number of sampled states and of sampled timings are equally important. We also identify the data set sizes required to reach a given accuracy. Finally, we quantify the severity of the residual misclassifications with an earth-mover distance on the confusion matrix.

AI.tldr: A feed-forward neural network recovers the use-number of a repeatedly-used XX spin-chain quantum state transfer channel from single-use Bloch-vector data with >90% accuracy, rising to ~95% with a U(1)-symmetric two-component representation.
AI.motivation: Repeated-use quantum state transfer departs from the single-use paradigm: memory accumulated in the channel between uses makes the map of the n-th use differ from use to use and carry a signature of prior uses. The paper asks whether this use number can be inferred from transmission data alone.
AI.method: The input to a simple feed-forward neural network is the set of Bloch vectors sent and received over a single use of an XX spin-chain channel. Exploiting the channel's U(1) symmetry, the authors introduce a reduced two-component representation of transmitted states. They characterise classifier dependence on training-data size and composition (sampled states vs. sampled timings) and identify data-set sizes needed for target accuracy; residual misclassifications are quantified via an earth-mover distance on the confusion matrix.
AI.result: Use-number identification exceeds 90% accuracy; the reduced two-component representation improves it to about 95%. Sampled-state count and sampled-timing count are comparably important, and required data-set sizes for given accuracy are identified.
AI.conclusion: Use number is recoverable from transmission data alone, and symmetry-informed state representations plus adequate sampling of states and timings yield near-95% classification accuracy, with residual errors quantified by an earth-mover distance on the confusion matrix.

title: Local Quantum Fault Tolerance Without Expansion
summary:
We study fault-tolerant quantum computation using a fixed, local error-correction rule and a geometrically simple code: the cubical $(d,d')$-Toric code with $d',d-d'\geq 2$, including the 4D Toric code. Under sufficiently weak local-stochastic Pauli noise, our construction uses noiseless, bounded-depth classical processing per physical time step. Its correction cycle acts only on the current syndrome, has constant depth, and is repeated unchanged during idle logical computation; it requires neither multiscale decoder states nor scale-dependent communication delays.
  Our proof treats errors and syndromes as chains in a cubical complex, combining geometric shrinking under the sweep rule with a space--time explanation-tree argument inspired by Toom's theorem. It does not rely on expansion. We establish three results:
  1.Explicit higher-dimensional sweep rule. We give a local algorithm for choosing sweep corrections on cubical $(d,d')$-Toric complexes, resolving the local-existence question of Kubica and Preskill.
  2. Fault-tolerant computation. We prove a circuit-level threshold theorem for noisy sweep cycles interleaved with logical gates. In particular, the 4D Toric code admits a fixed, constant-depth syndrome-based correction cycle without a multiscale decoder or expansion-based encoding. We do not claim constant total-depth overhead.
  3. Ideal decoding under local-stochastic noise. For an initial local-stochastic Pauli error of rate $p$ below threshold, $n^{d+1}$ noiseless sweep cycles recover the encoded state on a side-length-$n$ $(d,d')$-Toric code with probability at least $1-O(\operatorname{poly}(n))p^{Ω(n)}$, extending earlier guarantees for independent errors.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a fault-tolerant quantum computation scheme using a fixed, local, constant-depth sweep-rule correction cycle on cubical (d,d')-Toric codes (including 4D), proving a circuit-level threshold theorem and ideal decoding under local-stochastic Pauli noise without multiscale decoders or expansion assumptions.
AI.motivation: Existing toric-code decoders typically require multiscale decoder states, scale-dependent communication delays, or expansion-based arguments. The authors aim to show that a simple, geometrically local, constant-depth correction rule (the sweep rule) suffices for fault tolerance, addressing the local-existence question of Kubica and Preskill for higher-dimensional cubical complexes.
AI.method: Errors and syndromes are treated as chains in a cubical complex. The approach combines geometric shrinking under a higher-dimensional sweep rule with a space-time explanation-tree argument inspired by Toom's theorem, avoiding reliance on expansion. The correction cycle acts only on the current syndrome with constant depth, is repeated unchanged during idle computation, and uses bounded-depth noiseless classical processing per time step.
AI.result: Three results: (1) an explicit higher-dimensional sweep rule—a local algorithm choosing sweep corrections on cubical (d,d')-Toric complexes, resolving Kubica–Preskill's local-existence question; (2) a circuit-level threshold theorem for noisy sweep cycles interleaved with logical gates, notably giving the 4D Toric code a fixed constant-depth syndrome-based correction cycle without multiscale decoding or expansion-based encoding; (3) for local-stochastic Pauli noise of rate p below threshold, n^{d+1} noiseless sweep cycles recover the encoded state on a side-length-n code with probability at least 1 − O(poly(n)) p^{Ω(n)}, extending earlier guarantees beyond independent errors. The authors do not claim constant total-depth overhead.
AI.conclusion: Fault tolerance is achievable with a fixed, local, constant-depth sweep-rule correction cycle on geometrically simple cubical Toric codes under weak local-stochastic noise, without multiscale decoders, expansion, or scale-dependent delays.

title: Drive-tunable Floquet exchange spectroscopy with Hong--Ou--Mandel interference
summary: Floquet driving reshapes cavity spectra, but single-photon sideband populations do not reveal how it changes two-photon exchange. Here we show theoretically that delay-resolved Hong--Ou--Mandel (HOM) coincidences can probe this response in a collectively coupled cavity. A frequency-entangled signal photon scatters linearly from the driven cavity while its idler provides a delayed reference. Averaging over an unsynchronized drive phase removes coherence between different net output orders but preserves exchange interference within each order. Fourier transformation of the coincidence trace yields two drive-dependent exchange branches associated with the Floquet-polariton spectrum. As the drive changes, the branches shift and exchange weight; the dominant physical output order also changes, a transfer not reproduced by single-photon sideband populations. We further map the coincidence-trace response over drive frequency and amplitude and connect it to a count-model-dependent Fisher information. Floquet control thus adds a tunable exchange spectrum to HOM interferometry and gives quantitative targets for an experiment.

AI.tldr: Delay-resolved HOM coincidences can probe how Floquet driving reshapes two-photon exchange in a collectively coupled cavity, revealing drive-dependent exchange branches and a physical output-order transfer invisible to single-photon sideband populations.
AI.motivation: Floquet driving reshapes cavity spectra, yet single-photon sideband populations cannot reveal how driving alters two-photon exchange, so a two-photon-sensitive probe is needed.
AI.method: Theoretical study of a collectively coupled driven cavity probed by HOM interferometry: a frequency-entangled signal photon scatters linearly from the driven cavity while its idler provides a delayed reference; averaging over an unsynchronized drive phase removes inter-order coherence while preserving intra-order exchange interference, and Fourier transformation of the coincidence trace is analyzed.
AI.result: The Fourier-transformed coincidence trace yields two drive-dependent exchange branches tied to the Floquet-polariton spectrum; as the drive varies, these branches shift and their exchange weight redistributes, and the dominant physical output order transfers—a transfer not reproduced by single-photon sideband populations. The coincidence-trace response is furthermore mapped over drive frequency and amplitude and linked to a count-model-dependent Fisher information.
AI.conclusion: Floquet control adds a tunable exchange spectrum to HOM interferometry and provides quantitative experimental targets.

title: Execution bias, repeatability and mitigation cost in parameter-frozen molecular VQE energy evaluation
summary: A smaller statistical error bar need not mean a more accurate molecular energy. We evaluate noiselessly optimized molecular variational quantum eigensolver states on IBM Aachen and Pittsburgh, two 156-qubit Heron processors (provider-reported revision 3). Only energy evaluation runs on hardware, with parameters, layouts and compiled circuits frozen and dynamical decoupling disabled. A five-molecule pilot, three-molecule isolated cohort in three windows and known-state controls comprise 110 jobs and 28.2 billed quantum processing unit (QPU) minutes; the isolated cohort spans 30.2 h within a 31.7 h campaign. Raw 1024 O2 and BeH2 mean residuals exceed returned uncertainty by factors 12-32. Pittsburgh BeH2 cross-job standard deviation is 5.6 times mean returned uncertainty. The zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) package reduces O2 absolute residuals by 49.7% on Aachen and 83.5% on Pittsburgh at about fourfold charge. On Pittsburgh, twirled readout error extinction (TREX) removes 80 millihartree (mHa) per Raw 1024 job charge versus 50 mHa for ZNE. Controls reveal qubit-124 preparation or readout errors 5.4-5.6 times calibration; 13 mitigated energy point estimates fall outside the mapped spectrum, with no Raw counterpart. These results support workload checks and repeated measurements before additional sampling.

AI.tldr: A smaller statistical error bar does not imply a more accurate molecular energy: on two 156-qubit Heron processors, raw variational eigensolver residuals exceed reported uncertainty by 12–32×, and mitigation (TREX, ZNE) trades large charge for partial bias reduction while some mitigated estimates fall outside the physical spectrum.
AI.motivation: Practitioners commonly conflate statistical uncertainty with total accuracy in molecular variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) experiments; this work aims to test whether returned error bars on real hardware actually bound the deviation from reference energies, and to quantify the cost/benefit of error mitigation.
AI.method: Noiselessly optimized VQE states are frozen (parameters, layouts, compiled circuits) and evaluated on IBM Aachen and Pittsburgh (156-qubit Heron, revision 3) with only energy evaluation on hardware and dynamical decoupling disabled. A five-molecule pilot, a three-molecule isolated cohort measured across three windows, and known-state controls total 110 jobs / 28.2 billed QPU minutes (cohort spanning 30.2 h in a 31.7 h campaign). Raw 1024-shot runs are compared against TREX and ZNE, with residual-vs-uncertainty ratios and per-job charge efficiency assessed.
AI.result: Raw 1024-shot mean residuals for O2 and BeH2 exceed returned uncertainty by 12–32×; Pittsburgh BeH2 cross-job standard deviation is 5.6× the mean returned uncertainty. ZNE cuts O2 absolute residuals by 49.7% (Aachen) and 83.5% (Pittsburgh) at ~4× charge. On Pittsburgh, TREX removes 80 mHa per Raw-1024 job-charge versus 50 mHa for ZNE. Controls show qubit-124 preparation/readout errors 5.4–5.6× calibration, and 13 mitigated point estimates fall outside the mapped energy spectrum with no Raw counterpart.
AI.conclusion: Reported statistical error bars are unreliable proxies for molecular-energy accuracy on current hardware, and mitigation can introduce spectrum-violating bias. The authors recommend workload-level validation and repeated measurements before spending additional sampling budget.

title: High-Threshold Fusion-Based Quantum Computation with Optical Hybrid Qubits
summary: Hybrid discrete- and continuous-variable (DV-CV) encodings have been developed to overcome operational drawbacks of each individual encoding, while fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC) has emerged to address the practical challenges of scalability toward fault-tolerant photonic quantum computation. Here we introduce hybrid FBQC using small optical DV-CV hybrid resource states connected through hybrid fusions, to combine the advantages of both approaches. We develop protocols for directly generating these resource states without requiring local hybrid logic such as the Hadamard gate, together with a tailored decoding strategy that exploits the error information contained in individual hybrid-fusion outcomes. We demonstrate that hybrid FBQC achieves a photon loss threshold of 2.231% while requiring only 12 hybrid fusions per surface-code unit cell, substantially improving upon the 0.89% threshold and 60-fusion requirement of previous hybrid measurement-based scheme. These results establish optical hybrid FBQC as a high-threshold resource-efficient route to scalable fault-tolerant photonic quantum computation.

AI.tldr: Introduces hybrid FBQC using small optical DV-CV hybrid resource states connected through hybrid fusions, achieving a 2.231% photon loss threshold with only 12 fusions per surface-code unit cell.
AI.motivation: Individual DV and CV encodings each have operational drawbacks, and hybrid DV-CV encodings overcome these; simultaneously, FBQC addresses scalability challenges toward fault-tolerant photonic quantum computation. The paper aims to combine the advantages of these approaches.
AI.method: Hybrid FBQC built from small optical DV-CV hybrid resource states joined by hybrid fusions. Protocols directly generate these resource states without local hybrid logic such as the Hadamard gate, plus a tailored decoding strategy exploiting error information in individual hybrid-fusion outcomes.
AI.result: Photon loss threshold of 2.231% requiring only 12 hybrid fusions per surface-code unit cell, improving on the 0.89% threshold and 60-fusion requirement of prior hybrid measurement-based schemes.
AI.conclusion: Optical hybrid FBQC is established as a high-threshold, resource-efficient route to scalable fault-tolerant photonic quantum computation.

title: Adaptive Local Measurements For Quantum Learning Can Exponentially Outperform Nonadaptive Global Measurements
summary: Can measurements chosen adaptively, in response to earlier outcomes, be exponentially more informative than measurements fixed in advance? In many quantum settings, adaptivity helps at most polynomially; known exponential advantages require coherent measurements across copies or restricted measurements. We show an exponential advantage measuring one copy at a time, with no quantum memory kept between state copies, even when the nonadaptive learner may perform arbitrary global measurements on each copy. We construct explicit families of multi-qubit states in which a scalar parameter is encoded in one of exponentially many candidate observables, with an auxiliary marker indicating which one. An adaptive protocol identifies the relevant observable and then measures it using only single-qubit measurements and one round of adaptation. At fixed accuracy, it needs logarithmically many copies as the qubit count grows, whereas every nonadaptive protocol needs exponentially many. The same mechanism yields an exponential gap in local asymptotic minimax mean squared error constants, tight up to the exponential base. The states are separable and classical in label-dependent product bases; no entanglement or other nonclassical correlations are required. The gap comes from measurement incompatibility: the candidate observables cannot be measured jointly, so a fixed measurement must divide its information budget among them, while adaptivity selects the informative one. Accordingly, the separation disappears when the candidate observables commute, and cannot occur with fully observed classical samples. Measurement incompatibility thus emerges as a resource for quantum learning, distinct from entanglement and quantum memory, that classical feedback alone can exploit.

AI.tldr: Adaptive, one-copy-at-a-time measurements with single-qubit measurements and one round of feedback achieve an exponential advantage over nonadaptive protocols (even with arbitrary global measurements per copy) for estimating a scalar parameter encoded in one of exponentially many incompatible observables; the source is measurement incompatibility.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows adaptivity gives at most polynomial gains in many quantum settings, and known exponential separations require coherent multi-copy measurements or restricted measurement classes. The paper asks whether adaptivity alone, with no quantum memory and only single-copy access, can be exponentially more informative than nonadaptive global measurements.
AI.method: Construct explicit families of multi-qubit states where a scalar parameter is encoded in one of exponentially many candidate observables, with an auxiliary marker identifying which. An adaptive protocol uses the marker to select the relevant observable, then measures it via single-qubit measurements with one round of adaptation. Compare against optimal nonadaptive protocols allowed arbitrary global measurements per copy, analyzing sample complexity at fixed accuracy and local asymptotic minimax MSE constants.
AI.result: The adaptive protocol needs only logarithmically many copies in the qubit count at fixed accuracy, while every nonadaptive protocol needs exponentially many. The same mechanism yields an exponential gap in local asymptotic minimax MSE constants, tight up to the exponential base. States are separable and classical in label-dependent product bases (no entanglement needed). The separation vanishes when candidate observables commute and cannot occur with fully observed classical samples.
AI.conclusion: Measurement incompatibility is a resource for quantum learning, distinct from entanglement and quantum memory, exploitable by classical feedback alone. Adaptivity can be exponentially more informative than fixed measurements even under single-copy, memoryless, single-qubit-measurement constraints.

title: Fully Quantum Latent Diffusion for Synthetic Malware Records: Effective Denoising, Limited Class Information, and Costly Post-Selection
summary: Malware benchmarks are difficult to share, because the samples are harmful and a corpus can reveal the incidents of its holder, while synthetic substitutes can leak training records. Quantum diffusion models, however, have been evaluated only on images or quantum states, leaving the utility, privacy, and sampling cost of their samples unknown. In this research, we introduce a fully quantum latent diffusion model for malware records, in which a parameterized circuit with one mid-circuit measurement denoises amplitude-encoded latent vectors of opcode sequences without classical neural layers. On 17 malware families with ten seeds, we compared it with random states, a perfect generator, a parameter-matched classical control, and a classical latent diffusion model. The circuit lowers its denoising infidelity by 63\%, yet classifiers trained on its records reach a macro-F1 score of 0.11 on real records, against 0.08 for random states, 0.61 for a perfect generator, and 0.44 for a classical diffusion model of comparable size, and adding its records to real training data lowers the score from 0.635 to 0.593. Post-selected sampling accepts $3.0\times10^{-7}$ of runs, and a training penalty that raises the acceptance to 0.14 removes most of the denoising. No synthetic record copies a training record, and smoothing the decoded lengths lowers the area under the curve of a length-based membership test from 0.80 to 0.51, which a differentially private length histogram matches with a formal guarantee. These results indicate that quantum generators of shareable security data require a joint evaluation of utility, privacy, and sampling cost.

AI.tldr: A fully quantum latent diffusion model generates synthetic malware records, but joint evaluation shows poor downstream utility, negligible memorization risk, and prohibitive post-selection sampling cost.
AI.motivation: Malware corpora are hard to share (harmful samples, holder-incident leakage) and classical synthetic substitutes can leak training records. Quantum diffusion models have only been tested on images or quantum states, so the utility, privacy, and sampling cost of their generated samples are unknown.
AI.method: Introduces a fully quantum latent diffusion model for malware records: a parameterized circuit with one mid-circuit measurement denoises amplitude-encoded latent vectors of opcode sequences, with no classical neural layers. Compared against random states, a perfect generator, a parameter-matched classical control, and a classical latent diffusion model over 17 malware families with ten seeds; evaluates denoising infidelity, downstream macro-F1, memorization, a length-based membership inference test, and post-selected sampling acceptance.
AI.result: Denoising infidelity drops 63%, yet classifiers trained on synthetic records reach macro-F1 0.11 on real data (vs. 0.08 random, 0.61 perfect generator, 0.44 classical diffusion), and augmenting real data lowers score from 0.635 to 0.593. Post-selected sampling accepts 3.0e-7 of runs; a training penalty raising acceptance to 0.14 removes most denoising. No synthetic record copies a training record; length smoothing lowers membership-test AUC from 0.80 to 0.51, matched by a differentially private length histogram with a formal guarantee.
AI.conclusion: Quantum generators of shareable security data require joint evaluation of utility, privacy, and sampling cost; the model is privacy-preserving but offers limited utility and impractical sampling cost.

title: High bandwidth heterodyne sensing with bulk NV diamond
summary: Developing high performance portable sensors is of significant importance for both terrestrial and satellite communications, with quantum sensors offering potential advantages in sensitivity and bandwidth. The nitrogen vacancy center in diamond is a popular quantum sensing platform for its relative simplicity and wide range of acceptable operating conditions, but suffers a limited instantaneous bandwidth due to the narrow linewidth of the spin resonance. In this work, we first present a magnetic quantum sensing scheme utilizing heterodyne mixing with strong optical and microwave driving, achieving MHz-scale instantaneous bandwidth with a sensitivity of $548 \; \text{pT/}\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ in an active diamond volume of $ 2.5\times 10^{-4} \; \text{mm}^3$ with $2 \times 10^{11}$ NV centers. We then demonstrate expansion of the sensing bandwidth by employing a strong magnetic gradient and many individually modulated microwave control fields, expanding the single resonance bandwidth to 48 MHz with a peak sensitivity of $8.5 \; \text{nT/}\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$.

AI.tldr: A diamond NV-center magnetometer using heterodyne mixing under strong optical/microwave driving achieves MHz-scale instantaneous bandwidth at 548 pT/√Hz, and a magnetic-gradient plus multi-tone microwave scheme broadens single-resonance bandwidth to 48 MHz.
AI.motivation: Portable high-performance sensors matter for terrestrial and satellite communications, and quantum sensors promise gains in sensitivity and bandwidth. The diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center is attractive for its simplicity and wide operating conditions, but its narrow spin-resonance linewidth limits instantaneous bandwidth.
AI.method: The authors use a magnetic quantum sensing scheme based on heterodyne mixing with strong optical and microwave driving to widen instantaneous bandwidth. They further extend bandwidth by applying a strong magnetic field gradient together with many individually modulated microwave control fields.
AI.result: The heterodyne scheme reaches MHz-scale instantaneous bandwidth with sensitivity of 548 pT/√Hz in an active diamond volume of 2.5×10⁻⁴ mm³ containing 2×10¹¹ NV centers. The gradient/multi-tone approach expands single-resonance bandwidth to 48 MHz with peak sensitivity of 8.5 nT/√Hz.
AI.conclusion: Strong optical/microwave-driven heterodyne mixing and gradient-based multi-tone control overcome the NV linewidth bottleneck, offering a route to wideband, compact quantum magnetometers for communication applications, at the cost of reduced sensitivity when bandwidth is greatly expanded.

title: Fate of Quantum Magic
summary: Magic, a quantum resource distinct from entanglement, measures departure from states stabilized by products of Pauli operators. Such stabilizer states can be maximally entangled yet admit efficient classical description: quantum advantage requires magic. We develop a powerful framework to evaluate the degree of magic in generic many-body states. We use it to study the fate of magic under thermal and dynamical evolution. In the transverse field Ising model, we find a thermal sudden death of magic that saturates with system size, and occurs after the death of entanglement. We reach similar conclusions in generic spin chains, and in the Kitaev quantum spin liquid on the honeycomb lattice, where the threshold shows an intricate dependence on subregion shape. We then study how magic equilibrates after a quantum quench. In quenches of generic spin chains, the magic of a subregion typically dies before entanglement, contrary to thermal trajectories. An explanation is given in terms of the geometry of non-magical states. As a third type of trajectory, we examine the fate of magic with separation with an appropriate notion of non-local magic and establish a sudden death. Finally, we show how to experimentally witness a volume law of frame-robust magic in quantum materials by using neutron scattering.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a general framework to quantify magic (non-stabilizerness) in generic many-body states, and use it to characterize how magic dies and equilibrates under thermal, quench, and spatial-separation dynamics, plus propose a neutron-scattering witness for volume-law frame-robust magic.
AI.motivation: Magic is the resource that distinguishes stabilizer states—efficiently describable even when maximally entangled—from states enabling quantum advantage, yet its behavior in many-body systems and under dynamics is poorly understood compared with entanglement.
AI.method: A framework for evaluating the degree of magic in generic many-body states is developed and applied to thermal and dynamical evolution: the transverse field Ising model, generic spin chains, and the Kitaev honeycomb quantum spin liquid; post-quench equilibration of subregion magic is analyzed and interpreted geometrically via the structure of non-magical states; a non-local notion of magic is introduced for spatial separation; an experimental protocol based on neutron scattering is proposed.
AI.result: A thermal sudden death of magic is found that saturates with system size and occurs after entanglement death in the TFIM, with similar behavior in generic spin chains and shape-dependent thresholds in the Kitaev spin liquid. Under quenches of generic spin chains, subregion magic typically dies before entanglement—opposite to thermal trajectories. Magic under separation exhibits a sudden death for the non-local notion. A volume law of frame-robust magic is shown to be experimentally accessible via neutron scattering.
AI.conclusion: Magic exhibits abrupt, "sudden death" behavior distinct from entanglement across thermal, quench, and separation trajectories, with ordering relative to entanglement depending on the trajectory type; the framework enables quantitative many-body studies of non-stabilizerness and its experimental detection in quantum materials.

title: Individually Addressed Logical Pauli Measurements by QLDPC Surgery on a Trapped Ion Quantum Computer
summary: Quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) codes may lead to order-of-magnitude reductions in the qubit overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Achieving this improved overhead requires logical operations that selectively address individual logical qubits encoded within multi-qubit code blocks. Recently proposed architectures achieve this through QLDPC surgery, in which non-destructive Pauli measurements are performed using ancillary ''gadget'' systems transiently entangled with the code block, generalising lattice surgery. Here we implement QLDPC surgery on a [[10,2,3]] generalised bicycle code using Quantinuum's H2-2 trapped ion processor. A single-round surgery measurement using seven gadget qubits measures the $\bar{X}_1$ operator with a 0.72 [0.32, 1.41]% (95% credible interval) error rate and agrees with subsequent transversal measurement with 1.03 [0.60, 1.65]% error. Decoding across three rounds of syndrome extraction suppresses the gadget measurement error, reducing the error rate to below 0.26%. The syndrome after surgery confirms return to the code space and the unaddressed ''spectator'' qubit is preserved with error 0.21 [0.04, 0.67]% during the three-round measurement. We further demonstrate composition of conjugate basis gadgets by sequentially measuring $\bar{X}_1$ then $\bar{Z}_2$, reusing the gadget qubits, and obtain a 1.12 [0.60, 1.94]% error in the $\bar{Z}_2$ measurement. These results constitute a hardware validation of the generalised surgery primitive underlying Pauli-based computing for QLDPC architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally implements quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) surgery on a [[10,2,3]] generalised bicycle code using a trapped-ion processor, demonstrating selective logical Pauli measurements, error suppression via multi-round decoding, and preservation of spectator qubits.
AI.motivation: QLDPC codes promise large reductions in qubit overhead for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but realizing this benefit requires the ability to selectively address individual logical qubits within multi-qubit code blocks. The recently proposed QLDPC surgery primitive—a generalization of lattice surgery using ancillary gadget systems—had lacked experimental hardware validation.
AI.method: The authors implement single-round QLDPC surgery on a [[10,2,3]] generalised bicycle code on Quantinuum's H2-2 trapped-ion processor. A seven-gadget-qubit measurement is used to measure the logical operator X̄₁, with comparison to a subsequent transversal measurement. They additionally decode across three rounds of syndrome extraction and demonstrate composition of conjugate-basis gadgets by sequentially measuring X̄₁ then Z̄₂ while reusing gadget qubits.
AI.result: The single-round X̄₁ surgery measurement achieves a 0.72% [0.32, 1.41]% error rate (95% credible interval) and agrees with the subsequent transversal measurement at 1.03% [0.60, 1.65]% error. Decoding across three syndrome-extraction rounds suppresses the gadget measurement error below 0.26%. Post-surgery syndrome confirms return to code space, and the unaddressed spectator qubit is preserved with 0.21% [0.04, 0.67]% error over three rounds. The composed X̄₁-then-Z̄₂ gadget sequence yields 1.12% [0.60, 1.94]% error in the Z̄₂ measurement.
AI.conclusion: These results constitute a hardware validation of the generalized surgery primitive underlying Pauli-based computing for QLDPC architectures, confirming selective logical addressing, multi-round error suppression, spectator-qubit preservation, and gadget composition/reuse on real quantum hardware.

title: Time-Switching Energy-Harvesting Quantum Relay-Assisted FSO Communication with Displaced Squeezed Signaling
summary: This paper investigates a quantum relay-assisted free-space optical (FSO) communication system in which a decode-and-forward relay is powered by time-switching optical energy harvesting and forwards the decoded information using displaced squeezed signaling (DSS). To obtain a physically con sistent description of turbulence-induced loss for non-classical signaling, each hop is modeled as a pure-loss bosonic chan nel whose random transmissivity follows a truncated Gamma Gamma law, i.e., the Gamma-Gamma irradiance conditioned on the physically admissible range of a transmittance. Under this channel, coherent states remain pure, whereas squeezed states are mapped to mixed Gaussian states. Under Helstrom-optimal detection, the average error of the coherent hop is derived in exact Laplace-series form. For the DSS hop, we derive the output states, a closed-form Gaussian fidelity with rigorous two sided bounds on the Helstrom error, and prove the existence of a loss-aware optimal photon partition. Furthermore, we prove that optimized squeezing preserves both the turbulence-induced diversity order and the leading asymptotic constant of coherent relaying, so that its benefit is a finite-photon-budget effect, and that an interior throughput-optimal harvesting fraction exists. A covariance-preserving benchmark with an exact series representation yields an analytical upper bound on the achievable throughput whose absolute gap vanishes as the relay photon budget grows. Numerical results based on the exact mixed-state Helstrom error quantify the benefit of squeezing and the regime in which it is useful.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes a quantum relay-assisted FSO system with time-switching energy harvesting and displaced squeezed signaling, deriving exact and bounded Helstrom error expressions and proving squeezing preserves diversity order while yielding finite-budget gains.
AI.motivation: Non-classical signaling (squeezed states) in relay-assisted FSO links under turbulence lacks a physically consistent channel model and rigorous performance analysis; the paper aims to establish such a description and quantify when squeezing actually helps.
AI.method: Each hop is modeled as a pure-loss bosonic channel with truncated Gamma-Gamma transmissivity; coherent states stay pure while squeezed states become mixed Gaussian states. Exact Laplace-series Helstrom error for the coherent hop; for the DSS hop, output states, closed-form Gaussian fidelity with two-sided Helstrom bounds, and analysis of optimal photon partition, diversity order, and throughput-optimal harvesting fraction; a covariance-preserving benchmark gives an analytical throughput upper bound.
AI.result: Optimized squeezing preserves the turbulence-induced diversity order and leading asymptotic constant of coherent relaying (benefit is a finite-photon-budget effect); an interior throughput-optimal harvesting fraction exists; the benchmark's absolute throughput gap vanishes as relay photon budget grows; numerics quantify squeezing benefit and its useful regime.
AI.conclusion: Displaced squeezed signaling offers practically relevant, bounded gains over coherent relaying but no asymptotic advantage; the truncated Gamma-Gamma pure-loss model provides a rigorous framework for non-classical FSO relay analysis.

title: Reverse Quantum Annealing for Ground-State Energy Calculation in Molecule
summary: We present the results of our reverse quantum annealing computations of the ground-state energies of alkaline-earth monofluoride molecules. By partitioning the Dirac--Coulomb electronic Hamiltonian into sub-QUBOs and refining forward-annealing solutions through optimized reverse-annealing schedules, residual configuration errors are systematically minimized. The electronic ground-state wave functions and energies are obtained using the Quantum Annealing Eigensolver algorithm. This work provides a pathway for achieving sub-milliHartree chemical accuracy and advancing molecular electronic structure calculations in the quantum annealing paradigm.

AI.tldr: Reverse quantum annealing, combined with sub-QUBO Hamiltonian partitioning and an optimized reverse-annealing schedule, refines forward-annealing solutions to compute ground-state energies of alkaline-earth monofluoride molecules toward sub-milliHartree chemical accuracy.
AI.motivation: Forward quantum annealing solutions for molecular electronic structure retain residual configuration errors; the authors aim to suppress these and push quantum-annealing-based chemistry toward sub-milliHartree (chemical) accuracy.
AI.method: The Dirac–Coulomb electronic Hamiltonian is partitioned into sub-QUBOs. Forward-annealing solutions are refined via optimized reverse-annealing schedules, and ground-state wave functions and energies are extracted with the Quantum Annealing Eigensolver (QAE) algorithm.
AI.result: Residual configuration errors are systematically minimized, yielding ground-state energies and wave functions for alkaline-earth monofluoride molecules with improved accuracy approaching sub-milliHartree level.
AI.conclusion: Reverse annealing plus sub-QUBO partitioning is a viable route to sub-milliHartree chemical accuracy for molecular electronic structure calculations within the quantum annealing paradigm.

title: Beyond energy bounds: comparing Schrödinger eigenstates
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Core numerical code: https://github.com/Hronrad/ordered-schrodinger-eigenstates
summary: We derive eigenstate comparisons from ordered Schrödinger operators, extending energy bounds to overlaps, spatial distributions and nodes. For three form-ordered operators with discrete comparison ground states, suppose the upper ground-state energy lies in the lower operator's ground-state gap. Three comparison spectral values then bound all three squared ground-state overlaps and guarantee a simple discrete intermediate ground state. Related gap estimates control low-energy subspaces and individual excited-state overlaps under additional gap conditions. In one dimension and radially, a single crossing of the potential difference relative to the energy shift orders ground-state likelihood ratios and monotone observables; a nondecreasing difference suffices. The results cover asymmetric wells and shortened right Dirichlet walls, with coordinatewise comparisons for submodular reference potentials and coordinatewise nondecreasing perturbations. A two-sided Sturm argument orders corresponding internal nodes for nondecreasing potential differences, even between orthogonal one-dimensional excited states. For Yukawa ground states, Hulthén comparisons bound overlaps, radial moments and the density at the nucleus; the latter two-sided bounds hold for screening $0<δ<2/\sqrt6$. Optimizing scaled Hulthén majorants gives a lower bound of approximately $1.13611$ for $n^2δ_c(n,0)$, where $δ_c(n,0)$ is the critical screening for the $n$th $s$-wave bound state. This bound is optimal within that two-parameter comparison family.

AI.tldr: The paper turns order relations between Schrödinger operators into bounds on eigenstate overlaps, spatial densities and nodes, and applies the machinery to Yukawa/Hulthén ground states to obtain an optimal lower bound of about 1.13611 for the scaled critical screening constant n²δ_c(n,0).
AI.motivation: Classical comparison theory for Schrödinger operators orders energies (min–max, Sturm oscillation). The authors want to extend this ordering principle beyond eigenvalues, so that form-ordering of potentials also yields quantitative information on eigenfunctions — overlap between ground states, likelihood-ratio/monotonicity of densities, and node locations — and then deploy it to sharpen knowledge of critical screening for Yukawa-type potentials.
AI.method: Three form-ordered operators with discrete comparison ground states are studied; when the upper ground-state energy falls in the lower operator's ground-state gap, three comparison spectral values bound all three squared ground-state overlaps and force a simple intermediate ground state. Gap estimates extend this to low-energy subspaces and excited-state overlaps. In 1D and radially, a single crossing (or merely nondecreasing difference) of the potential difference relative to the energy shift orders ground-state likelihood ratios and monotone observables; coordinatewise arguments handle submodular reference potentials with coordinatewise nondecreasing perturbations. A two-sided Sturm argument orders internal nodes for nondecreasing differences, including orthogonal 1D excited states. For Yukawa ground states, Hulthén majorants give overlap, radial-moment and nuclear-density bounds for 0<δ<2/√6, and optimization over a two-parameter family of scaled Hulthén majorants is performed.
AI.result: Overlap bounds via three comparison spectral values; guaranteed simple intermediate ground state; gap-controlled low-energy subspace and excited-state overlap estimates; ordering of likelihood ratios and monotone observables under a single potential-difference crossing; node ordering for nondecreasing differences; two-sided Hulthén bounds on Yukawa overlaps, radial moments and nuclear density valid for 0<δ<2/√6; and an optimal-in-family lower bound n²δ_c(n,0) ≳ 1.13611.
AI.conclusion: Form-ordering of Schrödinger operators is a flexible tool for comparing eigenstates, not just energies, and yields sharp, optimal-within-family constraints on Yukawa critical screening, with potential for further refinement via richer comparison families.

title: Signatures of Narrowband and Ultrashort-Pulse-Like Probing in Coherent Anti-Stokes Raman Scattering Using Twin Beams and Sum-Frequency Generation Readout
summary: We theoretically investigate coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) driven by bright twin beams with sum-frequency generation (SFG) readout. Expressing the SFG output in terms of quantum-field correlation functions yields multiple correlation structures with distinct properties associated with different interaction pathways on the bra and ket sides. Among them, frequency correlations between the CARS probe and SFG gating fields enable the two fields to act collectively as an effective narrowband probe, avoiding probe-induced spectral convolution. When this behavior appears on either the bra or ket side, the other retains Raman relaxation information as if probed by an ultrashort pulse.

AI.tldr: Theoretical study of CARS driven by bright twin beams with SFG readout, showing that quantum-field correlation functions yield distinct correlation structures, and that frequency correlations between CARS probe and SFG gating fields create an effective narrowband probe avoiding spectral convolution.
AI.motivation: Conventional CARS suffers from probe-induced spectral convolution that obscures Raman relaxation information; the authors aim to exploit quantum correlations in bright twin beams to overcome this limitation in a nonlinear spectroscopic measurement.
AI.method: Express the SFG output of the twin-beam-driven CARS process in terms of quantum-field correlation functions, and classify the resulting correlation structures by their associated interaction pathways on the bra and ket sides.
AI.result: Multiple distinct correlation structures emerge corresponding to different bra/ket interaction pathways; frequency correlations between the CARS probe and SFG gating fields make the two fields act collectively as an effective narrowband probe, and when this occurs on one side (bra or ket), the other side retains Raman relaxation information as if probed by an ultrashort pulse.
AI.conclusion: Quantum frequency correlations in bright twin beams enable a scheme that avoids probe-induced spectral convolution while preserving ultrafast-pulse-like access to Raman relaxation dynamics, offering a route to correlation-enhanced nonlinear Raman spectroscopy.

title: Resonance and Transition-Channel Competition in Cavity-Assisted Floquet-State Stabilization
summary: Static coupling to a dissipative cavity has been proposed as a route to autonomously stabilize Floquet eigenstates. The cavity provides an energy-selective relaxation channel: when its photon energy matches a quasienergy difference modulo drive quanta, it mediates transitions between Floquet states, followed by irreversible photon loss. Here, we show that at intermediate driving frequencies, this resonance condition alone is not sufficient for stabilization. Instead, the steady state is controlled by the interplay between resonance selection and the cavity-induced transition strengths between Floquet states, which can either cooperate or compete. This interplay leads to successful stabilization, mixed steady states despite resonance, and complete breakdown near Floquet-zone hybridization. We further show that the same mechanism extends to multilevel spin-S systems, providing a general framework for understanding when static dissipation can reliably stabilize driven quantum states.
