AI.tldr: Resonance matching alone is insufficient for cavity-based Floquet stabilization at intermediate drive frequencies; steady states are set by the interplay between resonance selection and cavity-induced transition strengths, yielding stabilization, mixed states, or breakdown near Floquet-zone hybridization.
AI.motivation: Static coupling to a dissipative cavity has been proposed as a way to autonomously stabilize Floquet eigenstates via an energy-selective relaxation channel. The paper tests whether the resonance condition (cavity photon energy matching a quasienergy difference modulo drive quanta) is sufficient for stabilization at intermediate driving frequencies.
AI.method: The authors analyze the competition between resonance selection and cavity-mediated transition strengths between Floquet states, examining the resulting steady states. They extend the analysis from the basic two-level case to multilevel spin-S systems.
AI.result: At intermediate driving frequencies, the resonance condition alone does not guarantee stabilization. Depending on whether transition strengths cooperate or compete with resonance selection, the system exhibits successful stabilization, mixed steady states even under resonance, and complete breakdown of stabilization near Floquet-zone hybridization. The mechanism generalizes to multilevel spin-S systems.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a general framework for determining when static dissipation can reliably stabilize driven quantum states, showing that both resonance selection and cavity-induced transition strengths must be considered jointly.

title: Force Sensing in a Recoverable Bosonic Quantum Memory
summary: In continuous-variable quantum information, sensing and quantum error correction in the same mode face an intrinsic trade-off: sensors must accumulate weak external displacements, whereas bosonic codes typically suppress such shifts as errors. Here, we establish compatibility by constructing finite-energy bosonic codes that enable a single oscillator to sense an external force while actively protecting an unknown logical qubit. By encoding logical amplitudes across discrete wave-packet sites and capturing the force signal in a shared internal coordinate, we achieve an endpoint probe readout that is independent of the logical state under continuous photon loss $γ$. Crucially, binomial site recovery cancels packet-dependent probe distortions alongside logical errors: for a $(2r+2)$-packet code, memory infidelity is suppressed to $O(γ^{r+1})$ while residual memory-probe correlations scale as $O(γ^{r+2})$. Finally, superconducting quantum circuit benchmarks under competing photon-number dephasing and Kerr nonlinearity identify preferred encoding regimes for hardware implementation.

AI.tldr: The paper designs finite-energy bosonic codes that let a single oscillator simultaneously sense weak external forces and protect an unknown logical qubit, resolving the sensing-versus-error-correction trade-off via wave-packet-site encoding and binomial recovery.
AI.motivation: In continuous-variable quantum information, sensing and quantum error correction in the same bosonic mode are intrinsically incompatible: sensors must accumulate weak external displacements, while bosonic codes treat such displacements as errors to be suppressed. This work aims to make the two functions compatible within a single oscillator.
AI.method: Logical amplitudes are encoded across discrete wave-packet sites, with the force signal captured in a shared internal coordinate, yielding an endpoint probe readout independent of the logical state under continuous photon loss γ. A binomial site-recovery protocol cancels packet-dependent probe distortions together with logical errors. Superconducting-circuit benchmarks under competing photon-number dephasing and Kerr nonlinearity are used to identify preferred encoding regimes.
AI.result: For a (2r+2)-packet code, memory infidelity is suppressed to O(γ^{r+1}) while the residual memory–probe correlation scales as O(γ^{r+2}). Circuit benchmarks under photon-number dephasing and Kerr nonlinearity reveal preferred encoding regimes for hardware implementation.
AI.conclusion: Finite-energy bosonic codes enable a single oscillator to sense an external force while actively protecting an unknown logical qubit, with binomial site recovery canceling both logical errors and probe distortions, and superconducting benchmarks indicating favorable hardware regimes.

title: Geometric Rényi divergence and RLD Fisher information under quantum processes without definite causal order
summary: Quantum experiments without a definite causal order offer new ways to distinguish devices, estimate physical parameters, and communicate. We prove a common limit on these tasks: the geometric Rényi divergence at the output of a deterministic completely positive process cannot exceed the sum of the divergences of its individual channel uses. The inequality holds for every Rényi order in $(0,1)\cup(1,2]$ and any number of independently replaceable channels. Parallel experiments with separate reference-assisted inputs approach the bound, giving an exact equality after optimization over processes. We also prove an additive bound on the right logarithmic derivative Fisher information of parameter-dependent channels under every fixed process in this class. A resulting Cramér--Rao bound limits locally unbiased estimation precision without assuming a definite causal order, and an erasure-probability example attains the bound. The proofs for the geometric Rényi divergence and RLD Fisher information follow from the requirement that every independent choice of channels produce a normalized output. We show how this requirement controls positive local operations, and how small channel perturbations convert the divergence inequality into a Fisher-information bound, including for singular channels. Further applications give finite-use bounds on channel discrimination and exclusion, together with communication and private-state-generation converses when the processes preserve the relevant comparison conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the geometric Rényi divergence at the output of any deterministic completely positive process is bounded by the sum of the divergences of its individual channel uses, and derives an additive RLD Fisher-information bound yielding causal-order-independent Cramér–Rao limits for discrimination, estimation, and communication tasks.
AI.motivation: Quantum experiments with indefinite causal order enable device discrimination, parameter estimation, and communication, but a common quantitative limit governing these tasks across arbitrary processes was lacking.
AI.method: Establishes a divergence inequality (geometric Rényi divergence at process output ≤ sum over individually replaceable channels) for all Rényi orders in (0,1)∪(1,2], using the normalization requirement for every independent channel choice; converts the divergence inequality into an additive RLD Fisher-information bound via small channel perturbations, including singular channels.
AI.result: The inequality holds for any number of independently replaceable channels; parallel experiments with separate reference-assisted inputs approach the bound, achieving exact equality after process optimization; an additive RLD Fisher-information bound yields a Cramér–Rao bound for locally unbiased estimation without definite causal order, with an erasure-probability example attaining it; finite-use discrimination/exclusion bounds and communication/private-state-generation converses follow under the relevant comparison conditions.
AI.conclusion: Indefinite causal order does not overcome a fundamental additive limit: process outputs obey a divergence additivity bound, from which estimation, discrimination, and communication limits follow for the entire class of deterministic completely positive processes.

title: Beyond Direct Imaging: Quantum Measurement Design for Small-Target Detection in UAV Hyperspectral Sensing
summary: Small mineral patches can be spectrally distinct yet difficult to detect when diffraction mixes their light with the surrounding rock. Conventional hyperspectral detectors analyze recorded intensities, leaving an opportunity to recover target evidence through the optical measurement itself. We develop a quantum-assisted framework for exploiting this opportunity in prospective unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) hyperspectral sensing. A common radiometric and diffraction model describes direct imaging and spatial-mode measurements of the same light. The theory identifies target changes that survive background fitting and explains when mode measurements retain more detection information. It quantifies losses from mode mismatch and unresolved outputs, linking the quantum benchmark to finite receiver design. A common-basis result identifies when material spectra can share a spatial measurement at fixed geometry. An adaptive receiver uses an imaging pilot to select candidate modes and combines both stages in a full-region presence test. Simulations based on measured mineral spectra and published UAV acquisition scales demonstrate gains over complete direct imaging at a shared active-exposure budget, including pilot cost and optical loss. At matched empirical 1\% region-level false alarms, detection increases from 62.95\% to 69.65\% for a representative target. Paired analysis supports gains with registration uncertainty and, separately, under controlled nonuniform backgrounds. Calibrated mode errors reveal where measurement losses weaken or reverse the benefit. These results connect background identifiability to receiver choices and their operating conditions. They provide a framework for designing spatial measurements alongside spectral channels to detect small material features.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a quantum-assisted framework that uses spatial-mode (diffraction-aware) measurements instead of only recorded intensities to detect small mineral patches in UAV hyperspectral sensing, showing detection gains over complete direct imaging at equal exposure budget.

The theory identifies target changes surviving background fitting, characterizes when mode measurements retain more detection information, quantifies losses from mode mismatch and unresolved outputs, and gives a common-basis result for sharing a spatial measurement at fixed geometry. AI.result: At a shared active-exposure budget (including pilot cost and optical loss) and matched empirical 1% region-level false alarms, detection rises from 62.95% to 69.65% for a representative target. Paired analysis supports gains under registration uncertainty and under controlled nonuniform backgrounds; calibrated mode errors show where measurement losses weaken or reverse the benefit.
AI.conclusion: The results link background identifiability to receiver choices and operating conditions, providing a framework for co-designing spatial measurements alongside spectral channels to detect small material features in UAV hyperspectral sensing.

title: A VLSI-Like Design and Verification Flow for Quantum Circuits: A Case Study in PI Estimation
summary: This paper proposes a VLSI-like design and verification flow for quantum circuit implementation, covering four levels: behavioral modeling, register-transfer level (RTL), gate level, and full-circuit integration with quantum algorithms. Using quantum Monte Carlo methods for pi estimation as a case study, the proposed flow provides a systematic path from initial specifications to large-scale quantum circuit implementation. The paper highlights two key contributions. First, quantum digital design supports a broad range of applications beyond predefined circuit templates. This capability is particularly important for application-specific operations in algorithms such as Shor's, Grover's, and quantum amplitude estimation (QAE), and can significantly advance fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). Second, classical simulation shows that replacing random sampling with grid sampling can achieve a quadratic improvement in this pi-estimation case without quantum computation. This suggests that the quadratic speedup may arise from the grid sampling strategy rather than from the QAE circuit itself. By adapting conventional VLSI digital design principles, this four-level flow addresses a key bottleneck in quantum circuit design and enables flexible design initiation from multiple entry points, including specifications, RTL, and gate-level descriptions, paving the way for the practical deployment of quantum computing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a VLSI-like four-level design and verification flow (behavioral, RTL, gate-level, full-circuit integration) for quantum circuits, demonstrated on quantum Monte Carlo pi estimation, and shows that grid sampling alone yields a quadratic improvement, suggesting the QAE speedup may stem from sampling strategy rather than the circuit.
AI.motivation: Quantum circuit design lacks a systematic methodology from specification to large-scale implementation, and existing approaches rely on predefined circuit templates that limit application-specific operations needed for algorithms like Shor's, Grover's, and QAE. A structured design flow is needed to address this bottleneck and support practical FTQC deployment.
AI.method: Adapts conventional VLSI digital design principles into a four-level flow: behavioral modeling, RTL, gate level, and full-circuit integration with quantum algorithms. The flow is validated using a quantum Monte Carlo pi-estimation case study, complemented by classical simulation comparing random sampling against grid sampling.
AI.result: The flow provides a systematic path from initial specifications to large-scale quantum circuit implementation and supports flexible design entry points (specifications, RTL, gate-level). Classical simulation shows that replacing random sampling with grid sampling achieves a quadratic improvement in the pi-estimation case without quantum computation.
AI.conclusion: Quantum digital design enables application-specific operations beyond predefined templates, advancing FTQC. However, the quadratic speedup observed may originate from the grid sampling strategy rather than the QAE circuit itself, and the proposed four-level VLSI-inspired flow addresses a key design bottleneck, paving the way for practical quantum computing deployment.

title: Efficient Quantum Optimization via Dissipative False Vacuum Decay
summary: Efficient quantum solvers for computationally hard problems are highly desirable for near-term quantum platforms. Here, we propose a cavity-based dissipative quantum solver for a class of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems encoded in atomic-spin Hamiltonians with a few discrete single-spin-flip transition energies. We show that the cavity-based quantum solver exploits dissipative false-vacuum decay in configuration space to facilitate escape from metastable local minima in rugged energy landscapes. Numerical studies of MaxCut and Maximum Independent Set identify favorable parameter regions for ground-state preparation. Based on the finite-size scalings of the median mixing time and instance-averaged ground-state preparation probability, we estimate time complexities for our solver that are more favorable than those of standard Grover search. These results highlight cavity dissipation as a controllable resource for quantum optimization.

AI.tldr: A cavity-based dissipative quantum solver exploits false-vacuum decay in configuration space to escape local minima of NP-hard spin-Hamiltonian optimization problems, achieving estimated time complexities more favorable than Grover search on MaxCut and Maximum Independent Set.
AI.motivation: Computationally hard (NP-hard) combinatorial optimization is a key target for near-term quantum platforms, motivating efficient quantum solvers. The work aims to turn dissipation—typically viewed as a liability—into a controllable optimization resource for rugged energy landscapes.
AI.method: The authors propose a dissipative quantum solver in which an atomic-spin Hamiltonian encoding NP-hard problems (with only a few discrete single-spin-flip transition energies) is coupled to a cavity. The solver leverages cavity-based dissipative false-vacuum decay in configuration space, allowing the system to escape metastable local minima. Performance is assessed via numerical simulations of MaxCut and Maximum Independent Set, identifying favorable parameter regimes for ground-state preparation.
AI.result: Numerical studies identify favorable parameter regions for ground-state preparation. Finite-size scaling of the median mixing time and the instance-averaged ground-state preparation probability yields estimated time complexities more favorable than standard Grover search.
AI.conclusion: Cavity dissipation serves as a controllable and beneficial resource for quantum optimization, offering a promising route to efficient solvers for hard combinatorial problems on near-term quantum platforms.

title: NAKO: A Benchmarking Framework for Evaluating and Diagnosing Neutral-Atom Quantum Compilers
summary: Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors couple gate scheduling, atom placement, and parallel atom transport, so compiler decisions jointly determine physical execution costs. Evaluating these compilers requires attainable resource references and a way to trace excess costs to their causes. We present NAKO, a benchmarking framework that parameterizes circuits by qubit count, logical depth, and requested one- and two-qubit gate densities, and assigns attainable targets for Rydberg stages, routing intervals, and movement layers. Each benchmark is paired with an executable reference schedule; under the stated execution model, construction guarantees minimum Rydberg-stage and routing-interval counts, and minimum movement among schedules with the minimum Rydberg-stage count. Comparing compiler outputs with these references quantifies resource gaps, while reference mappings and intermediate physical states enable controlled interventions that trace excess costs to specific compiler decisions. In a 648-run evaluation of Enola and OLSQ-DPQA, NAKO identifies distinct bottlenecks. For Enola, placement scoring and cross-stage layout management contribute to excess movement; diagnosis-guided interventions reduce mean movement by 78.9% across five matched circuits. For OLSQ-DPQA, premature candidate selection and limited exploration of preparatory states produce avoidable entangling stages and routing intervals; four fixed-checkpoint continuations each eliminate one Rydberg stage and one routing interval without increasing movement. NAKO thus links resource targets backed by constructive optimality guarantees to controlled diagnosis and validation of compiler-specific resource savings.

AI.tldr: NAKO is a benchmarking framework for neutral-atom quantum compilers that pairs circuits with achievable resource targets and executable reference schedules carrying constructive optimality guarantees, enabling quantification and causal diagnosis of resource gaps.
AI.motivation: Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors couple gate scheduling, atom placement, and parallel atom transport, so compiler decisions jointly determine physical execution costs. Evaluating such compilers therefore requires attainable resource references and a mechanism to trace excess costs back to their causes.
AI.method: NAKO parameterizes circuits by qubit count, logical depth, and requested one-/two-qubit gate densities, and assigns attainable targets for Rydberg stages, routing intervals, and movement layers. Each benchmark is paired with an executable reference schedule that guarantees minimum Rydberg-stage and routing-interval counts, plus minimum movement among schedules achieving the minimum Rydberg-stage count. Reference mappings and intermediate physical states support controlled interventions.
AI.result: In a 648-run evaluation of Enola and OLSQ-DPQA, NAKO exposed distinct bottlenecks. For Enola, placement scoring and cross-stage layout management caused excess movement; diagnosis-guided interventions reduced mean movement by 78.9% across five matched circuits. For OLSQ-DPQA, premature candidate selection and limited exploration of preparatory states produced avoidable entangling stages and routing intervals; four fixed-checkpoint continuations each eliminated one Rydberg stage and one routing interval without increasing movement.
AI.conclusion: NAKO links resource targets backed by constructive optimality guarantees to controlled diagnosis and validation of compiler-specific resource savings, providing a principled benchmarking methodology for neutral-atom compiler evaluation.

title: Provably efficient experimental classification of quantum data with quantum kernels
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures for the main text, and 22 pages and 6 figures for the supplementary information
summary: Analyzing quantum systems is essential for quantum information processing, but can require exponentially many measurements without exploiting the structure of the system or task. Quantum machine learning offers a promising way to reduce this cost by learning from quantum data. Here, we theoretically establish a framework for efficient quantum-state classification and experimentally demonstrate the resulting scheme on a programmable photonic processor. Our analysis links learning efficiency to the structure of quantum data, without relying on a physical description tailored to each task. We derive sufficient conditions for accurate classification with a number of measurements polynomial in system size. We apply this guarantee to a resource problem in continuous-variable (CV) quantum computing: classifying stellar rank, a measure of non-Gaussianity. Experimentally, we implement the classification of single-mode CV quantum states with stellar rank zero and one. This is enabled by developing a programmable CV photonic processor capable of preparing and processing diverse Gaussian and non-Gaussian states and performing virtual projection onto such states, going beyond the Gaussian-only capabilities of most existing photonic platforms. The experiment demonstrates accurate classification despite experimental imperfections. Our results establish a theory-guided and experimentally validated framework for quantum-state classification that can be implemented on quantum devices available today.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework for efficient quantum-state classification whose sample complexity relates to the structure of the quantum data, and experimentally validates it by classifying the stellar rank (a non-Gaussianity measure) of single-mode continuous-variable states on a programmable photonic processor.
AI.motivation: Analyzing quantum systems typically requires exponentially many measurements unless prior structure of the system or task is exploited. Quantum machine learning is proposed as a route to reduce this cost by learning directly from quantum data, but a general, physically agnostic framework with rigorous efficiency guarantees and experimental validation is lacking.
AI.method: The authors establish a theoretical framework for quantum-state classification that links learning efficiency to the structure of quantum data without relying on task-specific physical descriptions. They derive sufficient conditions guaranteeing accurate classification with a number of measurements polynomial in system size, and apply this guarantee to a resource problem in continuous-variable quantum computing—classifying stellar rank. Experimentally, they build a programmable CV photonic processor able to prepare and process diverse Gaussian and non-Gaussian states and perform virtual projection onto such states, and use it to classify single-mode CV states of stellar rank zero and one.
AI.result: Polynomial measurement-complexity sufficient conditions for accurate classification are derived. The photonic processor, which exceeds the Gaussian-only capabilities of most existing platforms, achieves accurate classification of stellar rank zero versus one despite experimental imperfections.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a theory-guided, experimentally validated framework for quantum-state classification that is implementable on currently available quantum devices, and demonstrates a hardware capability for non-Gaussian state preparation, processing, and virtual projection in the CV setting.

title: Composable Device-Independent Quantum Digital Signatures
summary: Extending device-independent (DI) quantum cryptography to composably support all fundamental information security objectives is crucial for secure quantum networks. Achieving this goal requires composable quantum digital signatures (QDSs), which support integrity, authenticity, and nonrepudiation when integrated into quantum networks. Yet existing QDS protocols generally rely on assumptions about the underlying quantum devices, while their security analyses remain largely restricted to stand-alone settings, leaving related-key attacks on the underlying linear feedback shift register (LFSR)-based Toeplitz authentication unaddressed. Here, we establish the first composable security framework for QDS within constructive cryptography, and realize the corresponding ideal QDS resource by developing a DI-QDS protocol employing one-time universal hashing and multi-channel multiplexing. We further derive a related-key security bound for the underlying LFSR-based Toeplitz authentication, thereby establishing unforgeability while extending the forgery boundary considered in previous QDS security analyses. We also demonstrate the practical feasibility of our DI-QDS protocol under realistic quantum network conditions in the finite-size regime, with numerical simulations showing that it enables efficient signing of multibit documents over metropolitan-scale distances. Our results establish QDS as a composable cryptographic primitive and extend DI quantum cryptography to support the full range of information security objectives with composable security guarantees in future quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes the first composable security framework for quantum digital signatures (QDS) within constructive cryptography and realizes a device-independent (DI) QDS protocol with one-time universal hashing and multi-channel multiplexing, including a related-key security bound for LFSR-based Toeplitz authentication.
AI.motivation: Extending DI quantum cryptography to composably support all fundamental information security objectives is essential for secure quantum networks. Composable QDS provides integrity, authenticity, and nonrepudiation, but existing QDS protocols rely on device assumptions and are analyzed only in stand-alone settings, leaving related-key attacks on LFSR-based Toeplitz authentication unaddressed.
AI.method: The authors build a composable security framework for QDS in constructive cryptography, realize the ideal QDS resource via a DI-QDS protocol using one-time universal hashing and multi-channel multiplexing, and derive a related-key security bound for the underlying LFSR-based Toeplitz authentication to establish unforgeability.
AI.result: Finite-size numerical simulations show the protocol practically enables efficient signing of multibit documents over metropolitan-scale distances under realistic quantum network conditions, with unforgeability established beyond previous forgery boundaries.
AI.conclusion: QDS is established as a composable cryptographic primitive, extending DI quantum cryptography to support the full range of information security objectives with composable guarantees for future quantum networks.

title: Analytic Solutions To Fully Quantized Parametric Amplification
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, plus 111 pages of Supplemental Material. MATLAB code and Python notebooks included as ancillary files
summary: We derive analytic expressions for observable dynamics under the fully quantized trilinear Hamiltonian, governing quantum three-wave mixing and parametric amplification. Starting from a coherent pump and vacuum signal and idler, the calculation reorganizes the Heisenberg expansion into resummed depletion and return profiles, yielding directly evaluable expressions for all 1st-, 2nd- and 3rd-order correlations. The construction uses no parametric approximation or fitted parameters. Representative numerical benchmarks show errors of order $10^{-12}$ throughout the entire pump depletion, and below $10^{-3}$ across dozens of depletion-and-back-conversion cycles, up to the first total collapse of the oscillation. The first-depletion treatment additionally provides 4th-order correlations, accommodates bright squeezed-pump inputs and reveals phenomena important to future optical quantum technologies. The framework can be extended to higher moments.

AI.tldr: Analytic, resummed expressions for all first- to third-order correlations of the fully quantized trilinear (three-wave mixing / parametric amplification) Hamiltonian with coherent pump and vacuum signal/idler, without parametric approximation or fitting, accurate to ~1e-12 during first depletion and <1e-3 over dozens of depletion cycles.
AI.motivation: Standard treatments of three-wave mixing rely on the parametric (undepleted-pump) approximation or fitted parameters, which fail once the pump depletes. The authors seek exact, directly evaluable observable dynamics for the fully quantized trilinear Hamiltonian.
AI.method: Starting from a coherent pump plus vacuum signal and idler, the Heisenberg-picture expansion is reorganized into resummed "depletion" and "return" profiles, giving closed analytic expressions for all 1st-, 2nd-, and 3rd-order correlations. No parametric approximation or fitted parameters are used; the first-depletion treatment is extended to 4th-order correlations and to bright squeezed-pump inputs.
AI.result: Numerical benchmarks show errors of order 1e-12 throughout the entire pump depletion and below 1e-3 across dozens of depletion-and-back-conversion cycles, up to the first total collapse of the oscillation.
AI.conclusion: The resummation yields accurate analytic correlation dynamics valid beyond the parametric regime, exposes phenomena relevant to optical quantum technologies, and can be extended to higher moments.

title: Conditional Information Flow and Neural Representability of One-Dimensional Rotated Cluster States
comment: M.Sc. research paper, University of Waterloo (2026). 37 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables
summary: I study how measurement outcomes can remain conditionally dependent over long distances while the underlying state carries only a small internal memory, using one-dimensional rotated cluster states, whose exact matrix product state (MPS) bond dimension is $D=2$ at every rotation angle. Using exact MPS contraction, I compute the conditional mutual information (CMI) of two readout protocols: the entanglement-swapping endpoint CMI decreases from one bit at $θ=0$ to zero at $θ=π/2$, whereas a stationary bulk readout of the locally equivalent conventional cluster state vanishes at both limits. As an exact control, the spin-1 AKLT chain obeys $I_m=(4/9)\,3^{-m}$, so its CMI length equals its two-point correlation length, for an identifiable but non-generic reason. I then compare learners on the same $N=64$, $θ=0.35$ target. A positive autoregressive GRU learns the computational-basis Born distribution from a few thousand samples, but an exactly computable Bell-basis readout shows that this distribution does not fix the phases. A complex RBM reaches the $N=8$ ground state under an exact objective, while a short generic recurrent variational Monte Carlo pilot is still improving when its runs end. As a positive control, an MPS-induced recurrent model whose hidden state is the bond vector reaches the ground state to near machine precision at $χ=2$, whereas a $χ=1$ control fails. These results show that long CMI does not require a large bond dimension, and that building the small virtual memory into the architecture greatly eases optimization.

AI.motivation: The paper asks how measurement outcomes can remain conditionally dependent over long distances even when the underlying quantum state holds only a small internal memory. It aims to decouple the notion of long-range conditional dependence from large bond dimension, and to understand how such small virtual memory can be captured by learning architectures.
AI.method: The author studies one-dimensional rotated cluster states, whose exact MPS bond dimension is D=2 at every rotation angle, using exact MPS contraction to compute the CMI of two readout protocols. As exact controls, the spin-1 AKLT chain is analyzed (I_m = (4/9)3^{-m}). Learners are compared on an N=64, θ=0.35 target: an autoregressive GRU, an exactly computable Bell-basis readout, a complex RBM reaching the N=8 ground state, a generic recurrent variational Monte Carlo pilot, and an MPS-induced recurrent model whose hidden state is the bond vector, with χ=2 and χ=1 controls.

The AKLT chain's CMI length equals its two-point correlation length, for an identifiable but non-generic reason. The complex RBM reaches the N=8 ground state under an exact objective, while the generic recurrent VMC pilot is still improving when runs end. The MPS-induced recurrent model reaches the ground state to near machine precision at χ=2, whereas the χ=1 control fails.
