title: Pöschl-Teller type of Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonians: SUSY transformations
summary: The aim of this work is to define and investigate the generalized Jaynes-Cummings (JC) Hamiltonian by means of supersymmetric (SUSY) quantum mechanics methods. We have considered trigonometric and hyperbolic Pöschl-Teller (PT) potentials as two natural ingredients to modify the standard JC model. We show that these generalized JC Hamiltonians have a list of characteristics in common with the JC Hamiltonian, for example: matrix intertwining, excitation number symmetry, Rabi frequency, formulas for atomic inversion and classical and revival times. Therefore, we conclude that JC Hamiltonians can be considered as one example of a wider a class of generalized Hamiltonians which can be useful in broader interaction problems.

AI.tldr: The paper defines and analyzes generalized Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonians built from trigonometric and hyperbolic Pöschl-Teller potentials using supersymmetric quantum mechanics, showing they share key structural and dynamical features with the standard JC model.
AI.motivation: The standard Jaynes-Cummings model is a cornerstone of light-matter interaction, but it is useful to know whether its characteristic properties are special to it or belong to a broader class of models. The authors aim to embed the JC Hamiltonian in a wider family of generalized Hamiltonians that could serve broader interaction problems.
AI.method: Supersymmetric quantum mechanics methods are applied to construct generalized JC Hamiltonians, using trigonometric and hyperbolic Pöschl-Teller potentials as the modifying ingredients. The resulting models are then characterized and compared with the standard JC Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The generalized JC Hamiltonians share a set of features with the standard JC model: matrix intertwining, excitation-number symmetry, a Rabi frequency, and formulas for atomic inversion as well as classical and revival times.
AI.conclusion: The ordinary JC Hamiltonian is one instance of a wider class of generalized Hamiltonians obtainable via SUSY methods, which may be useful for broader interaction problems.

title: Optimal Linear Combination of Hamiltonian Simulation for Dissipative Dynamics
summary: Linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS) is an efficient method for simulating dissipative dynamics on quantum computers. The choice of the LCHS kernel controls the cost of the algorithm. We prove that the kernel family proposed by Ni and Ying~\cite{NY26} minimizes the LCHS query cost in the minimax sense. For target accuracy $ε$, the minimum cost is asymptotically $\frac{2\mathrm{e}}π(\ln\frac1ε-\ln\ln\frac1ε+o(1))$, with optimal leading constant $\frac{2\mathrm{e}}π$. Our lower-bound proof combines weak duality with a realization lemma that approximates extremal dual functions by matrix elements of dissipative evolutions.

AI.tldr: The Ni–Ying kernel family minimax-optimally minimizes the LCHS query cost, with an asymptotically optimal leading constant of 2e/π.
AI.motivation: In linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS), the choice of kernel determines algorithm cost, so it is important to establish which kernels are optimal.
AI.method: A lower-bound proof combining weak duality with a realization lemma that approximates extremal dual functions by matrix elements of dissipative evolutions.
AI.result: The kernel family of Ni and Ying is proved minimax-optimal for LCHS query cost; for target accuracy ε the minimum cost is asymptotically (2e/π)(ln(1/ε) − ln ln(1/ε) + o(1)), with optimal leading constant 2e/π.
AI.conclusion: LCHS query complexity is characterized up to lower-order terms, confirming the Ni–Ying kernel as minimax-optimal.

title: Adiabatic training of VQAs for entanglement detection
summary: This paper introduces a hybrid quantum framework for training Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) aimed at addressing the fundamental problem of entanglement detection using adiabatic quantum computing. This problem is of foundational significance in quantum information science and has been approached through both classical and quantum methodologies. We propose an adiabatic-inspired optimization strategy for training VQAs, which combines a discretization of the parameter space with a hierarchical segmentation scheme. The optimization problem is formulated as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model to leverage the capabilities of quantum annealing. Preliminary results are compared against classical neural networks and conventional VQA training techniques. The findings aim to stimulate further investigation and discussion within the scientific community regarding the efficacy and applicability of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum framework for training Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) via an adiabatic-inspired optimization strategy, formulated as a QUBO model to exploit quantum annealing, and applies it to the foundational problem of entanglement detection, benchmarking against classical neural networks and conventional VQA training.
AI.motivation: Entanglement detection is a foundational problem in quantum information science, previously tackled with both classical and quantum methods. Conventional VQA training suffers from optimization difficulties (e.g., barren plateaus, non-convex landscapes), motivating a new training paradigm that leverages adiabatic quantum computing and quantum annealing.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum framework combining (i) discretization of the VQA parameter space with (ii) a hierarchical segmentation scheme to produce an adiabatic-inspired optimization strategy. The resulting optimization problem is cast as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model so that quantum annealing hardware can be used to solve it.
AI.result: Preliminary experimental results are reported and compared against classical neural networks and conventional VQA training techniques for the entanglement detection task. (The abstract does not quantify the outcomes; it presents initial comparative findings.)
AI.conclusion: The work offers an adiabatic-inspired, QUBO-based hybrid approach to training VQAs for entanglement detection, with preliminary comparisons suggesting the approach is worth exploring. The authors intend the findings to stimulate further investigation and discussion on the efficacy and applicability of the proposed method.

title: Probabilistic imaginary-time evolution via compiled diagonal representations
summary: We introduce a probabilistic imaginary-time evolution scheme based on a compiled approximate diagonal representation of the Hamiltonian. A basis transformation is optimized offline. For a fixed compiled representation, the online circuit structure and gate count per attempt are independent of the imaginary time, and the same representation can be reused across different input states and evolution times. We derive a condition for enhanced success probability. Numerical tests show reduced online cost relative to termwise Pauli-based methods at a common accuracy threshold. We also examine how approximation errors and offline preparation costs affect the overall benefit.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic imaginary-time evolution (ITE) scheme using an offline-compiled approximate diagonal representation of the Hamiltonian, giving online cost independent of imaginary time and reusable across states and evolution times.
AI.motivation: Termwise Pauli-based ITE methods incur online cost that scales with the imaginary time and Hamiltonian terms; the authors seek a scheme with reduced and time-independent online cost.
AI.method: Compile an approximate diagonal representation of the Hamiltonian via an offline-optimized basis transformation. ITE is then performed probabilistically in this diagonal basis; a success-probability enhancement condition is derived, and approximation and offline preparation costs are analyzed.
AI.result: Numerical tests show reduced online cost versus termwise Pauli-based methods at a common accuracy threshold. A condition for enhanced success probability is derived, and the impact of approximation errors and offline preparation costs on the overall benefit is examined.
AI.conclusion: The compiled diagonal representation yields time-independent, reusable online circuits and lower online cost than termwise Pauli methods, with the trade-off governed by approximation error and offline compilation overhead.

title: Detection and Inhibition of Decoherence Through Collisions: A dynamical approach
summary: Quantum systems are intrinsically fragile and highly vulnerable to environmental noise, making the preservation of quantum states one of the fundamental challenges in realizing practical quantum technologies. We propose two noise-agnostic quantum state protection protocols based on a collisional model. The first protocol preserves quantum states of qubits without requiring complete prior knowledge of the underlying noise dynamics, and the second even protects a logical qubit under similar circumstances. These protocols provide robust protection for arbitrary single-qubit and entangled states against general noise processes. Furthermore, their capability to safeguard quantum states with an arbitrary number of qubits enhances the reliability, robustness, and scalability of emerging quantum architectures. These results establish the proposed framework as a promising approach for practical quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: A noise-agnostic quantum state protection scheme using a collisional model, with two protocols that preserve qubits and logical qubits without full prior knowledge of noise dynamics.
AI.motivation: Quantum systems are fragile and vulnerable to environmental noise, so preserving quantum states is a fundamental challenge for practical quantum technologies. Existing protection typically requires detailed knowledge of the noise.
AI.method: Two protocols based on a collisional model: the first protects single-qubit states without complete prior knowledge of the noise dynamics; the second extends protection to a logical qubit under similar conditions.
AI.result: Robust protection of arbitrary single-qubit and entangled states against general noise processes, and the ability to safeguard states with an arbitrary number of qubits.
AI.conclusion: The framework enhances reliability, robustness, and scalability of quantum architectures, offering a promising noise-agnostic approach for practical quantum information processing.

title: Error-Corrected Quantum Optimization via Rydberg Atom Array Embeddings
summary: Rydberg atom quantum optimizers naturally encode the maximum independent set problem on geometric graphs. However, to solve general combinatorial optimization problems on more complex topologies, an embedding is required to overcome the limited-range native interactions. Such embeddings use gadgets, specific arrangements of atoms, which inevitably introduce ancillary atoms. Here, we show that this apparent overhead instead provides an intrinsic resource for error correction. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Parity Architecture-based Rydberg embedding naturally forms a classical error-correcting code, a principle that extends to other Rydberg blockade-based embeddings. Within superatom substructures, exact Rydberg-excitation-number constraints provide local error syndromes at no additional hardware cost and give rise to a strictly nonlinear code. To correct bit-flip errors, we introduce the precisely tailored Cluster decoder, which exploits these local constraints and the underlying gadget structure. Numerically, this approach achieves an error threshold of $p_{\text{th}}\gtrsim26 \%$ across different layout geometries. Experimentally, on the QuEra Aquila QPU, the Cluster decoder recovers exact optimization solutions with an average success rate of $\gtrsim8\%$ for systems of up to 107 atoms, even when bare hardware and standard greedy post-processing find none. A Rydberg atom array embedding is therefore not merely a hardware mapping of an optimization problem, but a co-designed architecture for quantum optimization in which embedding, computation, and error correction emerge from the same physical structure.

AI.tldr: Ancillary atoms introduced by Parity-Architecture Rydberg embeddings are shown to form a natural classical error-correcting code, enabling a tailored Cluster decoder that achieves a ~26% bit-flip threshold and experimentally recovers exact optimization solutions on a 107-atom QuEra Aquila QPU.
AI.motivation: Rydberg-atom optimizers natively solve maximum independent set on geometric graphs, but general topologies need gadget-based embeddings that seem to impose an overhead of ancillary atoms. The authors argue this overhead can be repurposed as an intrinsic resource for error correction rather than a pure cost.
AI.method: The authors analyze Parity-Architecture-based Rydberg embeddings and show that the exact Rydberg-excitation-number constraints within superatom substructures act as local error syndromes at no extra hardware cost, yielding a strictly nonlinear code; they generalize this principle to other Rydberg blockade-based embeddings. They then design the Cluster decoder, exploiting these local constraints and the gadget structure to correct bit-flip errors, and evaluate it numerically across layout geometries and experimentally on the QuEra Aquila QPU.
AI.result: Numerically, the Cluster decoder reaches a bit-flip error threshold of p_th ≳ 26% across different layout geometries. Experimentally on QuEra Aquila, it recovers exact optimization solutions with an average success rate ≳ 8% for systems of up to 107 atoms, even in cases where bare hardware and standard greedy post-processing find none.
AI.conclusion: A Rydberg atom array embedding is not merely a hardware mapping of an optimization problem but a co-designed architecture for quantum optimization in which embedding, computation, and error correction all emerge from the same physical structure, turning apparent ancillary overhead into a built-in error-correction resource.

title: Optimized Dynamical Decoupling for Spin Ensembles with Large Inhomogeneities
summary: Spin ensembles show increasing promise for highly efficient quantum sensing and quantum technologies. However, protecting their coherent properties remains a significant challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) typically employs a sequence of fast pulses that aim to reduce the effect of unwanted system-environment interactions. However, the performance of the DD sequences typically suffers in spin ensembles, e.g., due to amplitude and frequency inhomogeneities and control errors. In this work, we compare the performance of an extensive number of DD protocols for coherence protection and quantum sensing in an ensemble of negatively charged NV centers under ambient conditions. We identify the optimal approach that uses rapid adiabatic passage pulses, which are robust to amplitude and frequency inhomogeneity, in combination with the variation of their phases. We experimentally demonstrate an improved signal contrast and an order-of-magnitude increase in memory time with the optimal sequence compared to the widely used XY8 with standard rectangular pulses. We also apply our approach for improved sensing of a weak oscillating field. While our particular demonstration is with NV centers in diamond, the optimized protocol is generally applicable to other spin ensembles and to systems with high amplitude and/or frequency inhomogeneities.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks a large set of dynamical decoupling (DD) sequences for coherence protection and sensing in an ensemble of negatively charged NV centers under ambient conditions, and identifies an optimal protocol that combines rapid adiabatic passage (RAP) pulses (robust to amplitude and frequency inhomogeneity) with phase variation, yielding higher signal contrast and an order-of-magnitude longer memory time than standard XY8 with rectangular pulses.
AI.motivation: Spin ensembles are attractive for quantum sensing and quantum technologies, but preserving their coherent properties is difficult. Conventional DD using fast rectangular pulses degrades in ensembles because of amplitude and frequency inhomogeneities and control errors, so a more robust DD strategy is needed.
AI.method: An extensive comparison of many DD protocols for coherence protection and quantum sensing is performed on an ensemble of negatively charged NV centers in diamond at ambient conditions. The optimal sequence uses rapid adiabatic passage (RAP) pulses, which are robust to amplitude and frequency inhomogeneity, combined with variation of their phases. Performance is benchmarked against the widely used XY8 sequence with standard rectangular pulses, and the approach is then applied to sensing of a weak oscillating field.
AI.result: The optimal RAP-based, phase-varied sequence delivers improved signal contrast and roughly an order-of-magnitude increase in memory (coherence) time relative to XY8 with rectangular pulses. It also improves sensing of a weak oscillating field.
AI.conclusion: RAP pulses combined with phase variation form a robust optimal DD protocol for ensemble coherence protection and sensing; although demonstrated with NV centers in diamond, the protocol is generally applicable to other spin ensembles and to systems with high amplitude and/or frequency inhomogeneity.

title: Quantum Query Complexity of Tournament Solutions
summary: A tournament solution records a set of winners from a tournament, that is, from the outcomes of all pairwise comparisons among $N$ alternatives. We study the quantum query complexity of computing tournament solutions when the outcome of each comparison has to be learned by a query. Classically, the picture is uniform: the Copeland set, the uncovered set and the top cycle all require $Θ(N^2)$ queries, and so does finding a single vertex of maximum out-degree. We show that the quantum query complexity of the top cycle can be computed with $\tildeΘ(N)$ queries, and a Condorcet winner can be found with $\tilde Θ(\sqrt N)$ queries. Finding a strong king requires $Θ(N^{3/2})$ queries, the same as finding a vertex of maximum out-degree. We also give a self-contained alternative proof of the known $Θ(N^{3/2})$ bound for finding a vertex of maximum degree, established by Gilani, Mande, Patro, and Raja. Our lower bounds reduce counting problems to tournament problems using Ambainis's adversary method. For the top cycle, we find a Hamiltonian path and locate the prefix forming the top cycle by divide and conquer.

AI.tldr: This paper determines the quantum query complexity of several fundamental tournament solutions, showing dramatic quantum speedups over the classical Θ(N²) lower bounds, and gives an alternative adversary-method lower bound for maximum out-degree.
AI.motivation: Tournament solutions (Copeland set, uncovered set, top cycle, Condorcet winner, strong king) are classically expensive: all require Θ(N²) queries when comparison outcomes must be learned by querying. The paper asks whether quantum queries can beat these uniform classical bounds and what the precise quantum query complexity of each solution is.
AI.method: Quantum query complexity analysis. Upper bounds: the top cycle is computed by finding a Hamiltonian path and locating the prefix forming the top cycle via divide and conquer, yielding Õ(N) queries; a Condorcet winner is found with Õ(√N) queries. Lower bounds: counting problems are reduced to tournament problems using Ambainis's adversary method to establish the Θ(N^{3/2}) bound for strong king and maximum out-degree. A self-contained alternative proof is given for the known Θ(N^{3/2}) bound of Gilani, Mande, Patro, and Raja.
AI.result: Top cycle: Õ(N) quantum queries (vs. Θ(N²) classical). Condorcet winner: Õ(√N) queries. Strong king: Θ(N^{3/2}) queries, matching the maximum out-degree vertex bound of Θ(N^{3/2}). A new self-contained adversary-method proof recovers the known Θ(N^{3/2}) lower bound for maximum out-degree.
AI.conclusion: Quantum queries break the uniform classical Θ(N²) barrier for key tournament solutions, with substantial separations for the top cycle and Condorcet winner, while strong king and maximum out-degree remain at Θ(N^{3/2}). The adversary-method reductions and the Hamiltonian-path divide-and-conquer technique provide a clean framework for tournament-solution query complexity.

title: Maximum-Entropy Ensemble of Quantum Subsystems with a Fixed Average State
summary: The reduced density matrices of Haar-random bipartite states form a fixed-trace version of the Wishart ensemble of random matrices, with an asymptotic eigenvalue density given by the Marchenko--Pastur (MP) law. We establish a similar universal form for the maximum-entropy distribution of mixed states subject to a fixed ensemble average, arguing that its eigenvalue density converges asymptotically to that of the correlated Wishart ensemble (CWE). The density is thus obtained by a free multiplicative convolution formula, which we apply to the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) with a thermal average state to derive a high-temperature leading-order correction to the MP law. We then consider measurement by a random POVM on the purification of the mixed reference state. We show that the resulting mixed-state ensemble is asymptotically equivalent to the CWE, and provide confirming numerical evidence. We return to the TFIM example to compute the entanglement of the system with the ancilla after measurement, and give finite-temperature Page curves for the average entanglement entropies.

AI.tldr: Maximum-entropy mixed states with a fixed ensemble average have an eigenvalue density converging asymptotically to the correlated Wishart ensemble (CWE), computed via a free multiplicative convolution; this is applied to the TFIM and to random-POVM measurement, yielding finite-temperature Page curves.
AI.motivation: Haar-random bipartite states produce reduced density matrices whose eigenvalues follow the Marchenko–Pastur law, but it is unclear what universal spectral form governs maximum-entropy mixed states constrained by a fixed ensemble average, and how measurement (random POVM) on a purification affects that form.
AI.method: Constructs the maximum-entropy distribution of mixed states subject to a fixed ensemble average and argues its eigenvalue density converges asymptotically to the CWE; derives the density through a free multiplicative convolution formula. Applies this to a thermal average state in the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) and analyzes measurement by a random POVM on the purification of the reference state, supporting claims with numerical evidence.
AI.result: The maximum-entropy ensemble's eigenvalue density tends asymptotically to the CWE density; for the TFIM a high-temperature leading-order correction to the MP law is obtained; the post-measurement mixed-state ensemble is shown to be asymptotically equivalent to the CWE, confirmed numerically; entanglement of system with ancilla after measurement and finite-temperature Page curves for average entanglement entropies are computed.
AI.conclusion: A universal CWE-based spectral law describes constrained maximum-entropy mixed states, generalizing the MP law, and provides a tractable tool for entanglement entropy and finite-temperature Page curves in physically relevant models and measurement scenarios.

title: Non-Asymptotic Bounds via the Nussbaum-Szkoła Mapping for Quantum Hypothesis Testing
summary: Quantum hypothesis testing concerns the discrimination between quantum states. This paper introduces novel lower and upper bounds for asymmetric quantum hypothesis testing based on the Nussbaum-Szkoła mapping. Together, these bounds provide a unified recovery of both converse and achievability results across all major asymptotic regimes, including large-, moderate-, and small-deviations. Unlike existing bounds, which either rely on technically involved information-spectrum arguments or suffer from fixed prefactors and limited applicability in the non-asymptotic regime, the proposed bounds arise from a unified framework and enable, in some cases, the direct use of classical results. It is further demonstrated that these bounds provide accurate approximations to the optimal quantum error trade-off function at small blocklengths. Numerical comparisons with existing bounds, including those based on fidelity and information spectrum methods, highlight their improved tightness.

AI.tldr: New lower and upper bounds for asymmetric quantum hypothesis testing derived from the Nussbaum-Szkoła mapping give a unified recovery of converse and achievability results across large-, moderate-, and small-deviation regimes, and accurately approximate the optimal quantum error trade-off at small blocklengths.
AI.motivation: Existing bounds for asymmetric quantum hypothesis testing either depend on technically heavy information-spectrum arguments, or suffer from fixed prefactors and limited validity in the non-asymptotic regime. A unified, tighter framework covering all asymptotic regimes is therefore needed.
AI.method: The authors construct lower and upper bounds on the asymmetric quantum error trade-off based on the Nussbaum-Szkoła mapping, which relates quantum states to classical probability distributions. This unified framework lets classical results be reused directly, and the resulting bounds are compared numerically against fidelity- and information-spectrum-based bounds.
AI.result: The bounds jointly yield both converse and achievability results in the large-, moderate-, and small-deviation regimes from a single framework; they provide accurate approximations to the optimal quantum error trade-off function at small blocklengths, and numerical comparisons show tighter behavior than fidelity- and information-spectrum-based bounds.
AI.conclusion: The Nussbaum-Szkoła-mapping-based bounds form a unified, technically accessible, and tight tool for asymmetric quantum hypothesis testing, valid non-asymptotically and recovering all major asymptotic regimes, with demonstrated numerical advantage over existing approaches.

title: Digital-Analog Quantum Neural Network with Long-Range Interactions
summary: Protocols combining single-qubit digital operations with analog quantum evolutions bypass large numbers of two-qubit entangling gates, offering a promising approach to variational algorithms and hybrid quantum simulation. Focusing on the digital-analog quantum neural network (DA-QNN) as a representative framework, this work demonstrates that incorporating long-range interactions enhances the efficiency of such hybrid algorithms. Within the analog blocks, an Ising model with power-law interactions is employed to generate entanglement, and this protocol is benchmarked across supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. Beyond discussing the effects of the transverse field and evolution time, the primary analysis focuses on how the interaction range governs the expressibility and trainability of the ansatz. For supervised image classification and many-body phase detection, long-range ansatzes match the performance of their short-range counterparts with fewer DA-QNN layers or shorter evolution times, owing to the rapid information propagation across the system enabled by nonlocal couplings. This resource reduction alleviates the classical optimization overhead and eases experimental implementation. In unsupervised phase detection, although the long-range ansatz does not outperform its short-range counterpart in every regime, the two ansatzes provide complementary signatures that jointly reconstruct the complete phase diagram. These findings establish long-range interacting platforms as a compelling resource for advancing practical, large-scale digital-analog quantum computing.

AI.tldr: Incorporating long-range (power-law) Ising interactions into digital-analog quantum neural networks (DA-QNNs) improves efficiency, matching short-range performance with fewer layers or shorter evolution times across supervised and unsupervised tasks.
AI.motivation: Digital-analog protocols avoid large numbers of two-qubit entangling gates by mixing single-qubit digital operations with analog evolution, making them attractive for variational algorithms and hybrid simulation. The paper asks whether the interaction range within the analog blocks can be exploited as a resource to further improve such hybrid algorithms.
AI.method: Uses the DA-QNN as a representative framework. Analog blocks implement an Ising model with power-law interactions that generate entanglement, and the protocol is benchmarked on supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. The transverse field and evolution time are examined, with the central analysis focused on how the interaction range governs the expressibility and trainability of the ansatz.
AI.result: For supervised image classification and many-body phase detection, long-range ansatzes match short-range counterparts with fewer DA-QNN layers or shorter evolution times, attributed to faster information propagation from nonlocal couplings. This resource reduction lowers classical optimization overhead and eases experimental implementation. In unsupervised phase detection, the long-range ansatz does not dominate in every regime, but the two ansatzes yield complementary signatures that jointly reconstruct the complete phase diagram.
AI.conclusion: Long-range interacting platforms are a compelling resource for practical, large-scale digital-analog quantum computing, improving efficiency and complementing short-range approaches.

title: Distributed Inner Product Estimation of Continuous-Variable Quantum States
summary: Continuous-variable distributed inner product estimation (CV-DIPE) compares unknown states prepared by distant bosonic and quantum optical systems. It supports benchmarking without efficient classical descriptions or joint measurements. We develop three CV-DIPE protocols for the natural class of energy-constrained continuous-variable quantum states, based on coordinated displaced parity, coordinated Haar measurements, and independent homodyne shadows. For arbitrary multimode inputs in this class, including entangled and non-Gaussian states, we establish truncation error bounds and worst-case sample complexity guarantees for the exact inner product. The leading terms of these bounds favor coordinated Haar measurements, whose global implementation is experimentally challenging. The three protocols provide certified inner product estimates for distributed continuous-variable systems from local measurement data.

AI.tldr: The paper develops three continuous-variable distributed inner product estimation (CV-DIPE) protocols for comparing energy-constrained bosonic states across distant labs, deriving truncation error and worst-case sample complexity bounds for arbitrary multimode inputs.
AI.motivation: Estimating inner products between unknown states prepared by distant quantum optical/bosonic systems is needed for benchmarking, but such states lack efficient classical descriptions and cannot be jointly measured. This motivates a distributed, local-measurement approach for continuous-variable states.
AI.method: Three CV-DIPE protocols are proposed: (1) coordinated displaced parity measurements, (2) coordinated Haar measurements, and (3) independent homodyne shadows. For arbitrary multimode, energy-constrained inputs—including entangled and non-Gaussian states—the authors derive truncation error bounds and worst-case sample complexity guarantees for exact inner product estimation.
AI.result: Rigorous truncation error bounds and worst-case sample complexity guarantees are established for all three protocols. The leading terms of these bounds favor coordinated Haar measurements, though their global implementation is experimentally challenging.
AI.conclusion: The three protocols yield certified inner product estimates for distributed continuous-variable systems using only local measurement data, providing a benchmarking tool that avoids joint measurements and efficient classical descriptions.

title: Bath-state (In)dependence of Non-Markovianity Measures in Quadratic Open Systems
summary: Open quantum system dynamics fail to fulfill the conditions of the Markov approximation when the environment and system timescales are close to each other. Such behavior of these systems can be characterized by several non-Markovianity measures, which are expected to vary with the environment parameters. In this work, we consider a fermionic quadratic open quantum system, establishing bath-state independence of the Breuer--Laine--Piilo and the Lorenzo--Plastina--Paternostro non-Markovianity measures. However, our analytical results reveal that the entanglement-based and divisibility-based Rivas--Huelga--Plenio measures, as well as the entropic Megier--Smirne--Vacchini measure, remain sensitive to the reservoir state, through both its temperature and its chemical potential. Modeling the reservoir as a free-fermionic chain, we derive an exact time-local master equation for a single fermionic site in contact with it. Our numerical results for this model confirm these findings and show that the BLP and LPP measures vanish identically only on the bound-state threshold, where the bath-sensitive measures nevertheless remain finite.

AI.tldr: For a fermionic quadratic open quantum system, the BLP and LPP non-Markovianity measures are shown to be independent of the bath state, while the RHP (entanglement- and divisibility-based) and MSV entropic measures remain sensitive to the reservoir's temperature and chemical potential, as confirmed by an exact time-local master equation for a single fermionic site coupled to a free-fermionic chain.
AI.motivation: When environmental and system timescales are comparable, the Markov approximation breaks down, and the resulting dynamics must be characterized via non-Markovianity measures. These measures are expected to depend on environment parameters, but whether—and how—each measure responds to the bath state was unclear, motivating a systematic study of bath-state dependence across different non-Markovianity quantifiers.
AI.method: The authors study a fermionic quadratic open quantum system and analytically examine the bath-state dependence of four non-Markovianity measures: Breuer–Laine–Piilo (BLP), Lorenzo–Plastina–Paternostro (LPP), Rivas–Huelga–Plenio (RHP, both entanglement- and divisibility-based), and the entropic Megier–Smirne–Vacchini (MSV) measure. The reservoir is modeled as a free-fermionic chain, and an exact time-local master equation is derived for a single fermionic site coupled to it, followed by numerical evaluation of the measures.
AI.result: The BLP and LPP measures are established to be independent of the bath state, whereas the RHP measures (entanglement- and divisibility-based) and the MSV entropic measure remain sensitive to the reservoir state through both its temperature and its chemical potential. Numerical results for the free-fermionic-chain model confirm these analytical findings and show that the BLP and LPP measures vanish identically only at the bound-state threshold, where the bath-sensitive measures nonetheless remain finite.
AI.conclusion: The non-Markovianity measures fall into two classes: bath-state-independent (BLP, LPP) and bath-state-sensitive (RHP, MSV). Since different measures respond differently to temperature and chemical potential, the choice of non-Markovianity quantifier must be made carefully when characterizing fermionic open systems; notably, at the bound-state threshold, the vanishing of BLP/LPP does not imply the absence of non-Markovianity, as the bath-sensitive measures remain finite there.

title: Identifying Logical Operations from Syndrome Histories for qLDPC Codes
summary: Syndrome histories are normally used to detect and correct errors in fault-tolerant quantum computation, but they can also reveal information about the logical operations executed during computation. We study logical-operation identification using syndrome histories alone or together with other classical measurement outcomes. We develop an exact inference method and a scalable approximation that account for unknown circuit faults and ideal measurement randomness. We evaluate automorphisms, logical Pauli measurements, T injections, and logical circuits combining these instructions on \([[18,4,2]]\) and \([[72,12,6]]\) bivariate bicycle (BB) codes under multiple noise models and error rates. A single logical instruction can be identified with over 94\% accuracy under circuit-level noise with error rates between \(10^ {-5} \) and \(10^{-3}\). We also achieve over 99\% accuracy for automorphism-based logical circuits and 78.32\% for logical circuits combining all three instructions. We further analyze identification ambiguities arising from insufficient or indistinguishable measurement information, fault timing, and approximation inference. Together, these results extend the role of syndromes beyond error decoding to identifying executed logical operations and circuits during fault-tolerant quantum computation. They also suggest that access to syndrome histories and related classical measurement outcomes may unintentionally reveal information about the executed computation.

AI.tldr: Syndrome histories, normally used for error correction, can also reveal which logical operations were executed in fault-tolerant quantum computation. The authors develop an exact inference method and a scalable approximation to identify logical operations from syndromes alone or with other classical measurement outcomes, achieving >94% accuracy for single logical instructions, >99% for automorphism-based circuits, and 78.32% for combined-instruction circuits on BB codes.
AI.motivation: Syndrome histories are conventionally exploited only for error detection and correction. The paper observes that they additionally leak information about the logical operations performed during computation, motivating a systematic study of logical-operation identification and the potential unintended information leakage from syndrome access.
AI.method: The authors formulate logical-operation identification using syndrome histories alone or jointly with other classical measurement outcomes. They develop an exact inference method plus a scalable approximation, both accounting for unknown circuit faults and ideal measurement randomness. They evaluate automorphisms, logical Pauli measurements, T injections, and logical circuits combining these instructions on [[18,4,2]] and [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle (BB) codes across multiple noise models and error rates, and analyze sources of identification ambiguity.
AI.result: A single logical instruction is identified with over 94% accuracy under circuit-level noise at error rates between 10^-5 and 10^-3. Accuracy exceeds 99% for automorphism-based logical circuits and reaches 78.32% for circuits combining all three instruction types. Identification ambiguities are traced to insufficient or indistinguishable measurement information, fault timing, and approximation error in inference.
AI.conclusion: Syndromes extend beyond error decoding to identifying executed logical operations and circuits during fault-tolerant quantum computation. Access to syndrome histories and related classical measurement outcomes may unintentionally reveal information about the executed computation, raising a leakage concern for fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

title: Dissipative controller as a hidden source of errors in quantum gates
summary: Quantum systems are typically controlled by classical devices that necessarily dissipate energy to the surrounding environment. By the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, this implies noise in the control field produced. We investigate the relationship between the resulting errors and the entropy produced by the macroscopic controller, working in the context of a concrete minimal model. In the most experimentally relevant regime of fast control and high fidelity, we find a tradeoff between dissipation and control errors. These findings are exemplified by perturbative calculations of the gate fidelity for simple gate implementations and of the fidelity of state transfer via shortcuts to adiabaticity in the Landau-Zener model. Our results quantitatively demonstrate that suppressing errors in quantum control typically comes at the cost of macroscopic dissipation, which is needed to tame fluctuations in the classical controller.

AI.tldr: Quantum control is performed by classical devices that dissipate energy, and by the fluctuation-dissipation theorem this generates control-field noise. Using a minimal model, the authors show a tradeoff between macroscopic dissipation (entropy production) and control errors in the fast-control, high-fidelity regime, illustrated by gate-fidelity and shortcut-to-adiabaticity (Landau-Zener) calculations.
AI.motivation: Classical controllers unavoidably dissipate, and fluctuation-dissipation implies correlated noise in the control field. The relationship between this entropy production and the resulting quantum control errors has not been quantified, motivating a systematic study in a concrete minimal model.
AI.method: A minimal model of a quantum system driven by a noisy classical controller coupled to a thermal environment is analyzed. Focusing on fast control and high fidelity, the authors derive a tradeoff between dissipation (entropy produced by the macroscopic controller) and control error, and verify it via perturbative calculations of gate fidelity for simple gate implementations and of state-transfer fidelity using shortcuts to adiabaticity in the Landau-Zener model.
AI.result: A quantitative tradeoff is found: in the experimentally relevant fast, high-fidelity regime, suppressing control-field fluctuations (and thus errors) requires increased macroscopic dissipation. Perturbative fidelity calculations for gates and for Landau-Zener shortcut state transfer confirm the predicted dissipation-error relationship.
AI.conclusion: Reducing errors in quantum control generally incurs a macroscopic dissipation cost needed to tame fluctuations in the classical controller, providing a quantitative link between control fidelity and thermodynamic entropy production.

title: Distributed Inner-Product Estimation for Continuous-Variable Quantum States
summary: Distributed inner product estimation (DIPE) is a fundamental task in quantum information, aiming to estimate the inner product between two unknown quantum states prepared on distributed quantum platforms. For multimode continuous-variable (CV) systems, the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space poses an additional challenge. In this work, we develop a CV-DIPE protocol using only local homodyne measurements at shared phase settings and classical communication. Under a known bound on the mean energy per mode, we derive explicit finite-sample guarantees and sufficient copy counts for estimating the full inner product to prescribed accuracy and confidence. The energy constraint yields an inverse-square truncation-bias bound, while Gaussian structure strengthens the tail control to exponential decay and improves the resulting accuracy scaling. Numerical simulations with Gaussian and non-Gaussian states illustrate the balance between truncation bias and statistical error and its dependence on mode number and energy. Our results enable independent CV platforms to benchmark their state preparations against one another, even when neither state admits a tractable classical description.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a continuous-variable distributed inner product estimation (CV-DIPE) protocol using only local homodyne measurements at shared phase settings plus classical communication, with finite-sample guarantees under a bounded mean energy per mode.
AI.motivation: Distributed inner product estimation is fundamental in quantum information, but multimode continuous-variable systems are hard because of their infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. Existing approaches lack explicit finite-sample guarantees for estimating the full inner product in this setting.
AI.method: Local homodyne measurements at shared phase settings on each distributed platform, combined with classical communication. Analysis under a known bound on mean energy per mode, with truncation-bias bounds derived from the energy constraint and refined using Gaussian structure to control tails; validated by numerical simulations on Gaussian and non-Gaussian states.
AI.result: Explicit finite-sample guarantees and sufficient copy counts are derived for estimating the full inner product to prescribed accuracy and confidence. The energy constraint gives an inverse-square truncation-bias bound, while Gaussian structure strengthens tail control to exponential decay and improves accuracy scaling; simulations show the bias–variance tradeoff and its dependence on mode number and energy.
AI.conclusion: Independent CV platforms can benchmark their state preparations against one another using the protocol, even when neither state has a tractable classical description.

title: Reversible photorefractive attack in continuous-variable quantum key distribution
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) offers information-theoretic security, but device imperfections introduce implementation vulnerabilities. Experimental evidence of the security consequences of transmitter vulnerabilities in continuous-variable QKD (CV-QKD) remains limited. Here, we experimentally investigate a reversible photorefractive attack in a local-local-oscillator CV-QKD system. Moderate blue-light illumination reduces the modulation variance of a lithium-niobate IQ modulator to a stable value without appreciably increasing estimated excess noise. The variance recovers after illumination is removed. We elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms and develop an attack that exploits recovery to compromise modulation calibration. Receiver measurements confirm that the resulting calibration mismatch leads to overestimated channel transmittance and underestimated excess noise. Key rate calculations based on measured parameters yield a positive estimated rate when the correctly calibrated rate is nonpositive. Recovery can also make the preceding manipulation harder to identify through later inspection. This work provides the first system-level experimental evidence that a reversible photorefractive response can be exploited to compromise modulation calibration in CV-QKD. These findings highlight reversible changes in quantum transmitters as a practical security concern, motivating security analyses and protection strategies that account for both optical perturbations and subsequent recovery.

AI.tldr: First system-level experimental demonstration of a reversible photorefractive attack on a local-local-oscillator CV-QKD system, where blue light modifies lithium-niobate modulator variance and its recovery to corrupt calibration and inflate the estimated key rate.
AI.motivation: QKD claims information-theoretic security, yet device imperfections create implementation vulnerabilities. While transmitter-side flaws in continuous-variable QKD are theoretically concerning, experimental evidence of their security consequences—particularly reversible, hard-to-detect ones—is scarce.
AI.method: Experimentally induce a reversible photorefractive response in a lithium-niobate IQ modulator of a local-local-oscillator CV-QKD system using moderate blue-light illumination, characterize the variance reduction and recovery, identify the underlying physical mechanism, and build an attack exploiting the recovery phase to induce calibration mismatch, verified through receiver measurements and key-rate calculations.
AI.result: Blue illumination reduces modulation variance to a stable value without appreciably raising estimated excess noise, and variance recovers once illumination is removed. The recovery-based attack causes overestimated channel transmittance and underestimated excess noise, yielding a positive estimated key rate where the correctly calibrated rate is nonpositive; recovery also obscures the manipulation from later inspection.
AI.conclusion: Reversible photorefractive responses in quantum transmitters are a practical security threat in CV-QKD, motivating security analyses and countermeasures that account for both optical perturbations and their subsequent recovery.

title: Inevitability of the Petz transpose map
summary: Bayes' rule is central to classical statistical inference: given a prior and a stochastic model, it determines the corresponding retrodictive conditional probabilities. In quantum theory, however, the question of whether an equally general rule of retrodiction exists and, if so, whether it is uniquely determined remains nontrivial. Here we prove that a retrodiction assignment defined for all priors and channels, which takes each predicted output state back to its prior, must coincide with the Petz transpose map if it is involutive, respects sequential and parallel composition, and agrees with unitary inversion. The theorem holds for channels between finite-dimensional full matrix algebras, with the input and output spaces restricted to the supports of the corresponding reference states. In particular, affinity under probabilistic mixtures and the characteristic square-root dependence on the reference states follow from these requirements rather than being postulated. Without involutivity, the remaining requirements characterize a family of doubly rotated Petz maps. Our result thus explains why the Petz transpose map arises in seemingly different areas of quantum theory: it is the unique quantum analogue of Bayes' rule compatible with these consistency requirements.

AI.tldr: A retrodiction rule valid for all priors and channels is uniquely the Petz transpose map if it is involutive, respects sequential/parallel composition, and agrees with unitary inversion; dropping involutivity yields doubly rotated Petz maps.
AI.motivation: Classical Bayes' rule gives retrodictive conditional probabilities from a prior and stochastic model, but quantum theory lacks a settled answer on whether a comparably general and uniquely determined retrodiction rule exists. The paper aims to characterize such a rule axiomatically.
AI.method: Axiomatic characterization: impose that the retrodiction assignment maps each predicted output state back to its prior, is involutive, respects sequential and parallel composition, and agrees with unitary inversion. Channels act between finite-dimensional full matrix algebras, with input/output restricted to supports of reference states.
AI.result: The axiomatized retrodiction map must coincide with the Petz transpose map; without involutivity, the remaining axioms characterize a family of doubly rotated Petz maps. Affinity under probabilistic mixtures and square-root dependence on reference states emerge as consequences rather than postulates.
AI.conclusion: The Petz transpose map is the unique quantum analogue of Bayes' rule compatible with these consistency requirements, explaining its appearance across apparently distinct areas of quantum theory.

title: Detuning-assisted cavity enhancement in spectroscopy
summary: Cavity-enhanced spectroscopy is a widely used experimental technique. We show that detuning the cavity frequency from the transition of interest can enhance the precision for dipole moment estimation by up to two orders of magnitude beyond the improvement when the cavity is resonant with the transition. We show this for both classical continuous-wave (CW) and pulsed single-photon probes, even in the presence of losses. We trace this enhancement to a detuning-controlled redistribution of information between the light- and matter-like polaritons, with losses determining the optimal branch. We show that this enhancement remains accessible using conventional photodetection and time-correlated single-photon counting.

AI.tldr: Detuning the cavity from the transition can enhance dipole-moment estimation precision by up to two orders of magnitude over the resonant-cavity case, for both CW and pulsed single-photon probes, even with losses.
AI.motivation: Cavity-enhanced spectroscopy is widely used, but conventional practice assumes the cavity should be resonant with the transition. The authors challenge this assumption, asking whether deliberate detuning can improve estimation precision of the dipole moment.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of dipole moment estimation using cavity-enhanced measurements, comparing resonant and detuned cavity configurations for classical continuous-wave and pulsed single-photon probes. The analysis incorporates losses and decomposes the enhancement in terms of information redistribution between light- and matter-like polariton branches.
AI.result: Detuning yields up to two orders of magnitude precision improvement beyond the resonant case, for both CW and pulsed single-photon probes and in the presence of losses. The effect arises from detuning-controlled redistribution of information between light- and matter-like polaritons, with the loss level determining the optimal polariton branch to exploit.
AI.conclusion: Deliberate cavity detuning is a practical route to substantially improved dipole-moment estimation. The enhancement is compatible with conventional photodetection and time-correlated single-photon counting, making it experimentally accessible.

title: Bounds for General $(r,δ)$-Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes
summary: We study general $(r,δ)$-quantum locally recoverable codes (qLRCs) without assuming purity or a stabilizer structure, and with arbitrarily overlapping recovery blocks. Using a selection lemma for multiple-erasure recovery, we establish a Singleton-like upper bound for general quantum subspaces. When $δ=2$, this bound reduces to the general single-erasure bound of Golowich and Guruswami. An integer optimization yields an explicit remainder correction that tightens the bound by up to $δ-2$. For pure codes, local decoupling and entropy arguments extend the parameter bound of Galindo et al., originally obtained for pure stabilizer codes constructed from Euclidean or Hermitian dual-containing classical codes, to arbitrary pure quantum subspaces. We also remove the partition assumption from several existing pure-code bounds for disjoint recovery blocks and obtain a further remainder correction by optimizing the budget. Finally, we analyze three families attaining these bounds: pure codes with overlapping recovery blocks and $d=δ$, which exhibit both a strict improvement of the pure-code bound and simultaneous equality in the pure-code and general bounds; impure codes with disjoint recovery blocks attaining the general bound; and an existing family of pure codes with overlapping recovery blocks and $d>δ$, which simultaneously attains all these bounds.

AI.tldr: The paper derives Singleton-like upper bounds for general (r,δ)-quantum locally recoverable codes without purity or stabilizer assumptions and with overlapping recovery blocks, extending prior single-erasure and pure-code results, plus remainder corrections and analysis of three extremal families.
AI.motivation: Existing bounds for quantum locally recoverable codes are limited: general single-erasure bounds (Golowich–Guruswami), pure stabilizer-code bounds (Galindo et al.) requiring Euclidean/Hermitian dual-containing classical constructions, and pure-code bounds that assume a partition into disjoint recovery blocks. A unified treatment for general (r,δ)-qLRCs with overlapping blocks and no stabilizer/purity structure was missing.
AI.method: A selection lemma for multiple-erasure recovery is used to prove a Singleton-like upper bound for arbitrary quantum subspaces with arbitrarily overlapping recovery blocks; an integer optimization produces an explicit remainder correction (up to δ−2). For pure codes, local decoupling and entropy arguments generalize the Galindo et al. parameter bound to arbitrary pure quantum subspaces and remove the partition assumption, with a further budget-optimized remainder correction.
AI.result: The general bound reduces to the Golowich–Guruswami single-erasure bound at δ=2; the remainder correction tightens the bound by up to δ−2. Three families are shown to attain the bounds: (i) pure codes with overlapping blocks and d=δ, exhibiting strict improvement of the pure-code bound and simultaneous equality in pure and general bounds; (ii) impure codes with disjoint blocks attaining the general bound; (iii) an existing family of pure codes with overlapping blocks and d>δ simultaneously attaining all these bounds.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified Singleton-like framework for general (r,δ)-qLRCs covering overlapping blocks and arbitrary (pure or impure) subspaces, generalizes and sharpens previous bounds via explicit remainder corrections, and identifies extremal families showing the bounds are tight and that purity/purity-gaps can be characterized.

title: QDMin: Coherent Quantum Minimum Finding for Nuclear Deformation Landscapes
summary: Locating the minimum of a nuclear collective landscape can require many interacting many-body calculations. QDMin (Quantum Deformation Minimum Finding) searches a parameterized Hamiltonian family with a coherent collective-coordinate register and an on-demand ground-energy threshold oracle. The oracle supplies the predicate required for quantum minimum-finding without first constructing the energy landscape point by point. We implement it for a schematic pairing-plus-multipole model using circuit-generated energy estimates during the search. In a four-point calculation, one Grover round raises the probability of the true minimum from 0.25 to 0.921. A $4\times4$ quadrupole--octupole-field calculation extends the complete circuit to two coordinates, although its minimum is first sampled in a round with zero Grover iterations. Its worst-case branch-preparation fidelity of 0.744 falls below the declared target, identifying coherent ground-state access as the current bottleneck. QDMin inherits expected $O(\sqrt{N_q})$ candidate-query scaling in the unstructured model; total advantage depends on the many-body oracle cost and remains unestablished.

AI.tldr: QDMin applies quantum minimum-finding (Grover-based) with a circuit-generated ground-energy threshold oracle to locate the minimum of a nuclear collective (pairing-plus-multipole) landscape without point-by-point construction.
AI.motivation: Finding the minimum of a many-body nuclear collective energy landscape typically demands many interacting many-body calculations performed point-by-point, which is costly. A quantum approach could reduce the number of candidate queries needed to identify the global minimum.
AI.method: QDMin searches a parameterized Hamiltonian family using a coherent collective-coordinate register plus an on-demand ground-energy threshold oracle that supplies the predicate for quantum minimum-finding. It is implemented for a schematic pairing-plus-multipole model using circuit-generated energy estimates during the search, with a coherent collective-coordinate register.
AI.result: In a four-point case, one Grover round raises the probability of the true minimum from 0.25 to 0.921. A 4x4 quadrupole–octupole calculation extends the complete circuit to two coordinates, but its minimum is first sampled in a round with zero Grover iterations. Worst-case branch-preparation fidelity of 0.744 falls below the declared target.
AI.conclusion: Coherent ground-state access is identified as the current bottleneck (fidelity shortfall). QDMin inherits expected O(sqrt(N_q)) candidate-query scaling in the unstructured model; the total advantage depends on the many-body oracle cost and remains unestablished.

title: Subsystem Spacetime Code
summary: Quantum error-correcting codes provide a powerful framework for analyzing and designing fault-tolerant Clifford circuits. In this work, we construct the subsystem spacetime code and use it to characterize the distances of Clifford circuits. We show that its gauge group can be explicitly constructed and classified using the masking properties of the instantaneous stabilizer groups and consists precisely of faults that are harmless to the circuit. We use this framework to identify where a dynamical code loses distance and to analyze how the fault distance changes when circuits are composed from smaller components. Our results provide a versatile tool for analyzing and designing fault-tolerant circuits, with potential applications to the construction of new dynamical codes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "subsystem spacetime code" to characterize fault distances of Clifford circuits, showing its gauge group is explicitly constructible/classifiable via masking properties of instantaneous stabilizer groups and corresponds exactly to harmless faults.
AI.motivation: Quantum error-correcting codes offer a strong framework for analyzing and designing fault-tolerant Clifford circuits, but a versatile tool is needed to characterize circuit fault distances, pinpoint where dynamical codes lose distance, and understand how fault distance behaves under composition of smaller circuits.
AI.method: Construct a subsystem spacetime code for Clifford circuits. Show that its gauge group can be explicitly constructed and classified using the masking properties of the instantaneous stabilizer groups, and prove this gauge group consists precisely of faults that are harmless to the circuit.
AI.result: The framework identifies where a dynamical code loses distance and enables analysis of how fault distance changes when circuits are composed from smaller components.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a versatile tool for analyzing and designing fault-tolerant circuits, with potential applications to constructing new dynamical codes.

title: Quantum communication: a discrimination approach
summary: We develop a state discrimination approach to unassisted quantum communication through a noisy quantum channel. Starting from the operational duality between entanglement recovery and state discrimination, we construct entanglement-generation codes with explicit decoders constructed from Petz recovery maps. The resulting error bounds hold for every number of channel uses and are expressed in terms of Petz-Rényi coherent information. For product sources, they yield exponential error decay at rates below coherent information.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a state-discrimination approach to unassisted quantum communication over noisy channels, yielding entanglement-generation codes with explicit Petz-recovery decoders, per-block error bounds in terms of Petz-Rényi coherent information, and exponential error decay below coherent information for product sources.
AI.motivation: Unassisted quantum communication through noisy channels lacks explicit, finite-blocklength coding schemes with tight error bounds; the work builds on the operational duality between entanglement recovery and state discrimination to obtain constructive codes.
AI.method: Constructs entanglement-generation codes whose decoders are built from Petz recovery maps, derived via the duality between entanglement recovery and state discrimination.
AI.result: Error bounds hold for every number of channel uses and are expressed in terms of Petz-Rényi coherent information; for product sources the bounds give exponential error decay at rates below the coherent information.
AI.conclusion: A state-discrimination framework yields explicit recovery-based entanglement-generation codes with any-blocklength guarantees, connecting Petz-Rényi coherent information to achievable exponential error exponents.

title: Rapid mixing for Gibbs samplers for quantum spin systems with all-to-all interactions
summary: Understanding when quantum many-body systems rapidly converge to thermal equilibrium is a central problem in quantum statistical mechanics. While spatial locality provides powerful tools for systems with an underlying geometry, fully connected models require estimates that accommodate interactions between every pair of spins. We study Gibbs-state preparation for two-local quantum Hamiltonians on arbitrary interaction graphs, including fully connected systems, via Lindblad dynamics that satisfies Kubo--Martin--Schwinger (KMS) detailed balance. Our approach is based on a quantum analogue of the classical Dobrushin condition, which controls the influence of local perturbations on the rest of the system. Using the quantum Wasserstein distance of order $1$, we quantify how these perturbations propagate under the dynamics and derive contraction estimates in a high-temperature regime controlled by the maximum total interaction strength per site. These estimates require no assumptions on spatial geometry or graph growth and yield mixing times logarithmic in the system size and the inverse error tolerance, uniformly over all initial states.

AI.tldr: Gibbs-state preparation for two-local quantum Hamiltonians on arbitrary interaction graphs (including fully connected models) via KMS-detailed-balance Lindblad dynamics, with mixing times logarithmic in system size and inverse error, derived from a quantum Dobrushin condition using the order-1 quantum Wasserstein distance.
AI.motivation: Spatial locality gives powerful mixing tools for geometrically local systems, but fully connected models involve interactions between every pair of spins and lack such geometric structure. The paper seeks thermalization/mixing-time guarantees that do not rely on spatial geometry or graph growth assumptions.
AI.method: A quantum analogue of the classical Dobrushin condition controls how local perturbations influence the rest of the system. Propagation of perturbations under the Lindblad dynamics is quantified via the quantum Wasserstein distance of order 1, yielding contraction estimates in a high-temperature regime governed by the maximum total interaction strength per site.
AI.result: Contraction estimates with no assumptions on spatial geometry or graph growth, giving mixing times logarithmic in the system size and in the inverse error tolerance, uniformly over all initial states, for arbitrary interaction graphs including fully connected systems.
AI.conclusion: A geometry-independent Dobrushin-type framework based on quantum Wasserstein-1 contraction enables efficient Gibbs-state preparation for two-local Hamiltonians on arbitrary graphs, extending rapid-mixing guarantees beyond spatially local models.

title: Quantum Computing through Computational Imaging: Representations, Measurement, and Inference
comment: v1: Supplementary code, data and web companion: https://doi.org/10.34965/enodo.i61162
summary: An algebraic correspondence between an imaging model and a quantum state does not specify a computational method: input access, measurement and decoding determine what can be returned. This exposition develops four distinctions for computational-imaging and engineering readers. It separates amplitude encodings of input values from encodings of complete candidate labelings, explaining why amplitude storage does not provide full-array readout. Complex-field interference motivates unknown-phase inference: complementary measurements resolve ambiguities that local Fisher information alone does not detect. Reshaping joint amplitudes into a matrix connects singular-value decomposition to pure-state entanglement, while distinguishing Schmidt rank from conditions for efficient classical simulation. In a four-pixel segmentation, an objective becomes a cost operator and a sampling circuit. One layer of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) lowers mean energy from $1.675$ to $0.686$ relative to uniform sampling, yet makes a nonoptimal labeling more probable than the optimum 0.484 versus 0.365. Archived IBM and IQM measurements illustrate a separate six-variable local boundary decision. Low-rank state reconstruction and selected quantum algorithms connect these distinctions to an end-to-end resource account. The derivations and reproducible numerical references assume complex linear algebra and probability, without prior quantum mechanics. The accompanying Seeing Amplitudes browser laboratory supports interactive exploration; the article remains self-contained and connects each representation to the estimate or decision it permits and the resources that output requires.

AI.tldr: Four conceptual distinctions are developed to clarify what quantum-amplitude imaging models can and cannot compute, illustrated by a four-pixel QAOA segmentation where one layer reduces mean energy but still favors a nonoptimal labeling.
AI.motivation: An algebraic correspondence between imaging models and quantum states does not by itself define a computational method; input access, measurement, and decoding determine what output is actually obtainable, so readers need explicit distinctions between representation and computation.
AI.method: Expository framework with four distinctions: (1) amplitude encodings of input values versus encodings of complete candidate labelings (amplitude storage ≠ full-array readout); (2) complex-field interference motivating unknown-phase inference via complementary measurements beyond local Fisher information; (3) reshaping joint amplitudes into a matrix linking SVD to pure-state entanglement, separating Schmidt rank from efficient classical simulability; (4) a four-pixel segmentation cast as cost operator plus sampling circuit, evaluated with one-layer QAOA and archived IBM/IQM measurements for a six-variable local boundary decision. Includes low-rank state reconstruction and selected quantum algorithms in an end-to-end resource account, supported by a "Seeing Amplitudes" browser laboratory.
AI.result: In the four-pixel segmentation, one QAOA layer lowers mean energy from 1.675 (uniform sampling) to 0.686, yet assigns higher probability to a nonoptimal labeling than to the optimum (0.484 vs. 0.365). Complementary measurements resolve phase ambiguities that local Fisher information alone does not detect. Schmidt rank is distinguished from conditions for efficient classical simulation.
